OpenBot from Source

The Architecture of a Governed AI Coworker Platform
Governance rides the protocol, not the framework; boundaries live in the deployment, not the model.
What makes a company dare to hand real tools to agents is not a smarter model but the action gateway that decides, records, then acts; one fenced computer per Bot; and protocol-agnostic integration.
A dissection of CopilotKit's open-source OpenBot: the React app, the Hono API, PostgreSQL, CopilotKit Intelligence, the AG-UI Bot endpoints, one Chromium computer per Bot, and the gateway that decides and records every action. This book is the sister volume to Claude Code from Source: that one answers "how a single agent thinks"; this one answers "how a fleet of agents gets governed".

Part I: Foundations

Before governance, the process must exist; before trust, we must know who is who.

Chapter 1: The Architecture of a Governable Agent Platform

From thinking to being governed

A single-process CLI agent like Claude Code answers the question "how does one agent think": one process, one machine, one tool loop, and a permission mode that governs at most one person sitting at a terminal.

OpenBot answers the next question: how does a fleet of agents get governed. It is CopilotKit's open-source platform for enterprise AI coworkers: a company keeps a stable of Bots on it, each with its own browser, its own login state, and its own tool grants, and employees @-mention them in channels the way they would a coworker. The sister book covered the first question in full; this book handles only the second, and that is the last time the comparison appears.

Why is governance an architecture problem and not a compliance document? Because the threat model changes the moment you hand real tools to an agent. A Bot that holds the company's Salesforce login, can open a shell, and can call MCP connectors is no chatbot; it has the access profile of an insider: one that never clocks out, lives in several replicas at once, and gets woken at three in the morning by a routine to do work. Without a governance layer, this platform is an incident waiting to be written into a postmortem. The questions a company has to answer are concrete: who made this action happen? Under which rule was it allowed through? What did it do while nobody was watching? And these questions come with no time buffer: the first compliance review, the first employee departure, the first 3 a.m. mistake: any one of them turns "no audit" from technical debt into an incident.

OpenBot's architectural bet fits in one sentence: governance rides the protocol, not the framework; boundaries live in the deployment, not the model. It also takes one aesthetic stance: it positions itself as a template, not a product. This chapter takes that sentence apart: first the full picture held up by six pillars, then a walk along the golden path of one channel message, then a stop to explain the three bets properly, and finally a map of the whole book. By the end, you will be able to place every later chapter back onto some segment of this map yourself.

The six pillars

OpenBot consists of six long-lived parts. Everything else (the twenty-plus boot refusals, the seven-gate tool pipeline, two-track memory) lives inside one of these six pillars.

The six pillars group into four planes: the user plane (app), the governance plane (server and PostgreSQL), the memory plane (Intelligence), and the execution plane (AG-UI endpoints, agent-computer, supervisor). This grouping is not a label pasted on afterwards; it corresponds to four distinct failure shapes. When the user plane breaks, people cannot see. When the memory plane breaks, conversations get silently forgotten. When the execution plane breaks, Bots have intent but no capability. When the governance plane breaks, the platform must refuse to work.

The governance plane is the only one whose failure must stop everything. That asymmetry is the tiering logic this book keeps returning to, and Chapter 2 has the complete list.

1. app (3010): the viewing surface, not a boundary. A React/Vite app: channels, Bot chats, live screen, settings and admin pages. It deliberately makes no authorization decisions: an allowlist in the browser is documentation, not control, and Chapter 14 shows this principle enforced strictly when it covers component rendering. The app's value is visibility: the live screen streams the Bot's browser to a human, who can grab the wheel at any moment.

2. server (3001): the home of governance. A Hono API service whose composition root, server/src/index.ts, is a single file of over 2,500 lines where auth, roles, the tenant package, coworkers, channels, policies, audit, credentials, plugins, components, and connectors all get wired. Concentrating the wiring in one file is deliberate: who depends on whom and who starts whom is checkable at a glance, and Chapter 2 takes the file apart along the four-layer entry chain. Every authorization decision is made in server, the least negotiable line in the whole architecture: the model may propose; only server may permit.

3. PostgreSQL + pgvector (5432): the single source of truth. Product data, audit rows, credentials, policies, grants, channels, components, page snapshots, the work_items queue: all in this one database. Postgres is not a convenience pick. In a multi-replica deployment, the truth must live where every replica can reach it, and append-only is enforced by database triggers rather than application code, because the application is not the only thing that can reach these tables (Chapter 6).

4. CopilotKit Intelligence: threads and memory. An external service holding persistent threads, memory, and the realtime gateway. OpenBot has no degraded path around it: "There is no SSE branch. Intelligence is a requirement of the product, not a tier" (server/src/copilot.ts:79-83). A deployment without it would silently forget every conversation, so a missing contract refuses the boot. Which capabilities are non-negotiable is written into the boot refusals; this is one sample of "the dependency list is a stance".

5. AG-UI Bot endpoints (4200 and up): Bots live behind a protocol. agent-bot (the proof of concept), agent-langgraph, and the agent-harness chosen at install time. A Bot is not a class inside server; it is any HTTP service that speaks the AG-UI protocol: LangGraph, Pydantic-AI, CrewAI, Mastra, ADK, or a hand-written server. That list sits in a comment at the top of the wiring code (server/src/copilot.ts:73-77). This is the physical form of "governance rides the protocol", and Chapter 16 is dedicated to the contract. What AG-UI itself is, Chapter 4 explains in full for readers who have not met it; for this chapter it is enough to know it is an event-stream protocol that carries turns, tool calls, and streaming output.

6. agent-computer + the supervisor, the container steward (4100 / 4500): one fenced computer per Bot. A container is a workstation: long-lived Chromium, a /workspace file volume, a shell, and a browser profile, with login state surviving across tasks. The supervisor is the only process in the whole deployment that holds the Docker socket, and it compresses that root equivalent into four verbs with a Bot as their subject: ensure, stop, reset, list. Container names derive from the Bot id rather than being supplied by the caller, so the caller can never even name a container. That is Chapter 9's first lesson.

Service Port Responsibility
app 3010 React/Vite UI: channels, Bot chats, live screen, settings, admin pages
server 3001 API, CopilotKit runtime, auth, tenant package, coworkers, channels, policies, audit, credentials, plugins, components, connectors
agent-computer 4100 Chromium, /workspace, browser profile, screenshots, snapshots, file tools
AG-UI Bot endpoints 4200–4202 agent-bot / agent-langgraph / agent-harness (the harness chosen at install time)
supervisor 4500 (host) / 4300 (container) creates, stops, resets, and lists each Bot's computer container
PostgreSQL + pgvector 5432 product data, audit rows, credentials, policies, grants, channels, components
CopilotKit Intelligence external persistent threads, memory, realtime gateway

Two deliberate absences deserve naming. First, there is no such thing as in-process Bot policy: the agent-computer's shell module says it plainly: "This file is the hands, not the judgement" (agent-computer/src/shell.ts:11-13). Judgment lives at the gateway; the computer is only hands. Second, the default deployment has no public ports: Compose binds every port to both the 127.0.0.1 and [::1] loopbacks, because the resolution order of localhost between the two addresses is platform-dependent, and binding only one leaves some machines mysteriously unable to connect (docker-compose.yml:27-33). The boundary starts at port binding, ahead of any firewall.

Two "why not merge them" answers are also worth remembering. Why doesn't memory just live in Postgres? Because threads and recall are Intelligence's product capabilities, while provenance, review state, and originator are OpenBot's governance fields. Chapter 15 shows how this grows into two tracks: Intelligence owns content and ranking; local rows own provenance and visibility.

Why is the computer a separate service instead of a tool class inside server? Because it holds real login state and must be fenced off on its own: its own network, its own capabilities, its own egress policy. The moment it merges into server, all of those boundaries degrade into in-process if statements.

The golden path: the life of a channel message

Follow one message end to end. A human @-mentions a Bot in a channel: "help me fill this form into the system". A channel is a persistent session mapped one-to-one onto an Intelligence thread, not a chat-room metaphor: opening a new channel opens a new thread.

Four places deserve a pause.

The direction of the return flow is the entrance of governance. Note that tool calls do not go from the Bot straight to the computer: action calls (browser, files, MCP) turn around, come back to server, pass the gateway, and only then may land on the computer. This return leg is the most valuable design in the whole platform: there is no direct trust between a Bot and its computer, and every action is a fresh authorization. Chapter 4 covers the full turn lifecycle, including how this return leg executes server-side on the headless paths (routines, Responsibilities, group chats).

A thread belongs to exactly one agent. Intelligence threads are owned by a single agent, and this hard constraint propagates all the way up into the shape of group chats: in a group session each Bot holds its own thread (group_bot_threads), while humans read a shared transcript (group_messages) (docs/architecture.md:171). Chapter 11 shows that Bot-to-Bot handoffs also land in the asked Bot's own session. That is a necessary consequence of thread ownership, not a product choice. The most interesting decisions in an architecture often look like this: one hard constraint at the bottom, one seemingly willful product behavior at the top.

Every audit row records who made it happen. A turn can be started by a person at a keyboard, or by a routine, a Responsibility, a memory import, another handoff, or the deployment itself. The audit row's initiator field distinguishes these six kinds (server/src/audit.ts:595-600; Chapter 6 lists all six and why each exists): actor tells you under whose authority it ran, initiator tells you whether anyone was watching at the time: "this is the only field that can tell an unattended run from somebody typing" (docs/architecture.md:61-65). A routine-triggered run executes under its owner's authority; read only the actor column and a 3 a.m. routine looks identical to the owner awake and typing. The initiator is the only field that separates the two.

The most counterintuitive of the six is deployment, and it exists so that person never over-reports. Boot rows and boundary refusals with no identifiable caller are caused by nobody; if they borrowed the default and were written as person, the reading "person means a person caused this row" would stop holding, and the column would over-report forever. With a dedicated deployment, a deployment that has never run a routine or a handoff shows person on every row, exactly as before the column was added, without one extra word. It also stays out of Chapter 6's "Nobody watching" filter: a boundary held at boot is work done on nobody's behalf, and counting it would only turn the filter into noise. Unattended work is a first-class scenario on this platform, not an edge case, and that filter exists for every case of running under someone's authority while that someone is absent.

Streaming is not decoration, and neither is stopping. A turn runs for minutes, and the event stream lets a human see what the Bot is doing instead of guessing at a spinner. The human's stop button punches back through three layers, from app to server to computer, and the abort must reach the browser "before a high-impact click lands" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:1557-1559). Governance covers both "may it do this" and "can we make it stop right now". The fan-out goes beyond the app too: the realtime gateway, a Phoenix channel, and OpenTag's after-the-fact SSE replay give the same turn events three exits, and Chapter 4 walks through each.

    The central mechanism: the action gateway

    Every "do something" call on the golden path eventually squeezes through the same pipe: govern() in server/src/computer/gateway.ts. The comment at the top of that file freezes the contract. It shows how the gateway ranks its own duties:

    ts
     * Reading a page is one thing; clicking a button on an external website is
 * another, and the difference is the whole product. The record is not a report written alongside the
 * work, it is the thing the action goes through, so it cannot be missing: an action that was not
 * recorded did not happen, because there is no path that acts without writing the row first.
 *
 * Three jobs, in this order:
 *
 *  1. Resolve the ref the caller sent into the element it actually points at, from the snapshot this
 *     server fetched. Never from what the caller said it was clicking.
 *  2. Ask the policy. Deny beats allow, an absent policy denies, and a broken rule denies.
 *  3. Write the row, whichever way the decision went, and only then act.

    — server/src/computer/gateway.ts:4-14

    The most important sentence in this book sits inside that comment: an action that was not recorded did not happen. The audit is the thing the action must pass through, not a report written after it; no path can act without writing the row first. The order cannot be swapped either: decide, record, then act. Why must the decision row be written before execution instead of backfilled after? Because a backfilled ledger always leaves a window: the action happened, the process died, the row was never written. Writing the row first and acting second closes that window to zero. The price is that refusals and failures must also land as rows, and that price is a feature, not overhead. An action that happened is visible in the transcript; an action that was refused exists only in the audit trail (Chapter 6).

    The decision order inside the gateway:

    The policy engine uses CEL expressions. Deny beats allow, and the semantics are fail-closed: a missing policy denies everything, a broken deny rule counts as a hit, a broken allow rule permits nothing. The context the rules see is full-field bound, meaning every field always exists and gets a neutral empty value when absent (docs/architecture.md:49-65):

    Field Meaning
    tool.name, intent the tool's name and the intent abstracted by effect (activate, type…)
    bot.id, actor.id which Bot, under whose authority
    page.url, page.host the current page
    element.ref, element.role, element.name, element.type the target element
    key, command, file.path, etc. keystrokes, shell commands, file paths
    mcp.server, mcp.tool, mcp.effect an MCP call's source and its read/write classification
    initiator.kind, initiator.id what started it: the only field that separates "unattended" from "somebody typing"

    The neutral empty value exists for a concrete case: deny: contains(command, "rm -rf") should not block every click just because a click has no command field. Chapter 5 covers this design.

    The factory default policy is a separate decision. Below is the complete definition of DEFAULT_ACTION_POLICY, which shows how permissiveness gets written out explicitly instead of hiding inside the engine:

    ts
    export const DEFAULT_ACTION_POLICY: ActionPolicy = {
  mode: "enforce",
  deny: [],
  allow: ["true"],
};

    — server/src/computer/policy-store.ts:52-56

    A conservative engine and a permissive configuration are two separate decisions, and the split is careful. The engine assumes silence means nothing is allowed, because a deployment that has not spoken has not yet said what its Bots may do. The factory config explicitly writes allow: ["true"], because a Bot that can see pages but touch nothing is not a product: the first thing a person asks it to do is fill in a form. Between the two, the enterprise gets dry-run mode: new rules first run on real traffic in a mode that records but blocks nothing, and the administrator switches to enforce after reading the audit trail and confirming. "A governance feature nobody dares switch on is not a governance feature" (server/src/computer/policy.ts:27-29). That sentence is why dry-run exists. Chapter 5 spends a whole chapter dissecting this pipeline, including the approval gate and the two semantically opposite 409s.

    In pseudocode, govern() has the same shape in any system that wants to copy it:

    ts
    // Pseudocode — illustrates the pattern
async function guard(call: ToolCall, ctx: RunContext) {
  const target = await targetStore.resolve(call.ref, ctx.snapshotId); // resolve against the server-held snapshot, never the caller's claim
  const verdict = policy.check({ ...ctx, target });                   // deny beats allow; absent means deny
  await ledger.append({ call, target, verdict });                     // write the row first: refusals are recorded too
  if (!verdict.permit) throw new RefusedByRule(verdict.rule);         // a refusal names the rule
  try {
    return await executor.invoke(target);                             // act last
  } catch (err) {
    await ledger.append({ call, outcome: "failed", err });            // a failure appends a row
    throw err;
  }
}

    The pipeline itself copies easily; what makes the pattern work is two things that are easy to lose when copying. The target is resolved from a snapshot the server holds, not from what the caller claims: "A gateway that decides on a label supplied by the model is theatre: 'never click Submit' is evaded by sending {ref: "e13", name: "Continue"}" (gateway.ts:16-18). The refs are opaque to the caller precisely so the mapping stays in server's hands. The timing of the refusal throw is designed too: the refusal for a stale ref deliberately happens after the decision row and before execution, because "refusing it before the row was written would be a way to act without appearing on the trail" (gateway.ts:657-660).

    Three architectural bets

    Bet one: governance rides the protocol, not the framework

    A Bot's harness (the shell its agent framework runs in) is replaceable: LangGraph today, Mastra tomorrow, a hand-rolled loop the day after. OpenBot's answer is to press the entire governance plane onto the protocol. Any endpoint that satisfies three contract clauses is a Bot: serve AG-UI; /health requires no auth; everything else verifies x-openbot-agent-token, and when the token is not configured the endpoint fails closed and refuses everything (Chapter 16). Governance information rides the protocol layer too: each turn's standing role is injected as a plain system message, the one thing every framework understands, while "which Bot this turn is for, which person, how deep a handoff chain" travels in a signed run assertion carried by the callback, so a Bot cannot relabel its own run.

    Why not govern at the framework layer? Because frameworks come and go, and the contract stays. If authorization logic were written into one framework's hooks, switching frameworks would mean rewriting the governance layer once per framework: N frameworks means N copies of audit semantics guaranteed to drift. Governance at the protocol layer exists in exactly one copy. The gateway knows neither LangGraph nor the Claude SDK; it knows "one tool call carrying a signed assertion". The contract's catalog is data, not documentation: one harnesses.json list, compiled straight into the Rust desktop binary and read through TypeScript on the web side. Frameworks whose official AG-UI support is still marked as in progress are not admitted; the contract does not take half-finished goods. This also explains why OpenBot refuses to write adapters: integration packages must be maintained by their own maintainers, and the platform only defines the contract. Otherwise what you own is a pile of forks, not an ecosystem.

    Bet two: boundaries live in the deployment, not the model

    "Asking the model not to do this" is a wish, not a boundary. OpenBot's boundaries all live in the deployment topology. Three examples. First, the network. PostgreSQL sits alone on the data network, for a reason written into a comment in the compose file. It records the defense left behind after someone actually reached the database from inside a Bot's computer:

    yaml
        # Off the network the Bots are on, because a Bot's computer is on it and a Bot has a shell.
    #
    # With no `networks:` anywhere, Compose puts every service on one network with DNS by service
    # name, so `agent-computer` could open `postgres:5432` and the credentials three lines below are
    # in this file. That is the audit trail, the policy store and the agent tables, reachable from
    # the one container whose whole job is to run what a Bot asks for. `agent-computer/src/shell.ts`
    # says it plainly: isolation is the container's job, a shell can reach whatever the container
    # can reach.

    — docker-compose.yml:4-11

    A Bot has a shell, a shell reaches whatever the container reaches, so the database network carries only two services, postgres and migrate, and nothing else gets in. Second, process capabilities: the Docker socket goes only to the supervisor, and the supervisor's HTTP surface has only four verbs with no pass-through: "The shared secret is not the boundary; the vocabulary is" (supervisor/src/index.ts:35-37). Even if the API server falls entirely, the worst action an attacker can express is "restart some Bot's computer", because nothing else can even be said. Third, egress: every computer runs an in-process egress filtering proxy with four modes, and by default nothing gets out until a policy arrives (Chapter 8).

    The third one needs one more sentence: an honest boundary declaration is itself part of the architecture. The egress proxy's comment admits it cannot stop a process that ignores the proxy variables and opens a raw socket: "That is the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy's job." It narrows the real network boundary rather than replacing it. Every defensive layer states what it defends against, what it does not, and whose job the remainder is. A vague boundary declaration turns into finger-pointing on the night of the incident; a written-down one turns into a real NetworkPolicy in a Helm chart. Chapter 9 walks this line to its end when it covers deployment topology.

    The same logic has a second face at boot: if the configuration does not hold up, refuse to boot. Placeholder encryption keys, a public address paired with single-machine mode, a missing Intelligence contract. Twenty-plus checks keep a deployment that "looks healthy but answers the wrong questions" outside the gate before the first request arrives (Chapter 2). Boundaries live in the deployment, starting before the process is born.

    Bet three: a template, not a product

    OpenBot is not a SaaS; it is a template you fork and then truly own. The tenant package seeds one company's personality, coworker roster, and channels into the database with five required files (brand.yaml, agents.yaml, channels.yaml, model.yaml, knowledge.yaml); one missing file refuses the boot, and the error message names the file (Chapter 2). The default tenant package is examples/fintech, a fictional fintech company: clone it and you have coworkers, channels, and skills, instead of an empty admin console.

    A template's honesty shows in which decisions it refuses to make for you. The route for asking a human for help is one such seam: the template answers only "ask this person in the channel", because that is the only answer a template can honestly give. A company has its own on-call rotation, and that route is handed in by the deployment, not hardcoded in the tool (docs/architecture.md:297-299). channels.allowed_groups is declared and stored but takes no part in authorization decisions: no login path populates users.groups, a rule with no input is just "a claim waiting for an identity provider", and the template does not pretend it is enforcing it (Chapter 3). Even the Helm chart's warmPool template exists but gets refused at install time: an unwired feature is not allowed to pretend it works (Chapter 9).

    The examples/ directory is itself a map of this stance. "Bot = AG-UI endpoint URL" is backed by three reference implementations that run as-is:

    • examples/fintech/: the default tenant package, with the brand, coworker roster, and channels of a fictional fintech company; Chapter 2 takes it apart along the boot chain;
    • examples/langgraph-bot/: a Bot built on LangGraph StateGraph (TypeScript);
    • examples/mastra-bot/: a Bot built as a Mastra Agent (TypeScript);
    • examples/pydantic-ai-bot/: a Bot built on pydantic-ai (Python).

    Three reference implementations across two languages and three frameworks, and the header comments say the same thing. langgraph-bot's version is "OpenBot knows it only as an AG-UI endpoint URL" (examples/langgraph-bot/src/index.ts:16-19). pydantic-ai-bot's version is the fullest: "OpenBot knows a Bot only as an AG-UI endpoint URL, so the language and framework behind that URL are the deployment's business, not the surface's" (examples/pydantic-ai-bot/src/app.py:9-10). mastra-bot points out that it and the LangGraph example "share no OpenBot-specific code beyond the AG-UI protocol" (examples/mastra-bot/src/index.ts:11-16).

    Zero shared code beyond the protocol is the most literal meaning of "riding the protocol". The architectural decisions they share each testify directly to this bet:

    • None of them uses a framework's official AG-UI client. @ag-ui/langgraph and friends are client-side packages meant for the CopilotKit runtime; a Bot must be the other end of the protocol, a server, so all three hand-write the SSE event stream directly with @ag-ui/encoder, the same way the built-in agent-bot does (examples/langgraph-bot/src/index.ts:21-24).
    • A Bot process never executes tools. Tools arrive with each turn's input.tools; the Bot emits a TOOL_CALL event and ends that run, and the OpenBot side executes through the governance gateway and opens a new turn carrying the result. "That is why this file can drive a browser it has no access to" (langgraph-bot src/index.ts:251-253). mastra-bot simply gives its tools no execute field at all: "nothing runs here" (mastra-bot src/index.ts:123-128). The return flow is a contract the Bot side keeps too, not a one-sided preference of server's.
    • They share the same anti-fabrication prompt word for word: "NEVER state what a page contains unless you have just read it with a tool in this conversation" (langgraph-bot src/index.ts:66, mastra-bot src/index.ts:42, pydantic-ai-bot src/app.py:34). The template writes "don't pretend to know" into the examples' default personality, so whoever forks is copying the right answer from line one.
    • Protocol details are done to production standard too. A pure tool-call turn has no text, so TEXT_MESSAGE_START is delayed until the first chunk; opening it early would leave an empty bubble (langgraph-bot src/index.ts:201-204). The SLOW_MS test hook deliberately stalls the stream so you can kill the process mid-way and verify the server survives a client agent dying suddenly (src/index.ts:184-188).
    • Auth is deliberately minimal. langgraph-bot and pydantic-ai-bot offer an optional REQUIRE_KEY compared against the authorization header; mastra-bot does not even have that. The examples demonstrate the shape of the protocol; formal token verification is a contract clause between the deployment and the endpoint, and belongs to Chapter 16.
    • Each Bot minds its own model-interface dialect. langgraph-bot infers from the BOT_MODEL name whether to enable the Responses API (src/index.ts:42-44); pydantic-ai is the opposite: it speaks only /responses, not /v1/chat/completions, and a gateway offering only chat completions cannot feed it (examples/pydantic-ai-bot/README.md:42-45). The contract governs the protocol's shape and does not standardize model tastes.

    Registration is the same too: write one remote-ag-ui line in the tenant package, with the endpoint interpolated from the environment as ${VAR:-default} (examples/pydantic-ai-bot/README.md:52-60 has the full snippet). Chapter 2 shows how this line deletes itself when not configured; the contract's full clauses (unauthenticated health check, token verification for everything else) are Chapter 16 material.

    The other side of the template: the list of what was not built is just as long, and every entry carries a reason. No recording of keystrokes while a human is driving. CAPTCHAs are never solved for a human. user-oauth credentials are exchanged fresh per call and never cached. The audit tables allow no TRUNCATE. A fair number of these were bought with incidents: the TRUNCATE ban comes from the lesson of a naive fix that failed open (Chapter 6), and not caching user-oauth credentials buys revocation that takes effect immediately, with no cache to evict (Chapter 12). This book keeps returning to these "no"s. Half of a governed platform's credibility comes from what it built; the other half comes from what it promises in writing never to build.

    Deep Dive: A single source of truth in a multi-replica world

    (Tech leads may skip this without losing the thread.)

    server is meant to run multi-replica, and that assumption seeps into every subsystem. The solutions converge on one move: put the fact in Postgres and keep the process forgetful. A page snapshot's ref-to-element mapping is stored in the database, not process memory, because "the snapshot these refs belong to was very likely taken by another replica" (gateway.ts:540-541). Unattended work all queues in a single work_items table, claimed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, with leases timed by the database's own clock. The database clock is a lesson bought by the "a node 90 seconds behind" incident (Chapter 10). The Helm chart's values.yaml carries one more reminder: running a single replica masks every bug that only horizontal scaling would expose.

    The broadcast of policy changes is the fullest worked example of this philosophy. Policies use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY to reach all replicas, but the notification payload is deliberately empty: it says only "the boundary moved", never "what it moved to". The reason is half semantics, half physics: "a rule list can outgrow NOTIFY's 8000-byte cap" (server/src/computer/policy-listener.ts:28-32), and a server that enforces the portion of the rules that fit in the notification is just a more concealed version of the original bug. So the table is always the truth, and a received signal means go re-read the table. Every accompanying mechanical detail serves the same premise: notifications get lost.

    • The listener holds one dedicated connection (postgres(url, { max: 1 })), because "LISTEN holds one for the life of the subscription: taken from the pool it would be a connection the rest of the server never gets back" (policy-listener.ts:12-15, 26);
    • Reconnects trigger a re-read too: NOTIFY reaches only the replicas listening at that moment, a replica that was restarting or disconnected misses the announcement, so the onlisten callback re-reads the moment the subscription is rebuilt. This was the incident caught by community issue #94 (policy-listener.ts:45-57);
    • When the signal arrives but the re-read fails, the server logs loudly and states plainly that it is enforcing old rules: "This server was told the boundary changed and could not re-read it, so it is still enforcing the previous rules" (policy-listener.ts:33-43);
    • The broadcast goes back to every server including the writer: "this is the other end, on every server including the one that wrote it" (policy-listener.ts:5-6). The server that changed the rule walks the same re-read path, one codebase and one fact across the fleet;
    • A failed broadcast in the other direction is equally non-fatal and only logged. A lost notification has reconnect as backstop, and the row in the table is the fact (policy-store.ts:181-200).

    Without this machinery, the failure is silent: the rule takes effect on only one of N servers, and nothing says so. "The admin screen reported success because the row really was saved, and the computer.policy_loaded audit row was written at boot, so both the screen and the trail agreed with each other and disagreed with what the fleet was enforcing" (policy-listener.ts:8-11). Screen and audit row agree with each other and both disagree with what the fleet actually enforces, so "a deny rule that stops roughly one action in N is worse than no deny rule, because it looks like it works" (policy-listener.ts:11-12).

    Chapter 5 returns to this line when it covers policy storage, broadcast, and replay. This Deep Dive is shared groundwork for at least four later chapters: when any chapter makes you ask "why does this also have to go through the database", the answer lives here.

    The map of the book: seven parts, nineteen chapters

    Part I: Foundations. Before governance, the process must exist; before trust, we must know who is who.

    • Chapter 1 (this chapter): The Architecture of a Governable Agent Platform: the six pillars, the golden path, the three bets.
    • Chapter 2: Startup as Boundary: Configuration, the Tenant Package, and Refusing to Boot: the full list of twenty-plus boot refusals, the tenant package pipeline, and the master table of fail-closed versus fail-open tiers.
    • Chapter 3: Identity and Access: Auth, Roles, and Removing a Person: auth, roles, the INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS floor, and the complete semantics of removing a person.

    Part II: The Governed Turn. The turn is the heartbeat; the gateway is the conscience; the audit trail is the memory.

    • Chapter 4: The Life of a Turn: The AG-UI Runtime: the AG-UI protocol, the browser and headless turn paths, thread leases, streaming fan-out.
    • Chapter 5: The Action Gateway: Decide, Record, Then Act: govern() in full, the CEL policy engine, the four layers of the approval gate.
    • Chapter 6: The Audit Trail: Who Did It, and What Started It: database-enforced append-only, the six initiator kinds, CSV export, and the audit's restraint.

    Part III: The Bot's Computer. Every coworker gets a computer. The computer is fenced, and a human can take the wheel at any time.

    • Chapter 7: One Computer per Bot: managed Chromium, ARIA snapshots and refs, mutual exclusion between human and Bot control, the shell allowlist.
    • Chapter 8: The Computer's Boundaries: Egress, Secrets, and Asking for Help: the egress filtering proxy, three defensive lines for secrets, CAPTCHAs never solved, Web Bot Auth.
    • Chapter 9: The Supervisor and the Deployment Topology: the supervisor's four verbs, the Compose / single-container / Helm shapes, the SPIRE identity layer.

    Part IV: Autonomy and Collaboration. When nobody is watching, work still happens, and we can still answer who asked for it.

    • Chapter 10: Unattended Work: One Queue and the Routines: one work_items table with seven consumers, routines, idempotency keys and fatigue rules.
    • Chapter 11: Bot to Bot, Bot to Human: handoffs where the grant is the routing table, signed assertions, failing loudly.

    Part V: Tools, Skills, and Components. Grant capability, never beyond the boundary.

    • Chapter 12: Plugins and MCP: The Capability Catalog and the Seven Gates: plugin_grants as one table holding three things, the seven gates of callTool, the three states of credential ownership.
    • Chapter 13: Skills and Tool Narrowing: the reliability turning point of tool count, three levels of skill ownership, narrowing that always fails open.
    • Chapter 14: Components: Answering in UI, Not Just Prose: answers as UI instead of prose; compiled and sandboxed component sources share one governance.

    Part VI: Memory and Learning. An agent without memory makes the same mistakes forever; memory without review is a compliance nightmare.

    • Chapter 15: Two-Track Memory and Automatic Learning: Intelligence owns content and recall; local rows own provenance, review state, and visibility.

    Part VII: Ecosystem and Cross-Cutting. Frameworks come and go; the contract stays. Surfaces differ; the boundary is one.

    • Chapter 16: The Framework Ecosystem: Fifteen Harnesses, One Contract: fifteen harnesses under one contract, with four representatives compared in depth.
    • Chapter 17: Security Boundaries: Two Keys and a Textbook Patch: the division of labor between two sets of keys, a textbook patch of the SSO plugin, the credential vault.
    • Chapter 18: Surfaces: Desktop, Mobile, and Voice: different forms, one boundary.
    • Chapter 19: Epilogue: Twenty Patterns for Governed Agent Platforms: twenty patterns collected, the three bets revisited, and where not to copy.

    The narrative spine (each chapter's opening, diagrams, and Apply This) reads end to end without the code blocks; the code blocks and Deep Dives are for the people who will build. A technical lead in a hurry needs only Chapters 1, 5, 7, 9, and 19.

    Apply This

    This chapter is an overview, so the transferable judgments are overview-level too. Five patterns, ordered by what to do first when you take them home.

    1. The action gateway: force every side effect through one pipe. The problem: an agent's tool calls are scattered across dozens of implementations, so authorization and audit never converge and "who did what when" has no answer. How to adapt: give every kind of side effect a single govern()-style pipeline: resolve (the target comes from server-held state, not the caller's claim), decide (evaluate policy, deny beats allow), audit (write the row first, refusals included), act (append a row on failure). The pitfall: two of them. Deciding on labels the model self-reports hands the boundary to the governed object, and "never click Submit" gets bypassed by a renamed button. Recording only successful actions is the second: refused attempts are the first rows you will read in an investigation.

    2. The vocabulary is the boundary. The problem: some process has to hold a dangerous capability (a Docker socket, production keys, payment rails), and the larger the holder's API surface, the larger the blast radius when it falls. How to adapt: compress the capability into a small set of verbs whose subject is a domain noun; derive resource names instead of accepting them; leave no pass-through endpoint. The auth token is the door lock; the verb surface is the wall. The pitfall: do not mistake a shared secret for a boundary. A secret is a thing that goes to zero the moment it leaks. Do not leave a "debug" straight-through endpoint either: it will quickly grow into the de facto boundary, with no audit.

    3. A fail-closed engine and an explicitly permissive factory config are two decisions. The problem: an engine that defaults to allow makes governance theater; an engine that defaults to deny with no way to rehearse means nobody dares turn it on, and governance exists in name only. How to adapt: make the engine deny by default and read broken rules in the strictest direction; write the permissiveness of the factory config out explicitly instead of relying on an implicit default; add a dry-run mode so new rules run on real traffic recording but not blocking, and switch to enforce after reading enough audit. The pitfall: do not hide an "unconfigured means allow" exception inside the engine. The safe reading of silence is "nothing is allowed", not "anything goes". A governance feature nobody dares switch on is not a governance feature.

    4. Isolate stateful things per entity, not in shared pools. The problem: agents hold real login state, workspaces, and browser profiles; once those are shared, any intent to authorize per entity dies: two Bots sharing one profile share login state, and "this Bot may access Salesforce" becomes unenforceable. How to adapt: one isolation unit per agent (container, volume, profile), with identity derived from the same fact that created it, not labeled on afterwards. The pitfall: the isolation unit itself is not the boundary. A profile isolates cookies, not the kernel, the filesystem, or memory. The real boundary has to come from topology (network segmentation, process capabilities, egress filtering), and each layer must write down what it does not defend against.

    5. Protocol first, frameworks second. The problem: frameworks change every half year and the governance layer gets rewritten along with them; N frameworks means N copies of audit semantics, guaranteed to drift. How to adapt: define a minimal contract: a protocol endpoint, an unauthenticated health check, verification for everything else. Governance information travels only on channels every implementation understands (plain system messages, signed assertions). Refuse to write adapters for any framework yourself; integration packages belong to their maintainers. The pitfall: do not let the harness hold authoritative state. The truth about conversations, grants, and audit belongs in your own database; what the framework holds is at best a cache.

    The next chapter starts where all of this starts: how a process proves it deserves a configuration before it is allowed to exist. Boot is itself the first boundary.

    Chapter 2: Startup as Boundary: Configuration, the Tenant Package, and Refusing to Boot →

    Chapter 2: Startup as Boundary: Configuration, the Tenant Package, and Refusing to Boot

    Chapter 1 gave the panoramic view: six pillars holding up an agent platform that can be governed, and a golden path carrying a channel message from a browser to a Bot's computer and streaming the answer back. That path rested on a premise left unsaid at the time: the process has to exist first, and it has to exist with the right boundaries. This chapter covers the earlier moment, from the process being launched to the first request being answered. What OpenBot checks, and what it refuses.

    For an ordinary web service, a misconfiguration means some feature misbehaves. For a platform that hands real tools to agents, a misconfiguration means a boundary has collapsed and nobody knows: the credential vault encrypts with a key printed in a public repository; every visitor is treated as the administrator; an operator mistypes a policy and the deployment "healthily" allows the very thing they just banned. What these failure shapes share is that the system does not go down; it only looks fine. OpenBot's answer is to compress every such interrogation into the boot moment: better not to start than to start with the wrong boundaries. config.ts states the program right at the top of the file: "Configuration the product cannot function without belongs at the boot boundary" (server/src/config.ts:1-5).

    This chapter follows the boot order. How the four-layer entry chain assembles the process; the single logic behind the twenty-plus refuse-to-boot checks in loadConfig(); then two samples worth reading closely, the reachability trichotomy of OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER and the tenant package's full pipeline from five YAML files to database rows. By the end, the book's thesis that boundaries live in the deployment rather than the model has its first literal footing: the facts of a deployment (addresses, keys, the administrator list) are interrogated at the boot boundary, and a deployment that cannot answer does not exist.

    The four-layer entry chain: before the first request is answered

    The server process's entry is a chain of four files instead of one, each layer doing exactly one thing:

    The first layer is so thin it almost does not exist, but its reason for existing is typical. This is the whole of production-entry.ts (server/src/production-entry.ts:1-8):

    ts
    /*
 * Bun resolves eventsource@3 through its `bun` export before its `require` export. The MCP SDK's
 * CommonJS SSE transport still requires eventsource, so the production process evaluates the ESM
 * module once before the runtime can reach that CJS require.
 */
import "eventsource";

await import("./index");

    It holds no business logic; it pre-empts a runtime quirk. Bun resolves eventsource@3 through its bun export ahead of require, and the MCP SDK's CJS SSE transport still uses require, so without the preload the process blows up mid-run. The file is worth remembering because the fix is "import once, at the right moment" rather than another layer of bundler configuration: the process's first line of code is spent on a deployment fact.

    The second layer, index.ts, is the composition root: 2,500-plus lines doing one thing in strict order, assembly. loadConfig(), the database connection, dozens of stores and services constructed one by one, createApp(...), startHttpServer(...).

    Most comments in the file do not say what something is; they say why this must come before that. The tenant package loads at index.ts:405 because "the package names the deployment and the channel store needs that name before it can mint a thread id" (index.ts:403-404); the peopleStore must exist before auth, because sign-in checks the deny list (index.ts:449-468). The composition root's correctness is made of ordering, and the comments are that ordering's documentation.

    The third layer, createApp() in app.ts, takes about thirty optional dependencies and assembles the Hono route tree. Each optional parameter's docstring states the degraded behavior when it is absent. Absence comes in two philosophies (no route vs 503), which is the subject of the failure-ladder section below. The fourth layer, http-server.ts, is the Bun.serve front door: ordinary requests pass to Hono, but WebSocket upgrades are intercepted before Hono sees them, and the guard is redone by hand. That hand-rolled pass is worth reading line by line; see the Deep Dive at the end of this section.

    Deep Dive: The hand-rolled guard on the WebSocket upgrade

    Why does the live screen's socket not connect straight to the agent-computer? Because computers authenticate with a shared token rather than a person's session, and must never be reachable directly from a browser: "so the socket terminates here, behind the same session guard as every other route, and this process opens a second socket inward carrying the token" (http-server.ts:66-72). The front door is both the end and the beginning of that socket. And an upgrade is not request/response: "Bun hands it over before Hono sees a body" (http-server.ts:74-76), so Hono's middleware chain does not exist for it, and the guard has to be redone by hand inside fetch (http-server.ts:100-173), answering five questions in order:

    1. Who are you? If resolveRequestActor(request) fails, 401: "An unauthenticated socket here would be the whole point of the proxy defeated" (http-server.ts:108-113);
    2. Which computer? If computerAccessCheck fails, 404. Being signed in is not enough; this socket carries that Bot's screen, and "without this, anybody signed in watches anybody's Bot work" (http-server.ts:114-124);
    3. Where does the upstream address come from? Only from computerGateway.locate (with checkComputerAddress), never from provider.locate: the upstream URL's query carries the COMPUTER_TOKEN, and a foreign host would walk away with a deployment-level token (http-server.ts:125-133);
    4. What if the computer cannot be found? Answer 502 and say so, never fall back to another Bot's computer: "Said out loud rather than falling back to another Bot's computer, which is the failure this whole path exists to prevent" (http-server.ts:144-153);
    5. What if the browser cannot keep up? Drop frames, do not queue them: "a frame the browser is too slow for should be dropped, not queued, because a stale frame is worse than a missing one" (http-server.ts:185-186).

    One more small mechanism: Bun accepts a single websocket handler, and the live screen and the channel push each need one, so the same handler demultiplexes on data attached at upgrade time: proxy sockets carry an upstream field, Hono sockets do not (http-server.ts:29-36, 84-89). This front door teaches every later chapter one thing: even when an entry bypasses the framework's middleware chain, "a request that got this far is authenticated" is still not treated as a fact.

    Refusing to boot: moving discovery to the cheapest repair moment

    loadConfig() reads every environment variable into an immutable DeploymentConfig; any failed check throws, and the process dies at boot. There are more than twenty such checks, all fail-closed. The representative ones:

    Configuration error What it costs if allowed through Source
    KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not a base64-encoded 32 bytes; or production still has the .env.example placeholder key The credential vault encrypts with a key printed in a public repository, and looks exactly like a healthy deployment config.ts:454-478
    Any OAuth provider's CLIENT_ID / CLIENT_SECRET not configured as a pair It blows up at the first sign-in, "the worst moment to discover it" config.ts:686-702
    A provider but no BETTER_AUTH_SECRET / BETTER_AUTH_URL, or a secret under 32 characters; a secret but no provider Half-configuration is the most dangerous shape config.ts:773-789
    Sign-in configured but INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS empty Everyone enters as a plain user, with no admin screen and no way to promote anybody config.ts:791-807
    One of the Intelligence trio (API_URL / GATEWAY_WS_URL / API_KEY) missing A partial set is more dangerous than none at all config.ts:948-968
    PORT and SERVER_PORT both set and disagreeing; or a typo like 30o1 Two names, one value: disagreement is an error config.ts:1290-1311
    AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS not an integer ≥ 1 A typo that silently became 0 would delete the audit trail rather than keep it config.ts:1247-1258
    AGENT_COMPUTER_POLICY invalid JSON or wrong shape The operator gets a "healthy" deployment that silently allows what they just tried to ban config.ts:1179-1197
    OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER + a publicly reachable address Every visitor is an administrator (the reachOf() section covers this) config.ts:505-537
    No IdP at all and single-user mode off Same as above; the only answer is to refuse the boot auth/dev-actor.ts:82-84
    Domain allowlist combined with a Microsoft multi-tenant tenant Under multi-tenancy the list "cannot hold" config.ts:838-854
    MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL without its paired token The managed Bot endpoint has no credential config.ts:657-666

    Every refusal corresponds to one question: if this error were allowed through, when would it surface, and in what shape. The comment on the INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS row says it plainest: "Refusing at start-up is the only cheap moment to catch that; the expensive one is after the first person has signed in" (config.ts:794-797). A deployment with sign-in configured but no administrator list lets everyone in as a plain user, with no admin screen anywhere and no place that could promote one. At boot this mistake costs a process exit; after the first person signs in, it costs database surgery.

    Three conventions cut across all of these checks.

    First, "unset" has one definition across the whole file: an empty string, once trimmed, counts as unset everywhere (config.ts:412-422). That convention makes "configured but not finished" a detectable state: an OAuth id/secret not in a pair, one of the Intelligence trio missing, all get caught. The Intelligence comment explains why a partial set is more dangerous than none: "it means somebody intended to configure Intelligence and got it wrong" (config.ts:938-941).

    Second, error messages are action instructions for the operator, not stack traces for a developer. The placeholder-key refusal attaches the fix command: "Generate one with: openssl rand -base64 32" (config.ts:466-470).

    Third, a security-relevant question can be asked only one way. Two gates used to disagree on trimming: one trimmed, one did not, so NODE_ENV=production (trailing space, preserved verbatim by Docker's env_file) tripped one gate and slipped past the other, and the gate it slipped past happened to decide whether the credential vault could encrypt with a key printed in a public repository. All production checks now go through a single isProduction() (config.ts:424-443). Chapter 17 has the full postmortem; the conclusion to keep here is that the same security question gets exactly one phrasing in the codebase.

    reachOf(): ask who can reach it, not whether this is production

    OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true means: this deployment has no sign-in, and every request is treated as the one administrator. .env.example ships with it on, because a clone should run; the README's deployment section hands the same .env to docker run. An address separates these two outcomes.

    The intuitive implementation looks at NODE_ENV and refuses single-user mode in production. OpenBot deliberately does not, and the comment says why (config.ts:488-492): the Dockerfile sets NODE_ENV=production for every container, and so does the Helm chart's local trial. Used as the gate, it would refuse a feature the chart itself advertises while failing to catch the genuinely dangerous combination. An earlier version of this check did use NODE_ENV, and the outcome was inverted: "NODE_ENV is unset by default, so the one case it had to catch was the one it let through" (auth/dev-actor.ts:14-16).

    The replacement question is direct: can anybody else reach it? The implementation is reachOf(), sorting every public address into three classes. The classifier's entry (server/src/config.ts:553-561):

    ts
    type Reach = "loopback" | "private" | "public";

function reachOf(raw: string): Reach {
  let bare: string;
  try {
    bare = new URL(raw).hostname.toLowerCase();
  } catch {
    return "public";
  }

    It shows the function's most important branch: if new URL() fails to parse, the address goes straight to public. The full decision tree:

    The middle class is the feature's real audience: 192.168.1.10 on a home server, a 100.x address handed out by Tailscale, openbot.local. None of them are loopback, and none are reachable by strangers. Refusing private networks along with public ones would refuse the feature's own users, and the operator's only way out would be to switch off the flag that describes reality accurately.

    So private is allowed, but every boot prints a loud warning (index.ts:2496-2503), and the comment explains why it is not made a quiet default: "A server that is not checking who is asking should never be a quiet default."

    Only public is refused. And the classifier's hardest rule is the catch branch in the code above: an address that cannot be parsed counts as public. The comment puts it in capitals (config.ts:550-551): "UNPARSEABLE COUNTS AS PUBLIC, and so does an unrecognised name. A value nobody could read is not a value anybody checked, and the safe reading of 'I cannot tell' is never 'it is fine'."

    This is the purest landing of the book's thesis. Same binary, same switch, and the boundary is decided by where this deployment is actually exposed, a deployment fact, rather than by an environment label inside the code. The boundary lives in the deployment. A library checks NODE_ENV; a platform checks reachability.

    The tenant package: five YAML files define a company

    After the environment variables, the boot chain reads the tenant package. OpenBot positions itself as "a template, not a product" (README:32): there is no hosted version to sign up for and no release artifact to depend on. You fork the repository, replace examples/fintech with your own coworkers, channels, and skills, and run it. The tenant package is that fork's diff surface: a deployment's brand, Bot roster, channels, model, and knowledge sources, all declared in one directory:

    File Required Contents
    brand.yaml required tenant.id, tenant.product_name (optional skin.stylesheet)
    agents.yaml required the Bot roster: id / name / title / role_description / type
    channels.yaml required the channel list and permitted_agents
    model.yaml required provider, credential_secret_ref, default_model
    knowledge.yaml required the knowledge source list (nothing consumes it yet; see the Deep Dive)
    skills.yaml optional skill declarations: slug / instructions / tools
    theme.css optional theme variables (validated against an allowlist)
    agents/*.yaml optional one or more coworkers per file, merged with agents.yaml

    The loading pipeline is a straight line, and any step failing refuses the boot:

    The validator is hand-written on purpose. The repository has zod available, but validateTenantPackage() uses four small functions (asRecord / asList / requiredString / stringArray, tenant-package.ts:278-311) because the error messages must name the file and the key. asList's docstring is the decision itself (server/src/tenant-package.ts:285-297):

    ts
    /**
 * A list a package must supply, named in the error when it does not.
 *
 * Cast without checking, a missing `agents:` reaches `.map` on `undefined` and the reader gets a
 * TypeError naming neither the file nor the key. Editing YAML by hand is the first thing somebody
 * does here, so getting it wrong has to produce a sentence they can act on.
 */
function asList(value: unknown, name: string): unknown[] {
  if (!Array.isArray(value)) {
    throw new Error(`${name} must be a list`);
  }
  return value;
}

    It shows a prioritization: a schema library can produce paths and type errors, but it cannot produce a sentence like "agents in agents.yaml must be a list" that a person with shaky hands can act on. Editing YAML by hand is always the first thing an administrator does with a tenant package, and the validator is written for that person. The pattern matters because it accepts the real distribution of configuration errors: most of them are typos and indentation, not semantic errors, and at this boundary the quality of the error messages is the quality of the product.

    Three validation rules show the most craft:

    • Reserved names. A Bot's id cannot equal a deployment route's reserved name (policy, fleet, policy-dry-run, server/src/computer/deployment-routes.ts:14). The computer router's bot-access guard steps aside for those names, so a Bot called policy would be treated as a deployment-level endpoint and served past the guard: "such a Bot would be served to anybody who can sign in without the guard ever being asked" (tenant-package.ts:382-390). And since only the package can give a Bot a self-chosen id (API-created Bots are always agent_<uuid>), refusing here closes the hole instead of moving it elsewhere.
    • Duplicate ids. Always refused, with a message that names both sources (tenant-package.ts:489-493): "Preferring one would make which coworker a deployment runs depend on the order a directory happened to be read in" (458-461).
    • Skill slugs. A skill slug referenced by an agent must come from the package's own skills.yaml; the loader deliberately does not check skills already in the database. A package cannot attach somebody else's instructions to its own Bots by naming their slug (545-552).

    How agents.yaml and the agents/ directory merge into one roster is likewise spelled out (collectAgents, tenant-package.ts:451-500):

    • Fixed order: the agents: list in agents.yaml first, then agents/*.yaml file by file in filename order. Only .yaml/.yml count; READMEs and editor leftovers are not parsed (readAgentFiles, tenant-package.ts:703-723);
    • The agents/ directory itself is optional: a missing directory returns an empty list, not an error (tenant-package.ts:706-711);
    • Each agents/ file can hold a single coworker document or a document with an agents: list (tenant-package.ts:484-487). The header comment states the directory's reason to exist: "a coworker somebody sends you is a file you drop in, not a fragment to paste into the middle of a file you already have" (tenant-package.ts:454-456);
    • Duplicate ids within one file are refused too (tenant-package.ts:476-479): the sync upserts row by row, so an unrefused duplicate would silently become whichever appeared later;
    • All files go through the same parseAgents, with error messages naming the agents/<filename> source: the validator's discipline that an error must point back to a file does not change in directory form;
    • Environment interpolation applies to agents/ files as well (tenant-package.ts:700-701), and the directory counts into the package checksum.

    One reconciliation rule exists specifically against read order: if the same id has an endpoint that interpolates to empty in one place and a complete declaration in another, the complete declaration wins. "A real declaration wins whichever file it is in, so the answer does not depend on the order a directory is read in" (tenant-package.ts:526-532). Together with the duplicate refusal that names both sources, every outcome of the merge is independent of the order the directory was read in, which is the most important certainty declarative configuration can offer.

    Each row of agents.yaml also carries a type contract. type has three values only, built-in / remote-ag-ui / remote-mastra, with the YAML kebab-case spellings mapping onto the database enum's snake_case (tenant-package.ts:365-375), and required fields fork by type:

    • built-in requires system_prompt: the Bot's persona travels with the package;
    • remote-ag-ui requires endpoint: the Bot's capability lives in the deployment;
    • remote-mastra may add remote_agent_id on top of endpoint, to name which agent on the other server (tenant-package.ts:436-440).

    avatar_seed is optional but must be non-empty if given; skills is a slug list, default empty. The type set is a closed vocabulary, and the loader refuses types it does not recognize. The price of that refusal (the whole file fails to load, the deployment does not come up) is exactly why picked-harness, covered below, dares to interpolate even type.

    The pipeline ends in a checksum: the five required files plus skills.yaml, plus the agents/ directory file by file, concatenated as filename\ncontents and hashed with sha256 (tenant-package.ts:783-791). Adding, removing, or editing a coworker all count as package changes; without the checksum a deployment would keep running the old roster while the repository already describes a different one. Note that theme.css is not in the checksum. That is a separate kind of decision, covered in this chapter's Deep Dive.

    ${NAME:-fallback} interpolation and a Bot that deletes itself

    Once the files are read, expandEnvironment() replaces ${NAME} and ${NAME:-fallback} with environment values before validation. The core of the interpolation (server/src/tenant-package.ts:335-345):

    ts
      return value.replace(
    /\$\{([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)(?::-([^}]*))?\}/g,
    (_, name: string, fallback: string | undefined) => {
      const resolved = environment[name];
      if (resolved !== undefined && resolved !== "") return resolved;
      if (fallback !== undefined) return fallback;
      throw new Error(
        `${filename} refers to \${${name}}, which is not set in this environment.`,
      );
    },
  );

    The semantics are three lines: use the environment value if it is non-empty; otherwise use the fallback; if neither exists, throw, with a message naming the file and the variable. An empty string counts as unset, the same convention as config.ts.

    The rationale is in the comment (tenant-package.ts:323-329): the address of the service behind a Bot belongs to the environment rather than the package, and the same package must work on a laptop, on staging, and on production; "An unset name is an error rather than an empty string".

    But "empty" gets two treatments here, and the difference is the design's essence. An unset variable is an error, because you declared you would provide it. A remote Bot whose endpoint interpolates to empty is handled differently: that declaration is discarded, and the id goes into omittedAgentIds, with same-named references in channels silently filtered (tenant-package.ts:396-403). This is the mechanism that lets the example packages carry a Bot nobody has configured yet: the fintech package has two such declarations (examples/fintech/agents.yaml:64-92). risk-analyst's endpoint: ${MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL:-} falls through by default and registers only once configured.

    picked-harness goes further and interpolates even type (${PICKED_HARNESS_KIND:-remote-ag-ui}). The package's comment explains this is no trick for its own sake: written as the literal remote-mastra, the whole package would fail to load on older servers that do not know that type, because the loader refuses an unknown type by refusing the entire file and the deployment does not come up. Interpolated, older servers see remote-ag-ui and load normally, unless somebody actually picks Mastra.

    A discarded Bot leaves no hole; it leaves a tombstone. On sync, the package-owned agent_profiles rows with no current declaration get a deletedAt marker, while the agents rows and conversation history stay as they were: "runtime tombstones preserve their readable history" (tenant-package.ts:841-842). The day the endpoint gets configured, the next sync clears deletedAt, the Bot comes back to life, and the history is still there.

    The reverse operation is deliberately absent: deleting an agents/ file from the package does not delete the Bot; the row stays, still owned by the package. The declaration stops; the existence does not. That is a deliberate seam between "the package is declarative configuration" and "the database is fact".

    Back to the book's thesis: type can be interpolated because the registration surface is a protocol, an AG-UI endpoint URL, rather than a framework. The package only declares "here is an endpoint that speaks AG-UI"; whether LangGraph or Mastra sits across from it is no concern of the loader. Governance rides the protocol, starting from the first line of the configuration file.

    The single-transaction seed: ownership encoded in SQL

    After validation, synchronizeTenantPackage() seeds the package into the database in one transaction (tenant-package.ts:795-1110): a defensive re-check of reserved names (against old packages, seeded before this check existed, that already planted a Bot called policy), upserting the deployment_packages row, tombstoning omitted Bots, upserting agent by agent, rewriting channel membership, syncing skills and grants. From then on the runtime reads only the database; the YAML is never read again. The tenant package subsystem holds no runtime state: it is a one-shot pipeline of file, validate, seed, plus a read-only status query (GET /api/admin/package).

    The upsert's phrasing is the most notable part of the seed. Ownership is encoded as a SQL-layer predicate rather than as an application-layer discipline. The agent-row upsert (server/src/tenant-package.ts:879-890):

    ts
            .onConflictDoUpdate({
          target: agentTable.id,
          setWhere: eq(agentTable.packageId, deploymentPackage.id),
          set: {
            name: agent.name,
            type: agent.type,
            configuration: agent.configuration,
            packageId: deploymentPackage.id,
            updatedAt,
          },
        })
        .returning({ id: agentTable.id });

    The mechanism: ON CONFLICT ... SET WHERE packageId = this package means that when the id collides but the row belongs to somebody else (a user-created Bot, another package), the UPDATE does not apply and RETURNING comes back empty. The code then throws "collides with a user-created agent" and rolls back the whole transaction (tenant-package.ts:892-895). "The package may only touch its own things" lives in the SQL predicate, where it survives the next contributor, rather than in "the sync function remembers to check first", which quietly stops working in that same contributor's hands.

    The same collision on the skills side is handled by skipping: when a package-declared slug collides with a skill a person wrote, the sync logs console.warn, skips, and continues booting (tenant-package.ts:1051-1061). The asymmetry is deliberate, and the comment gives the reason: "Anybody signed in may write a skill, so throwing would let one person stop the deployment booting by choosing a name" (1037-1039). Bot self-chosen ids can only come from the package, so a collision there is always an accident or malice and throwing is affordable; the skill namespace is shared with every signed-in user, so throwing hands any registered user a button that stops the deployment from booting. Before deciding whether a boot refusal is right, ask first: who else can write in this namespace?

    Grant retraction follows the same ownership logic. Package-issued skill grants are marked tenant-package in plugin_grants.granted_by; every other value is a real user id, so the two never collide (tenant-package.ts:168-173). On redeploy, all grants this package issued are deleted by that marker first, then re-inserted from the current YAML: a skill the package stops giving is taken back. Grants an administrator made by hand in the UI carry the administrator's id and are untouched by redeploys: "retracting somebody's deliberate decision is not something a redeploy should do quietly" (987-994).

    Finally, the nature of credential_secret_ref in model.yaml: it is a reference, not a value. The documentation writes this into the configuration-change procedure: "credential_secret_ref is a reference to a stored credential, not a credential value." (docs/configuration.md:1162) The credential itself is written into the credential vault by an administrator through the API (AES-256-GCM encrypted; Chapters 6 and 17 return to it), and the package only names the keyId. The credential value never enters the YAML, the package checksum, or the logs.

    Each time the key is needed, resolveModelApiKey resolves it on the spot (credentials.ts:259-279), along a fixed chain:

    1. Look up the newest live row in the credentials table by {provider, keyId} (readModelSecret, credentials.ts:459-479);
    2. On a hit, unwrap the AES-GCM envelope with KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY (decryptSecret; the envelope carries a version and an iv);
    3. On a miss, fall back to the OPENAI_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variables; a trimmed-empty string counts as absent, the same convention as in the refuse-to-boot section.

    Not caching is deliberate: "a credential rotated a moment ago is used by the next run" (index.ts:650-651). Once rotation finishes in the vault, the next run gets the new key, and there is no cache to invalidate. The write path is likewise closed inside the vault interface: an administrator writes on the Credentials page, and if a live row with the same key exists it is atomically rotated (createCredential, credentials.ts:560-591). Configuration goes into the repository, secrets go into the vault, and the two meet only on the reference's name.

    The model itself has an environment override layer: runtimeModelForEnvironment lets environment variables override the package's model.yaml (copilot.ts:221-251), in a fixed priority:

    • BOT_PROVIDER overrides the package's provider; written as an empty string it counts as openai, which is how the desktop client switches back to OpenAI;
    • BOT_MODEL applies only when the provider is anthropic, or openai with OPENAI_BASE_URL set;
    • Everything else uses the package's default_model.

    One deliberate asymmetry remains: when neither is set in the environment, the fallback default model for openai deliberately differs from the default in the shared spec (copilot.ts:209-219). Built-in Bots speak the Responses API and can afford newer models; remote Bots speak chat completions, where those models would refuse function tools. Defaults are chosen by the consumer's protocol capability, rather than one "latest" shared across all deployments. The package declares the default and the environment overrides the exception, the same division of labor as interpolation's "addresses belong to the environment".

    The failure ladder: refuse to boot, 503, or carry on quietly

    At this point the failure philosophy along the whole boot/runtime boundary can be collected into one table. The same "something went wrong" gets four tiers of handling, and the tier is decided by one question: would staying silent here amount to telling a lie?

    Where the failure happens Tier Behavior and reason Source
    Configuration validation (twenty-plus checks; see Refusing to boot) Refuse to boot The process dies at boot, the only cheap discovery moment config.ts
    Tenant package validation failure, sync collision Refuse to boot The transaction rolls back; a bad package means a wrong deployment, and no deployment is better tenant-package.ts
    Dependency absent (e.g. peopleStore) 503 Honest degradation: "nobody has signed in yet" and "this deployment cannot tell you" are two answers, and an empty list is a lie app.ts:282-288
    Every request when there is no IdP and no single-user mode 503 authenticationUnavailable always answers "No identity provider is configured." A healthy deployment never reaches it, because the boot phase already refused the combination (see Refusing to boot); it exists as depth for the "what if" app.ts:608-618
    Capability never built (e.g. worker) No route mounted "a deployment that never built a worker has no door for it, not a locked one" app.ts:323-325
    Model availability self-check fails Warn and continue At boot, ask the provider once whether this key can call this model, 5-second timeout, never throws; a custom BASE_URL is skipped outright (compatible endpoints often cannot answer a single-model query, so a 404 says nothing) model-availability-check.ts:91-122
    Boot audit row write fails Silent degradation .catch(() => undefined): "A deployment must not fail to start because its audit trail is unavailable" index.ts:535-543
    Sign-in audit write fails Fail-open Sign-in is not blocked: "A trail that is briefly unavailable must not lock everybody out" auth/index.ts:72-95
    Intent routing model fails Fail-open Falls to the default coworker: "a router that throws would turn 'we were not sure who to ask' into 'your message went nowhere'" routing/classify.ts:9-13

    The right two columns are the comparison that matters. An absent peopleStore answers 503 because an empty list would lie while 503 tells the truth; a worker that was never built simply has no door, rather than a locked one; the model self-check only warns because its failure signal is itself unreliable.

    The self-check row is the most elaborate cell in the warn-and-continue tier, and its endings are finer than the table can hold (model-availability-check.ts:91-122):

    • 404: log model-unavailable, with a fix suggestion;
    • 401 / 403: log model-credential-rejected, meaning the provider rejected the key itself;
    • custom BASE_URL: skip outright, because compatible endpoints often have no single-model query and a 404 says nothing;
    • no key configured: skip.

    Even a warning that does not block boot splits its answer into "the model does not exist" and "the credential was rejected", because the operator's next action is completely different for each.

    "No IdP and not single-user" is the only condition appearing in two tables: the boot checklist refuses it (see Refusing to boot), and at runtime requireUser's third form, authenticationUnavailable, answers every request with 503 (app.ts:608-618). The two layers are deliberate defense in depth: a normal deployment never reaches this branch, which exists for the unknown path of "somebody bypasses the boot check one day". The selector's comment also guarantees the other direction: "Checked first, and only ever true when there is no provider, so a configured deployment cannot fall back to it" (app.ts:612-613), so a deployment with sign-in configured cannot accidentally fall into the single-user form. The single-user mode's dev actor and the normal form createRequireUser's per-request table read are Chapter 3's subject.

    The most instructive contrast is the audit trail's two appearances. A boot audit row that cannot be written degrades silently; a sign-in audit write failure lets the login through. Then Chapter 5 shows the action gateway treating audit as a hard precondition of action, where even refused actions land a row. The same mechanism fails open on the telemetry path and fails closed on the boundary path. The tiers do not contradict each other; they are a precise sorting of which failure guards a boundary and which is only the boundary narrating itself.

    Deep Dive: Contract first, consumption later

    The tenant package hides three fields that are "validated but read by no one", and each is deliberate.

    knowledge.yaml is fully parsed and validated, yet has no consumer today. The comment at tenant-package.ts:220-228 explains: the Drive connector that used to consume it synced documents under a service account, so every answer came back as the deployment rather than as the person asking. The connector was removed, not repaired; the file stays in the contract because published packages already carry it and the validator should keep refusing broken ones. This is a fail-closed product decision: better to have no such feature than an overreaching version of it.

    allowed_groups in channels.yaml is validated, stored, and read by nothing. The schema comment and the docs both say so: the sign-in path never populates users.groups, and package channels never get membership rows, so a package-declared channel is unreachable today rather than open. With both ends of the control missing, the default picked the more conservative tier, and the docs say it plainly: "It decides nothing today, and a deployment that writes one must not treat it as an access control" (docs/configuration.md:1141-1151).
