    theme.css passes a miniature CSS firewall (comments stripped before evaluation, @import and url( banned, only :root / .dark blocks allowed, an allowlist of 32 variable names, tenant-package.ts:19-105) and then... has no consumer anywhere in the repository, and does not enter the package checksum. Unlike knowledge, this one left no honest comment behind: contract first, consumption later owes a sentence here, an asymmetry a reader of the source can chase the authors about.

    A reverse example: the catalog/ directory (the fintech package's definitions of ten candidate coworkers) is not read by the loader. It is a library of material you copy into agents/ to use. It used to load by default, and every fresh deployment booted into a dozen Bots nobody asked for; after the change to copy-to-use, "a fresh deployment opens on a short roster rather than a dozen Bots nobody asked for" (examples/fintech/agents/README.md). The template's sense of measure is here too: materials in full, defaults minimal.

    One more spot is easy to miss: when building the frontend, scripts/generate-app-config.ts validates the whole tenant package again, so a broken package cannot even build the frontend, but writes only the brand into the generated config. The sign-in page needs the product name and cannot wait for deploy time; things knowable only at deploy time, like the IdP list, are answered at runtime by the /api/capabilities projection. The same package is read at three moments: brand at build time, seed at boot time, projection at runtime. Each takes what it needs, and none reads what it should not.

    Apply This

    Every transferable pattern in this chapter revolves around one move: push boundary checks to the cheapest moment.

    Refuse at the boot boundary. Solves "configuration errors surfacing in their most expensive form at the most expensive moment". To adapt it: collect all configuration validation into one function that runs on the first line of main, and exit the process on any failure; write every error message as a sentence an operator can execute, with the file name, the variable name, and the fix command; specifically detect half-configuration (A set, B missing), because it means somebody meant to configure and got it wrong. The pitfall: alert fatigue. Where you can refuse, do not downgrade to a warning; a warning printed at every boot and read by no one is the same as nothing.

    The reachability trichotomy. Solves "the security check asks the wrong question": NODE_ENV answers what the process thinks of itself, reachability answers whether anybody else can reach it. To adapt it: turn security-relevant environment checks into classifications of deployment facts; use at least three classes (loopback / private / public), and do not kill the middle class, which is often the feature's real audience; anything unparseable goes into the most dangerous class. The pitfall: environment labels may be constants in your distribution channel (the Dockerfile sets production for everything), so asking them is asking nothing; and the classification logic must exist in exactly one place in the codebase, because two phrasings of the same question are the seed of an incident.

    Hand-written validators for actionable errors. Solves "a schema library's error messages assume the reader is a developer, while a configuration file's real reader is an administrator with shaky hands". To adapt it: on the boundary where a human hand-edits configuration, replace the schema library with small functions so every error names the file and the key; refuse duplicates while naming every source, instead of silently preferring one. The pitfall: do not carry the habit to internal API boundaries, where schema libraries are right. Hand-written validation holds only where the error message is the product, and written too often it becomes a second parser you have to maintain.

    Guarded upserts with ownership encoded in SQL. Solves "seed scripts overwriting user data past their authority" and check-then-act races. To adapt it: upsert with a setWhere (update only rows I own), and treat an empty RETURNING as a collision; choose throw-and-rollback or skip-and-warn by whether the namespace is shared with people, because throwing in a shared namespace hands any user a denial-of-service button; reclaim assets by a marker like granted_by, taking back only what you gave. The pitfall: do not SELECT first and then decide INSERT or UPDATE at the application layer, because the row can change owners between the two statements; the predicate must live inside the SQL itself.

    Configuration in the repo, secrets only as references. Solves the tension between "the same configuration must fit many environments" and "secrets cannot enter git". To adapt it: interpolate environment-dependent values with ${NAME:-fallback}, treat empty strings as unset and unset as an error; keep only the secret's name in configuration, put the body in an encrypted vault, and resolve on each use so rotation takes effect immediately. The pitfall: the semantics of an empty interpolation must be chosen explicitly. In this chapter an unset variable is an error while an empty endpoint withdraws the declaration, and both treatments are written into comments and docs. Passing an empty string downstream silently kneads "not configured" and "configured empty" into the same bug farm.

    Configuration and the tenant package answer "what is this deployment, and who is who", but getting the roster through the door is only the start. Chapter 3 answers how a deployment keeps answering "who is asking" on every request: how sign-in gets in, how roles are read, how the INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS floor acts as the backstop, and why the single button "remove a person" has to touch five tables and two locks.

    ← Chapter 1: The Architecture of a Governable Agent PlatformChapter 3: Identity and Access: Auth, Roles, and Removing a Person →

    Chapter 3: Identity and Access: Auth, Roles, and Removing a Person

    Chapter 2 showed OpenBot turning configuration into deployment shape: more than twenty checks that refuse the boot, and a tenant package seeded in one transaction and read only from the database at runtime. One entry on that refusal list got a reason but no follow-up: sign-in configured with INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS left empty kills the process at boot, because no screen anywhere can promote somebody once the deployment is running. Why does an email list matter enough to keep the whole process down? This chapter answers that question, and its reverse: once the list has let people in, how the platform keeps answering "who is asking".

    Identity is the foundation under every governance brick later in this book. The audit row's actor_user_id, the actor in the action gateway's evaluation, coworker (roster) visibility, a routine's owner: all of them first need to know who this is, and getting it wrong once has a concrete shape, one person running another person's private coworker and reading their threads. OpenBot's attitude toward identity is the same sentence as its attitude toward configuration: better to refuse an answer than to guess. Without this chapter's mechanics, every visitor to a deployment is an administrator. With them done half wrong, a removed person keeps working for days, until their cookie happens to expire.

    This chapter is also the thesis demonstrated on both faces. "The boundary lives in the deployment": who is an administrator, who may sign in, and which identity provider to use are all decided in the end by deployment configuration and database rows, never by a frontend screen or a claim inside a token. And "governance rides the protocol" meets a counterexample here: OpenBot's authentication stands on a popular library, Better Auth, and when the library's default model conflicts with enterprise semantics, OpenBot neither obeyed it nor forked it; it routed around the seams. By the end you will know how sign-in gets in, how roles are read, how the floor acts as the backstop, why the one button "remove a person" touches five tables and two locks, and why a deployment needs two sets of keys that never borrow from each other.

    The login surface: one library, four ways in

    OpenBot did not write its own session management, OAuth handshakes, or SAML parsing. Those are problems others have solved, and writing them again would only write them worse. It uses Better Auth for authentication, but depends on it through one narrow interface: the whole server's requirement of the auth library is one handler plus one api.getSession (server/src/auth/guards.ts:15-32).

    The interface has two implementations: the regular Better Auth instance (createAuth(), auth/index.ts:163), and a proxy that treats another OpenBot deployment as the authority in white-label mode (createOrganizationAuth(), auth/organization.ts:70; this chapter does not expand the latter). The session the interface returns carries an optional role field whose only reason to exist is the white-label path; that exception comes later in the chapter. The narrow interface is what makes every detour in the second half of this chapter legitimate: the library can be shimmed, wrapped, and replaced, because it was never the authority, only one end of the protocol.

    There are four ways in, each assembled differently, all facing the same checks once inside:

    Way in How it is assembled method tag at the door
    Google / Microsoft (Entra) Paired environment variables, Better Auth built-in providers oauth
    Okta OIDC discovery through the genericOAuth plugin: "Okta is not one place: every customer has their own issuer" (auth/index.ts:192-201) oauth
    Enterprise SAML / OIDC Registered at runtime, Better Auth sso() plugin sso-saml / sso-oidc
    SCIM 2.0 directory provisioning Enabled only when SCIM_BEARER_TOKEN is set scim

    The method tag in the third column is more than a statistic: it goes back on duty after the door. SSO-enforcement decisions branch on it, with sso-oidc/sso-saml/scim passing directly and every other method going on to the switch check (auth/index.ts:58). The break-glass flow in the floor section meets it again.

    Runtime-registered IdPs are routed by email domain: a person types their email address, and the part after @ decides which identity provider to ask (db/schema/core.ts:217-218). This routing table is a deployment fact: a company's own IdP is not something knowable at build time, so it lives in the database, registered by administrators at runtime, and there can be several. This "configuration or data" distinction becomes important later.

    The domain comparison itself is drift-proofed: the domain an administrator writes into the list and the domain in the provider-returned address must pass through the same normalizeDomain before they meet, because "Two copies drift, and the copy that misses an alias is the one that lets a credential endpoint through" (auth/email-domain.ts:22-30; the function normalizes with IDNA/UTS-46, the same rules browsers and resolvers use). One rule cannot mean one thing when written and another when matched. When the list is non-empty and the address yields no domain, the answer is always refusal (emailDomainAllowed, same file, 86-97): the safe reading of "I cannot tell" is never "let it through".

    Past the door, Better Auth's databaseHooks turn every sign-in into a pipeline:

    Two details are worth stopping for. First, the domain list and deny list are checked twice: user.create.before covers new accounts only, and session.create.before checks again on every sign-in of an existing account. Without the second pass, narrowing the domain list later would miss everyone who had signed in once (auth/index.ts:462-464). The refusal on that second pass is also fully formed: the hook throws FORBIDDEN with one true sentence, "Your access to this deployment has been removed." (auth/index.ts:490-497). Second, a refused sign-in still writes an audit row: session.refused is the only record of the attempt, because no user row was ever written and no session exists to inspect after the fact (auth/index.ts:414-415). The audited refusal is the most important row; Chapter 6 expands the principle, and here we see its shape at the login door.

    Audit writing itself is fail-open, and intentionally so: all sign-in audit goes through the single funnel record(), and these hooks run inside Better Auth, where throwing equals refusing the sign-in. "A trail that is briefly unavailable must not lock everybody out" (auth/index.ts:72-95). This does not contradict Chapter 5's action gateway, where audit is written before action and fails closed. The tiers differ: the gateway stops one action, the login door stops everyone's every day. The standard is not consistency; it is who pays when it fails.

    Spread the tier table out inside the identity subsystem and every cell has a source:

    • Fail-closed: ssoRequired() treats an unreadable setting as true (the break-glass section); a non-empty domain list with an unparseable address is refused by emailDomainAllowed (auth/email-domain.ts:86-97); the enterprise gate answers 503 when it cannot read a capability (admin/gate.ts:176-191); personHasAccess in the OAuth callback answers false whenever there is no peopleStore: "It also cannot remove anybody, which is exactly why guessing here would be a hole nothing else closes" (app.ts:1724-1728).
    • Fail-open: sign-in audit through record() (the previous paragraph); boot audit rows like computer.policy_loaded end in .catch(() => undefined), since a deployment must not refuse to start because its audit trail is unavailable (index.ts:535-543).

    Together the two columns are the identity layer's temperament: questions of entry and authorization have no safe default, so it refuses rather than answers; questions of bookkeeping have one, and the ledger never gets to lock the door in reverse.

    What lands in the database is more than audit rows. Treating the Better Auth handler as a black box, one sign-in's persistence surface across its hooks is five things, each with its own writer and failure semantics:

    What is persisted Writer Failure semantics
    user row Better Auth, clamped by the user.create before/after hooks No row unless the lists agree; writes session.refused
    session row Better Auth, with session.create.before re-checking the lists Throws FORBIDDEN if removed; no session is created
    role row Seeded by seedRole, replayed by applyConfiguredAdmin Both funnel into setRole's single-transaction delete-then-insert (expanded in the floor section)
    lastSignedInAt stampSignIn A write failure only logs; it does not block sign-in
    audit row one funnel: record() Fail-open (the previous paragraph)

    The fifth row is worth a closer look. The first step of session.create.after is stampSignIn, advancing users.lastSignedInAt to this sign-in's moment, written as greatest(coalesce(lastSignedInAt, at), at) (auth/index.ts:97-106, called at :501). The greatest semantics mean a late or replayed callback cannot turn the clock back, and running it twice equals running it once. The whole update is wrapped in try/catch, and a failure lands one structured sign-in-stamp-write-failed log line (auth/index.ts:110-119): the same tier of judgment as fail-open audit; an unwritable timestamp is not worth locking anyone out over. None of the five relies on implicit framework behavior: the user and session rows are written by the library and clamped by hooks, while roles, the timestamp, and audit are written entirely by OpenBot's own code. Every entry has a writer who can give a reason, so each kind can be audited and replayed on its own.

    One more refusal worth remembering: Entra's profile mapping falls back through email → upn → preferred_username, and when none yields an email it returns an empty object and lets Better Auth refuse the sign-in. "Being refused is a far better answer than being quietly admitted as somebody the deployment cannot recognise" (auth/index.ts:139-141). Why would Entra yield no email: a multi-tenant app's optional claims may never arrive, because an external user's token is minted by their own tenant and does not inherit this app's claim configuration, and the default tenant common is exactly multi-tenant. Better Auth maps email literally with no fallback, so on those deployments it is undefined (auth/index.ts:121-138). An identity system's manners have no "close enough counts as half a person" tier.

    The SCIM path deserves a paragraph of its own, as the only way in not initiated by a person: the directory provisions people in (person.provisioned lands an audit row) and writes group memberships into users.groups. That field is marked input: false, so no sign-in request can write it; only SCIM's projection can. Its readers are the group-based capability switch and the network policy, and the comment names reader and writer in the same place (auth/index.ts:271-279). The field's entire reason to exist is on the read side: it is the channel through which a directory affects capability decisions inside the deployment, but it never enters from a sign-in request and never becomes a role. Even the bearer token considers rotation: SCIM_BEARER_TOKEN_NEXT is accepted alongside the current one, so rotating the token does not stop the directory (auth/scim.ts:16, 133). But one line is drawn hard: "The OpenBot role (admin/user) is never taken from the directory" (auth/scim.ts:159-163). A directory may provision people and groups; roles are always the deployment's own decision. The directory is a source, never an authority; that is the floor mechanism seen from its other face: who gets to be an administrator is either named by configuration or granted on a screen, and there is no third hidden channel.

    The audit rows the login door leaves behind are identity governance's minimal vocabulary:

    Audit row When written Answers
    session.signed_in every successful sign-in who came in
    session.refused a refused sign-in who was kept out
    session.break_glass a list break-glass under SSO enforcement who broke the glass
    person.admin_by_configuration the moment a floor replay promotes who was promoted by configuration
    person.provisioned SCIM provisions a person who was provisioned by the directory

    Every governance story in the later chapters opens in this vocabulary.

    Two textbook workarounds

    Better Auth's SSO plugin assumes personal integration: the registrar's userId is stamped onto the sso_providers row, the list route shows only the registrar's own rows, deletion requires the same person, and rows cascade from the users table, so deleting a person deletes the whole company's sign-in. OpenBot's comment states the model error in full: "a company's Okta tenant is not the property of whichever administrator happened to paste the metadata in" (auth/identity-provider-store.ts:8-9). The error has two concrete identity consequences: a second administrator opens the Identity providers screen, sees an empty list, and re-registers a provider that already exists; and the person who set up the environment leaves, taking the company's login with them.

    OpenBot's response is to leave the library untouched and reroute at the seams: two route detours plus two supporting patches, one sentence each:

    • An admin check in front of the registration route. The library's SSO registration route hangs only sessionMiddleware, so any signed-in user could register an IdP for some domain. The patch shims the check ahead of the library's handler: a request hitting the set gets a fresh session and a live role lookup, and non-admins get 403 (app.ts:552-566).
    • Self-written full-table routes for list and delete. Admin-only routes query the whole table, so a provider registered by anyone can be seen and deleted, and deletion writes an audit row. Registration still goes through Better Auth: there is one parser for metadata and one storage place for the client secret (identity-provider-store.ts:17-19).
    • The foreign key changed to set null. sso_providers.userId went from cascade to onDelete: "set null", degrading userId into a note of who registered the row: the person leaves, the login lives (db/schema/core.ts:233-235).
    • An encrypting wrapper around the write-path adapter factory. The client secret and signing certificate in a provider's config sit in plain text columns, and the library offers no encryption hook. Wrapping the adapter factory is the only funnel that catches every read and write path: four methods must be wrapped (create/update/findOne/findMany), updateMany only if it exists (encrypt-sso-config.ts:174-175).

    Why call this textbook-grade: none of the four patches changes one line of the library, none explodes on a Better Auth upgrade, and each lands exactly on the point where the semantic error occurs: the placement of the permission check, the ownership, the lifecycle binding, the storage of secrets. The correct dose of a patch is exactly covering the error; one gram more and you are maintaining a parallel implementation for the rest of your life.

    Equally notable is the road not taken: fork. Forking an auth library means backporting every upstream security patch yourself and chasing every protocol evolution yourself, while everything that would buy, these four seams already bought. How exactly each seam is repaired, how the front check is shimmed, how the full-table routes are written, how the adapter is wrapped, is Chapter 17's material, expanded item by item.

    One authority, two projections

    Sign-in settles "who are you", but one run must answer two different questions about the same person: whose threads and memories are these, and which coworkers may this person run. OpenBot nails both questions to a single resolver, resolveRequestActor, the only one in the whole process. The comment explains why there is only one: "Answering them from different places is how one person ends up running another's private coworker, or reading their thread" (server/src/index.ts:256-262).

    ts
    // server/src/index.ts:271-285 (excerpt)
  const session = await auth?.api.getSession({ headers: request.headers });
  const user = session?.user;
  if (!user) {
    throw new Error("A CopilotKit run requires a signed-in user.");
  }
  const roles = user.role
    ? [user.role]
    : await roleRepository.rolesForUser(user.id);
  // ... (elided: throws when neither role exists)
  return {
    id: user.id,
    name: user.name ?? user.email ?? user.id,
    role: roles.includes("admin") ? "admin" : "user",
  };

    Watch where the role comes from: never the session claims. user_roles is a set table with (user_id, role) as its composite primary key, and "admin wins" is a read-side rule: any row saying this person is an admin makes them an admin. Every request reads the table live.

    The same authority casts two differently shaped projections outward:

    • identifyUser (index.ts:290-293) serves Intelligence's thread ownership; signed-out throws directly, because a thread must belong to somebody and there is no anonymous tier.
    • identifyActor (index.ts:307-314) serves coworker visibility grants; signed-out returns ANONYMOUS_ACTOR (index.ts:305), an actor with an empty id that owns nothing: it matches no private profile and is no administrator. This projection exists for /info: the runtime must be able to describe itself to deployment checks ("license invalid" and "chat silently broken" are two different answers), and describing itself needs no identity. But the anonymous actor never passes identifyUser, so acting still requires an identity. The asymmetry is deliberate: self-description is public, action is not.
    • A third variant, actorFor(ownerUserId) (index.ts:573-586), serves the headless paths that have no request, routines and approval continuations, resolving roles by owner. The comment emphasizes in capitals: "THE ROLE IS READ, NOT ASSUMED". Hardcoding role: "user" would make an administrator's routine unable to see admin-only coworkers, reporting "that Bot is no longer registered" about a Bot sitting right there in the chat.

    The HTTP side's requireUser middleware (auth/guards.ts:55-91) is the same discipline: every request's getSession carries disableCookieCache: true, and roles are read live from user_roles. The comment is one sentence: "Fresh, not the cookie cache: a role changed a moment ago has to apply to this request." (app.ts:555-556) This is a deliberate trade of performance for correctness: roles are low-cardinality, high-consequence facts, and one indexed query buying "demotion and removal take effect immediately" is worth it in any enterprise deployment. No session is 401; a session with neither role is 403. "Who are you" and "are you authorized" are two questions and two status codes.

    requireUser itself is a three-way choice made at assembly: one ternary decides this deployment's HTTP identity form before the process starts serving (app.ts:612-618):

    ts
    // server/src/app.ts:614-618
  const requireUser = config.singleUser
    ? createDevRequireUser()
    : auth && roleRepository
      ? createRequireUser(auth, roleRepository)
      : authenticationUnavailable;

    It shows identity form decided at assembly time: the three forms share one name, and downstream routes neither know nor need to know which one they are running on. Each form's behavior at the door:

    Form Assembly condition Behavior at the door
    createDevRequireUser() config.singleUser Asks no session; puts DEV_ACTOR straight into the context (auth/dev-actor.ts:88-95). On a dev machine, "who are you" has one fixed, honest answer
    createRequireUser(auth, roleRepository) a regular deployment The discipline above made concrete: fresh session, live role reads, 401/403 tiers
    authenticationUnavailable no IdP and not single-user Always 503, "No identity provider is configured"

    The third form is actually unreachable: Chapter 2's boot checks already refused the "no IdP and not single-user" combination, and the refusal message gives the reason in full, that on a deployment without sign-in every visitor is an administrator (auth/dev-actor.ts:82-84). Yet the middleware layer still writes it as an explicit third form instead of leaving an implicit undefined to explode at runtime. An "impossible" branch still gets a name, a status code, and an error message that tells the truth: the same family of honesty as Chapter 2's reachOf() counting the unparseable as public, with no unnamed cell in the tier table.

    The normal form's body is worth a read (auth/guards.ts:55-89): the two failures each say one true thing, 401 "Authentication required." without a session and 403 "Authorization required." with a session but neither role. What passes into context.var.actor afterward is the five-field {id, email, name, image, role}, and every sub-route then reads the same answer through the AppVariables type. There is no request-level cache object; every handler's stores live in the closure. Note the role check carries the projection shape too: session.user.role is used first when present, a claim signed by the white-label authority proxy, otherwise user_roles is read live, line-for-line isomorphic to resolveRequestActor's reading.

    The same file holds an anti-symmetric decision: requireAdmin departs from the middleware style and is a function called inside handlers, the caller writing const denied = requireAdmin(context); return denied ?? … (auth/guards.ts:91-99, usage at app.ts:836-839). Why not middleware: plenty of routes branch after requireUser anyway, and the administrator check sits inside each concrete route next to the action it protects, rather than mounted by path prefix with mounting order left to luck. When assembly finishes, this name is handed as-is to the enterprise controls' gate: app.use("/api/*", createEnterpriseGate(requireUser)) (app.ts:620), so capability switches and model allowlists stand on the shoulders of whichever of the three forms is running.

    One exception proves the rule: the AuthService interface's session has a user.role field, but the comment states it is "Set only by a server-verified organization authority" (auth/guards.ts:27-29). Only sessions proxied back from a server-verified authority deployment in white-label mode may carry a role. On the Better Auth path a role never travels in the session: tokens expire, get cached, get copied, and the right storage for this decision is the user_roles table plus one indexed query per request. Letting a high-consequence fact live where it can be changed immediately and take effect immediately is the identity layer's costliest and most worthwhile non-optimization.

    The floor: INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS end to end

    Now the opening question can be answered: why does an empty list refuse the boot. Because a role can come from only two places: this list, or a grant on a screen by someone who is already an administrator. With the list empty, the first person to sign in is a plain user forever, and no screen can promote them: "Refusing at start-up is the only cheap moment to catch that; the expensive one is after the first person has signed in" (config.ts:791-798). But the boot check is only the floor's first brick. The full chain has four links, each plugging one concrete hole:

    Seeding at account creation. When a new account lands, seedRole decides admin or user by whether the email hits the list (auth/index.ts:436-441). Note it matches by email, never by provider: in a deployment mid-migration, the same person comes from Entra this week and Okta next week, and to this list they are the same person.

    Replay on every sign-in, promote-only. This is the floor's core mechanism. Roles used to be written once at account creation: editing the list changed nothing for people already in the table, and no screen could fix it. applyConfiguredAdmin (auth/roles.ts:85-115) replays the list at every sign-in: a hit ensures the admin row exists, a miss leaves everything untouched. It only promotes, and only touches people the list names; everybody else's roles are the property of the admin screens, and a sign-in overwriting them would produce a screen that lies from the moment they come back (roles.ts:78-79).

    The replay also returns a value: whether this sign-in is the moment a promotion happened. If yes, it writes one person.admin_by_configuration audit row: "anybody who can edit the configuration can make themselves an administrator, and until this returned something there was no row anywhere saying it had happened" (roles.ts:81-84).

    Writing the role itself is a single-transaction "delete the rows that should not be there, then insert the one that should":

    ts
    // server/src/auth/roles.ts:45-50
  await database.transaction(async (tx) => {
    await tx
      .delete(userRoles)
      .where(and(eq(userRoles.userId, userId), ne(userRoles.role, role)));
    await tx.insert(userRoles).values({ userId, role }).onConflictDoNothing();
  });

    Why not one upsert: user_roles is a set table, and insert-without-delete leaves old roles behind; and if the delete-then-insert ran outside one transaction, a request on another process between the two statements would find this person with no role at all and 403 them, which reads as a permissions bug (roles.ts:35-38).

    The UI says 409 to the floor. Demoting somebody named in the list on the admin screen returns 409: "This deployment names that address in INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS, so they stay an administrator. Change the configuration instead." (app.ts:988-996) The reason: allowing the demotion would produce a screen that lies until the person comes back, since the floor promotes them again at the next sign-in. Removing access is likewise 409 (app.ts:1053-1061). There are also two self-lockout guards: nobody can remove their own administrator role or their own access (app.ts:1006-1011, 1065-1067), because on a deployment with one administrator, that is the whole deployment. A screen refusing to do something it cannot do is far more honest than pretending it can.

    Break-glass under SSO enforcement. Enterprise deployments often turn on "SSO required": social logins are refused outright. The switch has a disaster shape: if the IdP goes down or is misconfigured, every administrator is locked out. So the list has a second identity: the break-glass key.

    ts
    // server/src/auth/index.ts:58-70
  if (["sso-oidc", "sso-saml", "scim"].includes(input.method)) return "allow";
  let required: boolean;
  try {
    required = await input.ssoRequired();
  } catch {
    required = true;
  }
  if (!required) return "allow";
  if (input.email && isConfiguredAdmin(input.email, input.initialAdminEmails)) {
    return "break_glass";
  }
  return "refuse";

    The three judgments each take a position: when ssoRequired() cannot read the setting it is treated as true, failing closed, because settings that cannot be read refuse the sign-in; people on the list can always break the glass; and every break-glass writes a session.break_glass audit row (auth/index.ts:48-51). Break-glass is not a backdoor: a backdoor by definition is the one you cannot see, and this one leaves its name in the audit on every use. The break-glass comparison itself is normalized first: isConfiguredAdmin applies trim().toLowerCase() to both sides before comparing (auth/roles.ts:18-22), because the list is hand-edited and case and whitespace should not decide who gets to break glass.

    The moment the switch turns on, an old debt comes due: sessions are checked only at creation, and created sessions keep renewing as they are used. Unhandled, everyone who signed in with Google or a password stays inside forever. So saving "SSO required" triggers a batch sweep (auth/sso-required.ts:16-45): sessions of everyone without a registered IdP account are deleted, with three kinds kept: those who came through SSO (they can sign right back in anyway), those on the break-glass list, and the administrator currently clicking save, so the strike does not log out its own operator. The function is deliberately safe to re-run: after a failed attempt, retrying is running it again. A switch changes more than future entry rules; it has retroactive force over existing sessions. This is what "configuration is the boundary" looks like at runtime, not only at boot.

    Removing a person

    On the admin screen, "remove" is one button. Under the button lies this chapter's densest design, because nearly every step of a naive implementation is wrong:

    • Deleting the user row does not work: the next sign-in through the identity provider recreates it, with a new id and a history that does not remember being removed (db/schema/core.ts:243-248);
    • Blocking only the next sign-in does not work: the current session is alive, and a cookie can be good for days;
    • Deleting external account links does not work: the account on Slack becomes a guest that belongs to nobody.

    OpenBot's removal is two-phase. The first phase is the two things that must be pinned down, in one transaction:

    ts
    // server/src/people/store.ts:299-313 (excerpt)
      const [user] = await database
        .select({ email: users.email })
        .from(users)
        .where(eq(users.id, userId))
        .limit(1);
      if (!user) return;

      await database.transaction(async (tx) => {
        await tx
          .insert(revokedAccess)
          .values({ email: normalize(user.email), revokedBy })
          .onConflictDoNothing();
        await tx.delete(sessions).where(eq(sessions.userId, userId));
      });

    The deny list blocks the next sign-in, deleting sessions stops the current one: "Both halves matter" (people/store.ts:291-297). Note the deny list's key is the email, never the user id: the id gets recreated on re-login, and the address is the only thing that survives. The address is lowercased before storage, because the provider's choice of case is its own freedom, and two rows differing only in case mean a person half blocked (core.ts:242-251).

    For "the user row stays", the audit trail cooperates on the opposite flank: audit_events.actor_user_id deliberately carries no foreign key (db/schema/core.ts:435-439). The trail is append-only (Chapter 6 shows how database triggers enforce it), so any delete that would cascade into it is an update the triggers would refuse; with the foreign key attached, a person who ever did anything could never be deleted. What removal must erase is the person's ability to enter; the evidence that they were here stays. The two directions call for exactly opposite handling, and a deny list plus a foreign-key-less audit column take one end each.

    The second phase retires credentials and identity links, deliberately outside the first phase's transaction (people/store.ts:315-327). The reasons are written out in full: retiring credentials goes through the credential vault's own interface and writes its own audit rows, and what identity asks of the vault is itself only a narrow interface, Pick<CredentialStore, "revoke">, since retiring a person needs one verb (identity/retire.ts:14, 69). Holding the person's removal transaction open while all that completes would let an unrelated failure roll back the deny row and the session deletion, the two things that must never fail to pin. So the order is: bar the door first, collect the keys second. If the second phase throws, the first has already committed, and the audit trail shows a removal without its retirement alongside: an honest record of what happened, and removing once more patches it up.

    On the identity-links side, retireIdentityLinks (server/src/identity/retire.ts:67-136) shows the full form of concurrency discipline:

    Three layers of design each block something different. Link rows are not deleted: status becomes needs_reconnect and credentials are detached, because user_id deliberately has no foreign key, so the external account keeps resolving to the removed person and gets refused, "rather than turning into an unlinked guest" (identity/retire.ts:30-37). Messages from the removed person on Slack land on "refused", never on "anonymous". Two layers of advisory locks fix the ordering: the user-level lock first (issueChallenge takes it too, so a redemption code lands entirely before or entirely after the removal, never in parallel), then deletion of pending challenges (which waits for in-flight redeemChallenge calls to commit, so the links they wrote become visible; the challenges themselves live only 10 minutes, and a cleanup with a one-day threshold collects the expired, identity/store.ts:505-519), then the person's (provider, realm) locks in sorted order, matching the lock order of the link-writing paths to prevent deadlock (identity/store.ts:31-56). Audit and retirement share one transaction: one failure, including a failed audit write, rolls the whole thing back, and a retry starts over and re-audits every link. An older version that wrote the audit after the commit once lost the remaining links' audit rows forever in a failure, because the retry found every link already retired (retire.ts:39-44).

    My favorite part of this code is that the comment also writes down the gap it could not close: a writeLink arriving after the removal commits (an OAuth callback that already passed the session check) re-links that realm for this person, in active status. The responsibility for refusing it is explicitly handed to linkedUser's callers, the external-message paths in delivery and responsibilities/slack, which must re-check the deny list themselves (retire.ts:53-63; identity/store.ts:350-354). This is not a hole being disclosed; it is an engineer being honest about a concurrency boundary: locks can only order what they can hold, and for what they cannot hold, pin the responsibility on whoever can catch it.

    Retirement has two more closing moves:

    • Both halves run. Plugin connections (brokered accounts like Composio) and identity links belong to two subsystems, and retireOwnedAccounts runs both halves to the end before summarizing: one half throwing does not stop the other, and at the end an AggregateError naming both causes is thrown, because stopping there would leave every linked account's token alive while the retry hits the same refusal first (identity/retire.ts:138-170).
    • The reverse operation exists and is one line. restore just deletes the deny row (people/store.ts:332-343): sessions are not restored, sign in again; credentials are not restored, reconnect. Restoring a person's access is one line, because removal erased only access.

    SCIM deprovisioning speaks the same vocabulary: when the directory deactivates a person, the hook does one thing inside the provisioning transaction, writing the deny list first ("Deny-listing before the transaction commits errs toward refusing"), and the slow parts, connector retirement and computer shutdown, offboard asynchronously (auth/scim.ts:55-101).

    Conversely, when the directory reactivates a person, only deny entries SCIM itself wrote get lifted. The mechanism is a prefix: SCIM-written rows set revokedBy to scim:directory (SCIM_REVOKED_BY_PREFIX, auth/scim.ts:27, 70-75), and reactivation lifts only rows matching the prefix (scim.ts:106-111): "An administrator's removal stands until an administrator lifts it" (scim.ts:110). The source of a removal has sovereignty over its undo: the directory's removals are the directory's to lift, and an administrator's removals are an administrator's alone.

    A note on this screen's own read path. The people list uses keyset pagination with a base64url cursor of {lastSignedInAt, email}, deliberately not offset: offset re-reads and discards every row before it, page 50 is fifty times the work of page 1, and somebody signing in mid-pagination shifts every later row by one and hides another person entirely (people/store.ts:44-51). A corrupted cursor is treated as page one rather than an error, because there is nothing here worth refusing over (same file, 103-107). Default page 50, capped at 200, search terms capped at 200 characters (people/store.ts:82-93; app.ts:936-942).

    The same store also answers the login path's deny query: isRevoked(email) is the read port of the table session.create.before re-checks on every sign-in. And the lastSignedInAt in the cursor key is exactly the column the login pipeline stamps on every sign-in: read path and write path meet on the same column.

    One last look at how these tables behave on deletion; they are the whole chapter compressed:

    Table What it records When the person is removed
    users Better Auth's account rows Not deleted; deleting would be recreated
    sessions live sessions deleted immediately
    revoked_access removed emails (the primary key is the email) one row inserted; revokedBy is not a foreign key, since administrators too may be removed one day
    user_roles the role set cascades with the user, but it no longer matters, since the deny list blocks first
    sso_providers runtime-registered IdPs userId set null; the company's sign-in is unaffected
    identity_links external account links needs_reconnect + credentials detached; row kept
    credentials credentials this person held revoked (revoked_at); row kept for audit

    Two sets of keys

    The identity layer has one last deployment-level fact: secrets are encrypted under two sets of keys that never borrow from each other. KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is the key for formats OpenBot owns: the credential vault's envelopes, stored website passwords, SSO provider configs, and the signing keys for a few derived uses. BETTER_AUTH_SECRET is deliberately reserved for Better Auth's own use: the OAuth access/refresh tokens from Google/Microsoft/Okta sign-ins are encrypted with the library's own encryptOAuthTokens: true (auth/index.ts:356-368). Why do login tokens not enter OpenBot's own vault: the library's encryption knows every path tokens take in and out, tolerates existing plaintext in the columns, and follows the library's own upgrade lifecycle; hand-rolling encryption inside somebody else's storage layer is how rows become permanently unreadable. The division of labor is the trust boundary: each key answers only for data in a format it owns. Chapter 17 has the full discussion of envelope formats, derived subkeys, and SSO config encryption.

    Apply This

    This chapter's patterns all revolve around one move: taking "who is this, and do they belong here" back from session claims, library defaults, and frontend screens, into the deployment's own database and configuration.

    1. One authority, projections everywhere. What it solves: when different sides of the same person (thread ownership, authorization scope) are answered from different code paths, what drifts out is a permissions bug, one person running another's private coworker. How to adapt it: the system has exactly one resolver for "who is this", and everything else is its projection; tighten each projection to its consumer, so the action side throws when signed out and the description side gets an anonymous who owns nothing. The pitfall: projections must not derive from each other; the anonymous projection's default permissions must be zero, since one millimeter wider makes it a backdoor; headless paths (timed jobs with no request) re-resolve by owner and never hardcode a role.

    2. Route around a library's seams instead of forking it. What it solves: a dependency's domain model conflicts with your semantics (personal integration vs deployment property); changing the library means maintaining it, obeying it means swallowing wrong semantics. How to adapt it: find the narrow passages the library must pass through, route front-checks, adapter factories, foreign key declarations, and reroute only at the points where the semantic error occurs; keep what the library gets right (parsing, storage) as-is and compress the patch surface to the minimum. The pitfall: a generic wrapper layer over the library is signing up for a worse parallel implementation; re-review every seam on each dependency upgrade, because a seam's shape is the library's internal fact; write down why the library default is wrong at each detour, or the next person deletes it as redundant.

    3. A configuration floor, replayed at every entry, promote-only. What it solves: break-glass-grade grants (first administrator, emergency entry) written once at account creation stop reacting to configuration changes, with no screen to fix them; plus the "last administrator locks themselves out" shape. How to adapt it: make such grants configuration assertions replayed at every authentication; the replay only promotes and only touches people the list names, leaving everything else to runtime screens; the moment a promotion happens lands an audit row, since anybody who can edit configuration can make themselves an administrator and that must have a row to show. The pitfall: the UI must refuse demotions of floor-listed people (409 plus a truthful error), or the screen lies; every use of the break-glass path writes audit, because an invisible emergency entrance is what a backdoor is.

    4. Removal is a state machine, not a DELETE. What it solves: deleting the account row does not work (the next sign-in recreates it), blocking new sign-ins alone does not work (the old session lives for days), deleting external links does not work (old identities become anonymous guests). How to adapt it: key the deny list by the external identity (email), never the internal id; delete sessions and write the deny entry in one transaction, both halves indispensable whatever their order; retire credentials outside the must-pin transaction, leaving an honest record on failure that a retry can patch; set external account links to "needs reconnect" instead of deleting them, so old identities keep resolving to "refused" rather than to "does not exist". The pitfall: do not touch other subsystems' interfaces inside the removal transaction, since an unrelated failure must not roll back the access revocation; write the lock ordering into comments and keep it consistent with the opposing paths; undo must distinguish sources, a directory's removal being the directory's to lift and an administrator's the administrator's.

    5. Read roles live, and pay the query fee for high-consequence facts. What it solves: cached roles delay demotion and removal, and a permission revocation that takes effect late is nearly no revocation. How to adapt it: low-cardinality, high-consequence security facts (roles, deny lists, grant rows) are read from the database per request with session caches disabled; save caching for high-cardinality, low-consequence reads. The pitfall: never bake roles into sessions or JWT claims, where they are fossils from the moment of issuance; decide the tier for read failures in advance, here 401/403, fail-closed, because identity questions have no safe default; and accept the decision's price, one indexed query per request, writing down in a comment why you pay it.

    The next chapter enters the book's heartbeat: a turn leaves the browser, streams back through AG-UI, and every tool call along the way passes the action gateway. The actor in the gateway's evaluation context and the actor_user_id in the audit rows are both the nail this chapter drove in: once identity is wrong, every layer of governance above governs the wrong person.

    Part II: The Governed Turn

    The turn is the heartbeat; the gateway is the conscience; the audit trail is the memory.

    Chapter 4: The Life of a Turn: The AG-UI Runtime

    Chapter 3 showed how OpenBot turns "who are you" into an unforgeable fact: one resolver, resolveRequestActor, answers identity and authorization together; the administrator floor only goes up; removing a person is a precisely ordered sequence of deletes and denials. Identity is the static foundation. What makes an enterprise nervous is the dynamic part: when someone tells a Bot "send this report to Finance," what actually happens inside the system over the next few minutes?

    This chapter dissects those minutes. A turn begins with one sentence from a person, passes through the protocol, a lock, an event stream, and at least one run, and ends with a reply persisted in the channel, or with one of the six other endings. What breaks without this machinery? Without the thread lock, two concurrent turns write events into each other's runs. Without outcome settlement, a turn that stopped to wait for an approval gets recorded as "said nothing." Without one rigorously executed cleanup block, a 3 a.m. routine locks a person out of their own conversation with no screen to explain why.

    By the end of this chapter you will understand three things: the minimal kernel of AG-UI (this book does not assume you have read it); how the browser path and the unattended path share that kernel; and why the book's central bet, that governance rides the protocol, can hold at all. The protocol is the only way in and out of a turn, so every governance point hangs on its boundary.

    Catching up: the minimal AG-UI kernel

    AG-UI is CopilotKit's open protocol, and it fixes one thing: the shape of the conversation between an agent and an interface. The minimal kernel fits in one sentence: the client POSTs a RunAgentInput, and the server streams back an event stream. The input carries threadId (which conversation), runId (the identity of this run), messages (history plus the new message), tools (what is available this turn), plus context and forwardedProps (pockets the caller stuffs for the agent; the latter is handed back to client code untouched, and Chapter 11's signed run assertion rides that pocket). OpenBot's turn engine records in a comment how the run side rebuilds the input from these fields (toolkit/src/run-turn.ts:692-696).

    The returning stream has four categories:

    Category Representative events The question it answers
    Lifecycle RUN_STARTED / RUN_FINISHED / RUN_ERROR Is the run alive, and how did it end
    Text TEXT_MESSAGE_START / CONTENT / END What the Bot is saying
    Tool calls TOOL_CALL_START / ARGS / END / RESULT What the Bot is about to do, and what came of it
    Custom CUSTOM Anything the protocol did not foresee (approval suspension rides on it)

    One thing outside the four categories earns its own paragraph: frontend tools, the key to the second half of this chapter. A tool's declaration travels in the input, but its execution can happen on the client. When the model decides to call a frontend tool, the run ends on purpose (RUN_FINISHED carrying outcome: interrupt), the browser executes the tool and renders the result, and then a new run starts, carrying the tool result back into the conversation.

    This yields a book-wide vocabulary rule: a turn is not a run. A turn is the question-and-answer the person perceives; a run is one request-and-event-stream at the protocol layer. A turn that touches the browser is a row of runs on the wire: the Bot requests a click, the run ends, the browser answers, the next run begins carrying the answer. The frontend comment says it plainly: the agent reports itself idle in every one of those gaps, "the truth about the wire and a lie about the turn" (channel-chat.tsx:572-577). The wire is true and the turn-level statement is the lie; any code that hangs the UI lifecycle on run signals will announce the turn's end in the middle of the turn.

    For clarity the diagram omits the Intelligence gateway that forwards events in between; the section on the three fan-out channels adds it back.

    One turn = one or more runs + the client-side actions between runs. Remember this inequality; every design later in this chapter stands on it.

    On the frontend, the inequality takes the shape of a pair of counters rather than a boolean: turnsInFlight decides whether the next message sends or queues, and runsInFlight decides how far the Stop button can reach (channel-chat.tsx:559-586). Two facts, one counter each, because the component's buttons can start a second turn while the first is still going.

    Two paths, one kernel

    A turn has two ways to be born in OpenBot. The browser path: someone hits Enter in a channel, the React app POSTs to /api/copilotkit/*, passes the session guard and Chapter 3's resolveRequestActor, and arrives at the CopilotRuntime assembled by mountCopilotRuntime (server/src/copilot.ts:1695). The headless path: a routine fires on schedule, a Bot hands off to another Bot, a Slack message gets paired. There is no browser and nobody watching, but the turn must land on the same thread, because the person will read it in the channel tomorrow morning. The toolkit's createTurnRunner drives this path (toolkit/src/run-turn.ts).

    The kernel the two paths share is deeper than it looks: the same agent registry (rebuilt per request; a private Bot must not exist for anyone else), the same system prompt assembly, the same sanitizeSeededHistory, the same middleware chain, and the same action gateway. Whoever executes a tool, adjudication and audit travel the same road (Chapter 5 opens this up). The only difference is who drives the run and who holds the lock.

    The rebuilt registry produces three kinds of agent (copilot.ts:90-138): built_in gets wrapped as BuiltInAgentWithSaneHistory; remote_ag_ui and remote_mastra get dialed as remote agents and then wrapped in middleware; and one kind you might not expect, unavailable, for a Bot that was deleted while its thread still exists. Its run() throws the reason directly: refuse at the endpoint rather than contact it, because a deleted coworker has no endpoint worth contacting and the person deserves the reason, not a transport error (agents.ts:325-329, paraphrased). The registry is more than a lookup map you call when an entry exists; even absence has behavior in it.

    There is an invisible discipline on the assembly side too: the runtime clone()s the agent before every run, and the base class's clone copies only base-class fields. So the three toolkit classes each hand-write clone(), copying private fields and the middleware list back through a cast (agents.ts:186-206, 285-300). The comment owns the reasoning: nothing registers middleware on built-in Bots today, and the hand-written clones exist so that when something does, it does not get lost in the clone. An insurance premium paid for a use case that does not exist yet, written down in a comment.

    The headless path builds the agent as the owner through the same actorAgentResolver (index.ts:1520-1556): the role is read out, not assumed, and Chapter 3's ruler is reused unchanged. If the Bot does not exist, a named RoutineBotNotRegistered is thrown, and the fatigue rule disables the routine after ten consecutive failures: exactly the right handling for a routine pointing at something that is never coming back.

    One assembly detail on the browser path is worth remembering: the CopilotKit handler mounts at the root path and brings its own basePath. Mount it under /api/copilotkit and you get a double prefix: Hono strips the prefix, the handler strips it again, every route lands on /api/copilotkit/api/copilotkit/*, and /info answers 404. The browser reports "Runtime info request failed with status 404" while the server logs stay blank (app.ts:1351-1356). Where a framework convention collides with server route semantics, incidents all grow quiet.

    The headless path is more instructive, because OpenBot made a decision there that most teams dare not make: copy the framework's private engine by hand. Inside the CopilotKit package sits runCanonicalChannelAgent, the package-private headless turn engine, not exported. OpenBot copied it into run-turn.ts and added exactly one thing, getOrCreateThread: idempotent, with the 409 race of concurrent creation already handled, safe on the first firing and the thousandth. A routine may be the first thing that ever touches a thread; on the browser path the first message creates the thread as a side effect (run-turn.ts:631-650).

    Why not mount a second mountCopilotRuntime and POST to your own run route? The file header admits this works perfectly well for identity: identifyUser and identifyActor are both injectable, and Chapter 3's double projection is reused unchanged. The option was rejected on information. The run route returns {threadId, runId, joinToken, realtime} at gateway-JOIN; the caller learns "the turn started" and nothing else. No completion signal, no reply text, no failure; recovering any of them requires a second transport. Strictly more moving parts in exchange for strictly less information (run-turn.ts:11-19). This is the textbook case of "what was not built": the runner-up option was not unusable; it could not answer the questions the caller must answer.

    The cost is recorded just as honestly: five ɵ-prefixed private methods (ɵgetRunnerWsUrl and ɵgetRunnerAuthToken at assembly, plus ɵacquireThreadLock, ɵrenewThreadLock, and ɵcleanupThreadLock for the lock lifecycle), with the request and response interfaces restated by hand. A renamed field will not blow up the type checker. It will pass against your own restatement and then get silently dropped on the wire. "That is what the test file is for" (run-turn.ts:27-29): the companion tests are tripwires, so a framework upgrade blows up the test first, not production. The header even records the runtime version the copy was checked against at birth, and the pinned dependency in the manifest is already newer (run-turn.ts:4, toolkit/package.json). The gap hangs there as a standing risk, not hidden as a scandal.

    The parameter comment of createTurnRunner is documentation in its own right (run-turn.ts:76-96). Five parameters, each declaring its governance role:

    • ownerUserId: the actor the run asserts; grants and connections resolve to them.
    • routineId: the audit trail names who fired this turn, rather than the owner.
    • runId: the durable delivery id; the lock, the runner, and the events reuse the same value.
    • depth: the chain depth of Bot-to-Bot handoffs; a person's turn defaults to 0.
    • onText: an incremental callback for surfaces that can show an in-progress turn.

    One reef the copy had to get right: threadId and the message list are assigned on the agent, not merely stuffed into the input. The runner calls agent.runAgent(input, …), and runAgent rebuilds the RunAgentInput from this.threadId, this.messages, and this.state, taking only runId, tools, context, and forwardedProps from the object it was handed (run-turn.ts:690-701). Passing only the input actually blew up once in handoff delivery: the Bot ran against an empty conversation, answered "how can I help" to a question it had never seen, and the transcript displayed the question directly above the answer (handoff-delivery.ts:316-324, paraphrased). When you copy a private engine, calls of exactly this kind are the most dangerous: type-correct, semantically empty.

    The copy's dependency surface is deliberately written as documentation too: three ports, IntelligenceLike, RunnerLike, and EventStream (run-turn.ts:122-177), together with ports.ts, named after the methods this file calls and nothing more. They are what lets tests drive every exit path without a gateway, and an honest list of how much a headless turn actually depends on CopilotKitIntelligence. Dependencies named down to the method level give an upgrade diff something to check against.

    Intelligence has no alternative. CopilotKit Intelligence owns durable threads, memory, and learning, and OpenBot's runtime always runs in Intelligence mode. The comment above the assembly function says it absolutely:

    typescript
    // server/src/copilot.ts:79-82
 * There is no SSE branch. Intelligence is a requirement of the product, not a tier: it owns
 * durable threads, memory and learning, and a deployment without it silently forgets every
 * conversation. config.ts refuses to boot without the full contract, so by the time this runs the
 * settings are present and this file has one mode.

    What this comment shows is a failure shape moving house: "missing Intelligence" moves from a production incident (a deployment silently forgetting every conversation) forward to a boot failure. Chapter 2's refuse-to-boot list contains this entry, so we do not expand on it here. Why it matters: the premise of governance riding the protocol is a protocol stack with exactly one shape. Keeping an "SSE degradation branch" means keeping a second code path, and a second path needs a second set of governance, a second audit, and a second runtime answer to "which one did it take today." A dependency that must exist for the process to boot is far cheaper than one that degrades gracefully.

    The defensive wrapper on the Intelligence client

    "There is no SSE branch" turns Intelligence into a hard dependency, but a hard dependency does not oblige you to trust every failure shape it has. Intelligence is a process on the other side of the network: it can 404, it can 401, and it can answer an entitlement read with "not configured."

    OpenBot wraps five defensive layers around this hard dependency on the client side. They are the client-side mirror of governance riding the protocol: every failure on the protocol boundary has a designed landing shape, and no layer changes the protocol; each one catches a failure's semantics on the client side of the line.

    A new thread's 404 is an empty history, not a 500. Thread ids are minted before the thread exists (the platform creates it on the first run), so reading the history of a brand-new conversation is a normal opening move, and the platform's answer is 404. The runtime's own handler catches everything and returns a bare 500, so every new chat manufactures one 500 with a stack trace. The fix is IntelligenceKnowingANewThread (toolkit/src/copilotkit/agents.ts:344-352): it overrides only getThreadMessages and, through historyOrEmpty, turns this one 404 into a 200 of {messages: []}.

    Why a subclass and not a wrapper: the base class's state lives in #private fields, JavaScript's hard privacy, which no outside object can touch. A wrapper would have to forward every method to an instance whose state it cannot hold; extends leaves the other methods on the instance that owns the fields and swaps out only this one. Coverage of exactly one method is the most honest part of the fix: it does not pretend to understand the runtime's other behavior.

    Judge by shape, not by type. isMissingThread (toolkit/src/thread-history.ts:20-26) matches name === "PlatformRequestError" plus status === 404, and never uses instanceof: the class never left the package's export map, so there is no type to test against. The name is set by the constructor and the status is a number on the instance; checking both keeps out an unrelated error that happens to carry a 404.

    The comment pins the boundary: "404 ONLY, and nothing wider." A 500 means an outage or a bad key; answering it with an empty history tells the browser "the conversation is gone" and invites the person to start over. The fault being fixed is noise; the fault that must not be introduced along the way is this one. historyOrEmpty also deliberately takes the read as a function parameter instead of folding it into the subclass, so the decision can be tested against a function that actually throws. The previous version (#71) fixed it by re-implementing the middleware in the test file; the test kept passing after the real code was deleted (thread-history.ts:28-37). A tripwire must be tied to the real code path, the same lesson as run-turn.ts's.

    A Proxy preserves the receiver. observeIntelligenceAuthentication (server/src/intelligence-client.ts:9-56) wraps the client in a Proxy: methods go through Reflect.get and Reflect.apply so the original receiver survives, the #private bill again. A resolved promise clears the intelligence connection-failure flag, with two exceptions: getRuntimeEntitlements and getInspectorMetadata may be served from cache, so they cannot count as authentication evidence.

    The failure side is equally precise: a 401 records intelligence_authentication_failed; a 403 does not. A 403 may be a permissions or entitlement decision; only refused authentication demands fresh credentials. The observation layer invents no semantics: it catches the SDK's typed HTTP error before the runtime handler flattens it into a generic 500, and translates it into a flag operations can act on.

    Build a second instance on purpose. When OpenBot itself asks Intelligence a question (whether a thread the browser remembers still exists), it does not borrow the client from the runtime; createIntelligenceClient builds another one (server/src/intelligence-client.ts:72-82). The constructor stores settings and opens no connection, so the cost is one object, while reaching into the runtime for the client it built would bind you to a module's mount order. The routine path likewise builds its own pair of client and runner (index.ts:664-685). The second instance buys decoupling, not waste: mount order must not become a precondition for correct behavior, and two consumers reading the same three settings need the settings to agree, not the instances.

    The entitlement boot check: ask once, do not block, never throw. A self-hosted Intelligence without a license answers every entitlement read with RUNTIME_ENTITLEMENTS_SELF_HOSTED_MISCONFIGURED, and the features gated on it, memory first among them, are then silently refused: conversations run as usual, nothing fails loudly, and OpenBot's own logs carry no reason. So at boot, ask once and log it (server/src/intelligence-entitlement-check.ts); each of the three known codes has its own fix text.

    The fix text stresses the same sentence: the license belongs to Intelligence's own deployment, and "setting it on OpenBot alone is not enough." This is the easiest place to misconfigure, so the fix text also names where the keyhole is. The self-hosted banner reads the same answer on page load, but only when banners are enabled, so it cannot be the thing that reports this. Ask once, do not block boot, never throw. That is the most restrained shape a boot check can have: it reports, then steps aside.

    Defense Where the failure shape lands Source
    IntelligenceKnowingANewThread New-thread 404 → a 200 of {messages: []}, not a bare 500 toolkit/src/copilotkit/agents.ts:344-352
    isMissingThread By shape: 404 only, no 500, no instanceof toolkit/src/thread-history.ts:20-26
    observeIntelligenceAuthentication Proxy preserves the receiver; 401 gets named, 403 does not server/src/intelligence-client.ts:9-56
    createIntelligenceClient A second instance; the runtime's client is not shared server/src/intelligence-client.ts:72-82
    Entitlement boot check Ask once, do not block, never throw; three codes, three fix texts server/src/intelligence-entitlement-check.ts

    None of the five layers changes the protocol, and none hides a failure: the 404 lands as empty history because it was already equivalent to empty; the 401 gets named because only it demands new credentials; the entitlement speaks loudly because silently missing memory is the hardest failure to read.

    Client-layer governance and gateway-layer governance use the same ruler: failure shapes are designed, not endured. Chapter 15 will show the other half of this wrapper: the recall path for memory and learning, and its philosophy of degrading every failure to undefined.

    The thread lock: the turn's lease

    On the browser path, the runtime holds the lock and the runtime releases it. The headless path took the lock's lifecycle over, and the file header says it plainly: "A bug in it is not a failed routine, it is a thread the person cannot chat in" (run-turn.ts:31-33). Correctness depends on the lock. While the lock is held, the person's next browser message is refused with a 409 "Thread lock denied" for an entire TTL. A leaked lock means "It locks somebody out of their own conversation, at three in the morning, for a reason no screen explains" (run-turn.ts:893-898).

    Before touching the lock there is an admission check: admission({ownerUserId, agentId, signal}) runs the pause guard first (a paused Bot starts no turn, and a pause that lands mid-turn aborts the signal it returned), then the enterprise controls: the "Use Bots" capability switch and the model allowlist. Browser runs meet these at the HTTP gate; headless turns never pass that gate, so every headless turn meets the same check here, and a refusal throws a named CapabilityRefusedError (server/src/agents/turn-admission.ts:12-28). An admission failure is not a lock failure: it happens before any resource is allocated, so there is nothing to clean up.

    First, what the lock is. It is a platform resource: Redis-backed, keyed by thread, NX semantics (refuse when held rather than queue), visible to every replica. The in-process map IntelligenceAgentRunner.threads is only a local fast path, which is why the runner is built once at assembly and reused globally: one instance per turn would shatter that map, and two concurrent turns would rush past the local check and collide on the platform lock instead of failing cheaply here (run-turn.ts:43-49). This is the literal meaning of "boundaries live in the deployment": the correctness of mutual exclusion rests on Redis and a TTL, not on any single process's memory.

    Even failure classification is deployment-level discipline. The comment's own words are the rule: "ONLY A CONFLICT MEANS 'NOT NOW'. Everything else is raised." When acquire fails, only a 409 reads as "not now": return null and let the caller wait and retry; everything else throws (toolkit/src/copilotkit/thread-lock.ts:73-91). The reason, from the comments: if platform-unreachable and dead-token also returned null, they would all read as contention. Every hop retries to exhaustion, everyone is told the question was never answered, and the only evidence is a warning line that looks like a busy conversation. Throw, and the person gets a sentence that states the real reason.

    Then, the lock's identity. runId is minted once at the start of a turn, and the same value goes to acquire, every renew, runner.stop, and cleanup (run-turn.ts:618-627). Re-minting it or reading it again is how you end up keeping one lock alive with renew while cleanup releases a different one: two ways to die from the same bug family.

    The numbers are worth listing, because each has a source:

    Number Value Why
    Lock TTL 120 s Fixed platform value; the comment admits 20 was once requested and never took effect (limits.ts:30-33)
    Heartbeat interval 15 s 120 seconds survives about seven failed renewals at a 15 s heartbeat; at 20 s a single miss loses the lock (limits.ts:35-39)
    Headless turn timeout 5 min The time budget of one turn (limits.ts:10)
    Abort backstop grace 5 s abortRun is a no-op while the agent build has not resolved; the backstop settles (limits.ts:12-20)
    Event persistence ack 60 s Platform-side deadline; a run that is not acked in time fails (run-turn.ts:36-38)

    keepLease (toolkit/src/lease.ts) is the heartbeat primitive. There are only two ways to lose the lock: a renewal refused with a 409 (the lock has a new owner), or more than lifetimeMs − everyMs elapsed since the last successful renewal (LockLapsedError, checked per tick rather than on failure, because a pending renewal never fails; lease.ts:44-48). Everything else (network errors, 5xx, 401) is skipped and waits for the next tick:

    typescript
    // toolkit/src/lease.ts:83-92
    const asked = now();
    void renew().then(
      () => {
        // A renewal that lands late still only extends the lock from when it was asked for.
        if (heartbeat !== undefined) renewedAt = Math.max(renewedAt, asked);
      },
      (error: unknown) => {
        if (isLockConflict(error)) lose(error);
      },
    );

    What this shows is a deliberate divergence in renewal tolerance: the runtime's own channel runner stops on any renewal error, while keepLease recognizes only the 409 and the time window. Why does it dare? The comment gives the chapter's best reason: a turn stopped by network turbulence gets retried from the beginning, and a Bot that has already sent the email will send it again (run-turn.ts:356-359).

    Re-running is not free; the side effects replay. The TTL exists so that turbulence shorter than it rides through, instead of stopping the turn and starting over.

    And every path (success, throw, timeout, heartbeat failure) flows into the same cleanup. The file header calls this finally block "the single most important thing in this file," and one read shows the title is earned:

    typescript
    // toolkit/src/run-turn.ts:900-906
      lease.stopHeartbeat();
      if (cancelTurn) signal?.removeEventListener("abort", cancelTurn);
      if (signal?.aborted) await stopPromise;
      if (deadline !== undefined) clearTimeout(deadline);
      if (backstop !== undefined) clearTimeout(backstop);
      spoken.unsubscribe();
      await lease.release();

    Seven lines, and every ordering decision matters: stop the heartbeat first (stop renewing a dying lock), then remove the listener, wait for the stop to settle, clear the timers, unsubscribe, and release the lock last. release never rejects: when cleanup itself is unreachable, the TTL is the backstop, and a second failure never replaces the real one. The pattern matters because it is the cure for the occupational disease of headless systems: the failure shapes of cleanup deserve more design than the main flow. A main-flow failure is seen by someone; a cleanup failure becomes a lock nobody knows exists.

    The lock's life has only three states (idle, held, lost), and lost ends the turn; there is no fourth way out:

    Current state Event Next state
    Idle acquire (NX: conflict refuses rather than queues) Held
    Held Renewal succeeds every 15 s Held
    Held Renewal refused with a 409 (the lock has changed hands) Lost
    Held No successful renewal within lifetimeMs − everyMs (LockLapsedError) Lost
    Held release in the finally (never rejects) Idle
    Lost stopTurn + raise Turn ends

    Settling the outcome: where failure arrives disguised as success

    The turn has run its course. What kind of ending was it? The question is harder than it looks, because in OpenBot's runtime, failure does not travel the error channel.

    The Intelligence runner reports a failed run like this: it emits a RUN_ERROR event and then completes the observable normally; the error callback is reserved for socket breaks and persistence failures (run-turn.ts:833-839). A RUN_ERROR not caught in next arrives as a successful completion, and the turn looks like a Bot that answered nothing. The browser side is another onset of the same disease: copilotkit.runAgent catches everything, reports through emitError, and returns {result: undefined, newMessages: []}, indistinguishable from "finished but had nothing to say" (channel-chat.tsx:531-536). The headless tool middleware has a mirror of it: asynchronous execution errors are uniformly converted to RUN_ERROR (code OPENBOT_HEADLESS_TOOL_ERROR) and then completed, again not the error channel (headless-tools.ts:315). Two processes, the same lesson: promise rejections and observable errors are both untrustworthy; failure arrives disguised as success. The frontend's fix is a turnFailure ref written by the subscription, checked by deliver after the finally, which then throws: "A TURN THAT DID NOT HAPPEN FAILS THE SEND, which is the only way anything upstream can tell" (channel-chat.tsx:727-729). The server's fix is to converge outcome judgment into a single function.

    settle (run-turn.ts:462-501) is the sole authority on a turn's outcome, with a fixed decision order. Its first three branches:

    typescript
    // toolkit/src/run-turn.ts:462-468
export function settle(evidence: TurnEvidence): TurnOutcome {
  if (evidence.failed) return { kind: "failed", error: evidence.failed.error };
  if (evidence.heartbeatError !== undefined)
    return { kind: "lockLost", error: evidence.heartbeatError };
  if (evidence.stopped) return { kind: "timedOut" };
  if (evidence.waiting)
    return { kind: "suspended", suspension: evidence.waiting };

    Seven outcomes, eight decision branches: suspended has two arrival paths, the explicit CUSTOM event and a spare riding on the interrupt metadata for when the CUSTOM event does not survive the Intelligence relay (the section on frontend tools explains who puts that spare there).

    Two places in the order are not arbitrary. First, interrupted comes before empty: a turn that "asked a question and then said nothing" satisfies both conditions, and "finished without saying anything" is a lie about a turn that actually stopped to ask (run-turn.ts:458-460). Second, lockLost and timedOut both await stopped before reporting: a stop you requested yourself must actually settle, not merely have been requested (run-turn.ts:518-525). The choice of reply text is equally political: take the diff first (what is new in agent.messages, which is persisted and is what the person will read in the channel), with the streamed chunks only as a fallback. Only what is persisted counts as said; the priority itself is a governance position.

    Judgment and propagation share one naming discipline: HeadlessToolSuspension, ThreadBusyError, RoutineBotNotRegistered, and CapabilityRefusedError are all discriminated by name.
