    Note that DB appears twice in this diagram while C appears at most once: one action produces at most two audit rows (decision plus outcome), and the action itself may never happen. The trail's completeness ranks ahead of the action's completion.

    "A refusal is a row too" applies beyond the gateway. A refused MCP callback writes mcp.callback_refused; a refused credential rotation writes credential.rotation_refused, whose reason to exist is written straight into the event vocabulary's comment (audit.ts:54-62): the refusals are the interesting ones. Record only successes, and an attempt to retire a key nobody told you to retire leaves no trace at all. The vocabulary also preserves an incident report: mcp.call_succeeded used to be written before the network call, so a call that died on the vendor's side left behind a "success" row. The comment's conclusion belongs in the design document of any audit system (audit.ts:144-148): "A trail that is confidently wrong is more dangerous than one that is silent, because it is used to rule things out".

    The list of refusal rows is wider than the policy engine's verdicts. When rows like mcp.callback_refused, routines.dispatch_refused, and session.refused happen, no policy has judged anyone, and the latter two have no Bot present at all. But the "what did this deployment block" filter needs them: for each of these three classes, the audit row is the only evidence anywhere that somebody tried, because the wire answer to all of them is the same deliberately vague refusal (outcome.ts:23-27).

    Append-only lives in the database

    The audit table's "insert, never change" is not application-layer discipline; it is enforced by the database. The reason is in the header comment of migration 0007: the application is not the only thing that can reach this table (migration scripts, the psql in an operator's hands, some service added next year), so the guarantee must live in the table itself. "'we deleted the rows about the incident' must stay impossible".

    The guarantee was tightened over three migrations, each closing a real bypass.

    0000, the birth certificate. The initial schema already carries the prevent_audit_event_mutation() function and the row-level trigger audit_events_append_only (0000_schema.sql:391-406), and UPDATE and DELETE both RAISE EXCEPTION. The header comment of 0000 names it as one of two things that must be preserved by hand: drizzle-kit's generate does not produce triggers, and nobody will warn you if the trigger gets lost while merging migrations.

    0007, a small window. Enterprise buyers demand retention policies, and this table becomes the deployment's largest within weeks of real use. So DELETE is allowed under strict conditions, and the conditions must be declared loudly by the deleting party: inside a transaction, set_config('openbot.audit_retention_days', N, true), where the third argument true confines the setting to the current transaction so the permission cannot leak beyond the statement that declared it; and the row must be older than N days, with rows inside the window refused no matter what the setting says. UPDATE stays refused under all conditions: retention may remove history, and may never rewrite it.

    0012, the bypass closed. Row-level triggers do not fire on TRUNCATE. After 0007, every UPDATE and DELETE was refused while TRUNCATE audit_events could empty the whole table in one statement and return success. 0012 closes the gap with a statement-level trigger, and makes the two triggers share one function: the refusal is written in one place and cannot drift into two versions.

    sql
    -- server/drizzle/0012_truncate_is_not_a_way_around_append_only.sql:26-40 (excerpt)
-- Answered before anything else is read, so no setting and no missing OLD record can change it.
IF TG_OP = 'TRUNCATE' OR TG_OP = 'UPDATE' THEN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'Audit events are append-only';
END IF;

-- `true` so a session that never set it reads NULL instead of raising, which is the ordinary case
-- and has to stay a plain refusal.
retention_days := nullif(current_setting('openbot.audit_retention_days', true), '')::integer;
-- ... (wrapped in BEGIN/EXCEPTION: a failed read is treated as NULL)

IF retention_days IS NULL OR retention_days < 1 THEN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'Audit events are append-only';

    The part of this migration most worth reading line by line is its review of the naive fix. The intuitive way to write it appends the TRUNCATE branch at the end of the function: read the retention-window setting first, do the row-age comparison, and only then ask the operation type. A statement-level trigger has no OLD record; if the control flow reaches the OLD.created_at >= ... comparison first, that is a comparison against NULL, the IF fails, and control falls through to RETURN OLD: TRUNCATE is let through. Worse, that path only becomes reachable after the retention sweep has set a window, exactly the state that happy-path tests never reach. This is a textbook fail-open. The 0012 comment compresses the lesson into one sentence: "Answering TG_OP before the setting is read removes the path rather than guarding it". So in the real code the TG_OP check sits on the first line of the function body, before any setting is read (with a row-age check after it: OLD.created_at must be older than the window, 0012:42-44).

    The full decision tree:

    The retention sweep: the only delete allowed

    The only legal caller of DELETE is sweepAuditTrail (audit-retention.ts:60-114). Every engineering detail comes from the same constraint: this is a table that every action writes to.

    • One sweeper per deployment. A session-level advisory lock (the fixed number 4192004) picks the winner. The lock cannot go through the shared connection pool: a session lock belongs to one connection, and a pool would take the lock on one connection and try to release it on another, leaking the lock. So the sweep uses its own max: 1 connection, released by disconnecting in a finally, and a mid-run throw does not leave the lock inside the database.
    • Small batches. 5000 rows per batch, at most 200 batches per run, scoped by a ctid subquery: every statement is short, and the table stays writable between statements. A deployment that has never swept may have years of rows to delete, and it should not lock its own audit table offline for that.
    • Off by default. With no retention days configured, the sweep does not start at all. "Deleting somebody's audit trail because a default said so is the worse failure of the two" (audit-retention.ts:10-12): a deployment that has not thought through its retention policy should keep everything.
    • Failures are only logged. "The trail is intact; it is only larger than the policy asks for" (audit-retention.ts:168-175).
    • A plain, self-aware cadence. Once an hour, first run 60 seconds after startup (audit-retention.ts:134-135), with the timer unrefed so it does not hold the process open. It uses an ordinary setInterval rather than the leased work_items queue from Chapter 10, and the header comment of work.ts spells out the exemption: sweeping with setInterval is safe only because deleting old rows twice is the same as deleting them once. Operations without that idempotency belong on Chapter 10's queue.

    One failure orientation here deserves naming, because it points the opposite way from Chapter 2. Chapter 2's configuration parsing is conservative in the style of "anything unparseable counts as public" (fail-closed); this chapter's sweep is "anything undeletable stays". The two rules are one rule: failure falls toward the safer state, and which state is safer depends on the nature of the data. For credentials and grants, fail closed; for evidence and trails, fail keep.

    Who did it vs who started it: the six initiator kinds

    actor_user_id answers "with whose authority"; the initiator_kind/initiator_id pair added in 0028 answers a different question: who started it. Why must these be two columns? Routines run with their owner's authority, and Bot-to-Bot handoffs run with the authority of the person who started the conversation. Looking only at the actor column, a routine running at three in the morning looks identical to its owner awake and typing. The architecture doc defines the problem precisely (docs/architecture.md:91-94): in an interactive run someone is present, and that person will notice a wrong tool call; an unattended run has nobody present, and the latter is exactly the class that most needs to be findable.

    There are six initiator kinds:

    initiator_kind initiator_id Meaning
    person none someone is present. The default
    deployment none the deployment itself: startup rows, boundary refusals where the caller cannot be identified
    routine routine id fired on a schedule, with the owner's authority, nobody present
    responsibility Responsibility id a standing Responsibility was triggered, also with nobody present
    memory memory source id memory import: reading a connected app, with the source owner's authority
    handoff the handing-over Bot's id initiated on behalf of another Bot

    The Nobody watching filter in the audit interface is exactly those four kinds, routine + handoff + responsibility + memory: every case of "running with someone's authority while that someone is absent". Two deliberate exclusions are more interesting than the inclusions:

    • deployment is not in the filter: the boundary held at startup is not work done on anyone's behalf, and counting it as unattended would turn the filter into noise.
    • deployment exists so that person never over-reports. Startup rows and the two unauthenticated boundary refusals are started by nobody; if they borrowed the default and were written as person, the reading "person means a person started this row" would stop holding, and the column would start over-reporting. A deployment that has never run a routine or a handoff shows person on every row, exactly as it did before the column was added, and not one word more.

    Nobody watching is not a standalone button; it is one of five preset views on the audit screen (audit.tsx:51-63):

    • Everything: no filter, the full list in reverse time order.
    • Computer actions: only computer.action_allowed.
    • Blocked: all refusal-type events (REFUSED_EVENT_TYPES).
    • Did not happen: rows like action_failed, action_stopped, and handoff_failed, the ones not refused but not happened either (DID_NOT_HAPPEN_EVENT_TYPES, outcome.ts:57-87).
    • Nobody watching: filtered by initiator, the four kinds above.

    The first four split by event type; the last splits by initiator. The reason Blocked and Did not happen are two families is written in the list's comment (outcome.ts:51-56): the boundary stopping something and the Bot being asked but failing to answer are two faults with two fixes, and only one of them is "the deployment working as configured". This row of views also carries the repair of a drift incident: row colors and filters once each maintained their own list, and the two had drifted, so a row could count as a refusal in one list while being painted "Allowed" in the other, or vanish from the "what did this deployment refuse" view entirely. Now "what kind of row is this" is answered in exactly one place, @/lib/audit/outcome (audit.tsx:43-50).

    The initiator's trustworthiness comes from how it travels: it rides in a signed run assertion, in the same bag as the handoff depth depth (Chapter 11 expands the mechanism), signed by the deployment and carried along the handoff chain. A Bot cannot relabel its own run, because the assertion is signed by the deployment. And a kind the deployment does not write is interpreted as person rather than preserved: an unfamiliar value is better downgraded to "someone present" than allowed into the trail impersonating a fact. There is one more invariant on the handoff chain: origin is always the root.

    The minting and carrying of the assertion are also designed (callback-token.ts:107-142). The comment on the initiator field explains why it shares a bag with depth: a handoff is one run on one pod handing over to another run on another pod, and the process that knows "this run was started by a routine" is the one that claimed the routine, not the one that writes the row. So the answer must travel with the signature: "a Bot cannot relabel its own run as a person's". The assertion reaches the agent through forwardedProps rather than HTTP headers: headers are consumed by the framework's HTTP layer and are gone by the time a tool call needs them, while forwardedProps is the part of an AG-UI run that the framework hands back to client code. The assertion also carries a ten-minute validity (RUN_TTL_MS, callback-token.ts:45), and expired ones cannot be replayed.

    Holding the assertion means holding the answer, so the parties writing audit rows do not have to be told one by one: a tool call, a handoff offered or refused at the handoff desk, a Bot that stops to ask a person, a stuck stream, all speak of the same initiator (architecture.md:115-124). Computer actions carry it too: for runs with no browser attached (routines, Responsibilities, group-chat turns), the computer tools live on the server side, Bot and person are bound before the model produces any arguments, and the gateway writes the run's initiator onto every decision row.

    ts
    // server/src/audit.ts:574-585
export function handoffInitiator(
  fromBotId: string,
  source: AuditInitiator | undefined,
): AuditInitiator {
  const root = source ?? PERSON_INITIATOR;
  if (root.kind === "handoff") {
    return root.origin
      ? { kind: "handoff", id: fromBotId, origin: root.origin }
      : { kind: "handoff", id: fromBotId };
  }
  return { kind: "handoff", id: fromBotId, origin: root };
}

    origin either inherits the previous hop's origin or fixes the current root (a person, a routine) as the origin; it never starts a new one. The comment explains why (audit.ts:570-572): a source that is itself a hop but has no origin passes no origin down, and inventing one here would be read as fact. However deep the chain, "who started this in the first place" is always one field away.

    The write path: redact twice, broadcast after

    All writes go through the same path, recordAuditEvent then store.insert, and the payload is redacted twice: once at the entrance, once inside insert. The doubling is deliberate: it means "no call path can bypass it". Redaction matches key names against a 29-word list (audit.ts:18-48: token, secret, password, tool_arguments, result, content...), after two normalizations, lowercasing and stripping non-alphanumerics, so encryptedValue and encrypted_value both get caught, and a hit replaces the whole value with "[REDACTED]".

    ts
    // server/src/audit.ts:754-763
const row = {
  ...event,
  ...initiatorColumns(initiator),
  payload: redactAuditPayload(event.payload) as Record<string, unknown>,
};
await database.insert(auditEvents).values(row);
for (const tap of auditTaps) {
  try {
    tap(row);

    Only after the insert succeeds are all AuditTaps notified (OTel/SIEM export, Action Recording): the order guarantees that what streams out is always what the trail holds. And a throwing tap is only logged, never affecting the write: "streaming a row must never fail writing it" (audit.ts:741-745). The broadcast can never hurt the ledger in return.

    The consumers hanging on the tap are worth naming: OpenTelemetry/SIEM export and Action Recording (kept 90 days, admin/controls.ts:64) both register via addAuditTap (audit.ts:746). The audit screen is the only human-facing read surface, but it is not the only reader: the built-in components' botActivity and recentRefusals data functions read this table directly (architecture.md:209), so Chapter 14's component governance does not need to maintain a second "who did what". The reads differ; the rows read are the same.

    The write path has one more entrance-shape detail: code that should not hold the database gets an AuditSink (audit.ts:702-714), a narrow interface with only a record method, which internally still goes through recordAuditEvent, so redaction applies to this side road too. Whoever wants to write audit does not need to touch the store, and whoever can touch the store has no second write path.

    The subtlest spot on the write path is not in audit.ts but in the credential vault. A refused rotation lands a row too (credential.rotation_refused), and the row must carry the refusal reason; but this row is written after the transaction rolls back (credentials.ts:623-624: "the row survives the failure it describes"), so the reason must be extracted through reasonWithoutStatement. Why extract? A drizzle query error message starts with Failed query: <full SQL> and attaches all bound values, and among the values bound to that insert is the freshly encrypted secret envelope. The audit table is append-only, gets exported, and is kept for the whole retention window: "a secret landing there is not one anybody can take back out" (credentials.ts:626-636). This comment also preserves a public admission of error: the previous version of the comment claimed that only the vault's own messages could reach here, but rotation runs three statements, and a DrizzleQueryError thrown by any of them is not the vault's own message. Keeping the correction inside the comment is normal for this codebase, and it is the audit mindset seeping into writing habits.

    Deep Dive: The read path is defended just as hard

    (Readers in a hurry can skip this; the main line resumes in the next section.)

    Audit reads have one entrance, the admin's GET /api/admin/audit-events, but the defensive density matches the write path. The list uses a (created_at, id) two-column keyset cursor, base64url-encoded JSON. The decoding side, decodeCursor (audit.ts:827-846), treats the string the caller sent as an adversary: the id must look like a UUID, createdAt must Date.parse, and on return both fields are rebuilt: "nothing else the caller packed into the cursor travels on into the query". The history lesson is written in the comments: a bad cursor once escaped as a DrizzleQueryError and left as a 500 carrying the full SQL and bound values; now it is always a 400, because an unreadable cursor is the caller's thing to fix.

    There is an even more hidden pitfall: created_at keeps microseconds, while a JS Date stops at milliseconds, so a cursor built from a Date points slightly before its row, and rows within the same millisecond would never appear on any page. The timestamp inside the cursor is therefore generated SQL-side as microsecond text with to_char(..., 'US') (audit.ts:936-944). Filters behave the same way: ?initiatorKind=nonsense narrows to "matches nothing" (sql\false``) instead of widening to no filter: "On the record of whose credential was spent on what, handing back everything is the wrong direction to fail" (audit.ts:866-883). The code that reads the audit also defends against the audit being misread.

    The cursor is the entrance-side defense; error messages are the exit-side one, and the latter is its own module: db/query-failure.ts, with a single responsibility, answering "the database failed; what can we quote outward". It recognizes query failures by shape rather than by class: query and params as own properties count (query-failure.ts:33-41), because drizzle's DrizzleQueryError is reachable only through a deep import, is not on its published surface, and instanceof cannot reach it. Once recognized, it keeps only cause.message, truncated to 400 characters; if the shape does not match, it falls back to one fixed sentence: "The database gave no reason this deployment can quote." (query-failure.ts:86-91). The reasonWithoutStatement the credential rotation used in the previous section is this module's exit (query-failure.ts:67-69): query failures get the stripped wording, everything else gets error.message. The header comment explains why it is its own file (query-failure.ts:1-12): this logic used to be a private function in plugins/store.ts, until the rotation path started writing error messages into audit rows, an append-only table kept for the whole retention window. It sits under db/ because "it depends on nothing, so it cannot close a loop". This pairs with decodeCursor's 500-turned-400: one keeps an incoming string from carrying a query along, the other keeps an outgoing error from carrying a statement along.

    The whole read entrance, auditQueryFromUrl (audit.ts:972-1017), gathers the same paranoia in one place: limit defaults to 50 with a cap of 100 (strictly parsed through parsePageLimit), and any invalid from, to, or cursor is a 400. Audit queries have no best-effort mode.

    Taking the trail out: CSV export

    The audit screen is the only read surface, but compliance pulls, incident timelines, and policy-block statistics all need evidence files. Export goes through the same route with ?format=csv and the same query function (app.ts:840-904), so the downloaded file and the on-screen table agree on the same set of filters, and there is no "two exports, two truths". There are four layers of defense, each aimed at a real attack surface.

    First, formula injection. Audit rows are full of text that people and Bots control: names, URLs, target ids. Spreadsheets execute cells that start with = + - @ (or a leading tab/CR) as formulas. CSV injection is an OWASP-listed attack, and audit exports are among its fattest targets. toCsvCell prefixes such cells with ', so they open as text:

    ts
    // server/src/audit.ts:1057-1068
function toCsvCell(value: string): string {
  const text = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/.test(value) ? `'${value}` : value;
  if (
    text.includes('"') ||
    text.includes(",") ||
    text.includes("\n") ||
    text.includes("\r")
  ) {
    return `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"`;
  }
  return text;
}

    Note the exemption reasoning in the comment (audit.ts:1048-1056): JSON payloads start with {, timestamps and ids start with digits or letters, so nothing the trail writes itself is ever modified; only the shapes an injector chooses are.

    Second, a cap and a truncation signal. Exports are capped at 5000 rows (paged through at 500 per page), and when the cap is hit the response carries an X-Audit-Export-Truncated header (with the actual row count as its value) and the interface says so plainly, sending the reviewer to narrow from/to instead of quoting half a trail as complete evidence.

    Third, the export itself goes on the books. Every export writes an audit.exported row recording who took it, how many rows, under which filters, and whether truncated. The vocabulary comment says it in one sentence (audit.ts:375-378): the trail is evidence, and who copied how much of it under which scope is evidence too.

    Fourth, the payload stays one JSON column. Flattening it into an unknown number of columns only invites the spreadsheet to misread it; the already-redacted payload travels as a single column.

    The columns are a fixed twelve (audit.ts:1033-1046), refusing the "flatten as many columns as there are payload kinds" route; the cap and page size are named constants (AUDIT_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS = 5_000, AUDIT_EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE = 500, audit.ts:1030-1031); readAuditExportRows (audit.ts:1108-1131) pages through and honestly reports truncated. Two tail details: when the cap is hit, what you get is the newest 5000 rows, so half the evidence is at least the most recent half; and an unrecognized format parameter, like any broken audit query, is a 400 (architecture.md:129-139).

    One contrary decision is worth holding up for comparison. Chapter 5's policy dry-run replays audit history against a candidate policy, and that endpoint writes not a single audit row: "a trail row for every what-if would bury the rows that record what actually happened" (computer/routes.ts:753-756). What goes on the books and what does not is decided by "what will a future reader do with this row", not by "how convenient is it to write".

    Audit restraint: what is deliberately not recorded

    An audit table naturally tempts its owners to record everything. OpenBot deliberately records less in at least five places, each with its reason stated first:

    Not recorded Recorded instead Why
    typed text which field was filled, and the character count form fields are the home of passwords, card numbers, and one-time codes
    file contents the path a file body is as sensitive as typed text
    command output the full command text "A command IS the action"; the output is this pair's file body
    keystrokes during a human takeover the takeover's start, end, and reason the whole reason a takeover exists is to let the person enter what nothing else should keep
    secret values "N characters" "Length, never content" (gateway.ts:977)

    The comments behind the first two rows spell out the philosophy (gateway.ts:1251-1256): audit.ts's redaction would indeed catch a key named text, but relying on that means the secret was put into the payload first and then caught in passing. Simpler and stronger is that it is never put in. Redaction is the net; restraint is not throwing things into the net. The asymmetry between command and output is the same reasoning: a trail that only records "the Bot ran something" answers no question anyone would ask, so the full command is recorded; the output is content and is not.

    The human-takeover row deserves expanding. Human keyboard and mouse input goes through /human/<kind>, the only action path in the gateway that writes no audit rows (gateway.ts:983-1004): the takeover itself is an audit event (computer.control_taken / control_released), but every key the person types during it is deliberately not recorded. The route layer's comment gives the reason (computer/routes.ts:496-502): "the reason a takeover exists is to let them enter the thing nothing else should keep". Recording those keystrokes would destroy the feature in the name of the feature. The price is that the gateway layer must re-validate the kind (an allowlist of click/type/key/scroll): this path writes no rows, so a kind tampered into ../exec would hit another endpoint of the computer API carrying the deployment's computer token, leaving no trace. A path that writes no rows needs harder validation.

    By the same token, takeover-class events get rows but skip policy (gateway.ts:752-760): a rule that can lock a person out of their own browser mid-login is worse than anything it prevents. The audit's role changes here too: it becomes a factual record of who held the wheel, when, and why, rather than evidence of permission.

    This "rowed but not policed" list is worth naming: writeControlEvent (gateway.ts:1425-1455) covers nine computer events, help_requested / help_cancelled / control_taken / control_released / secret_requested / secret_supplied / stopped / reset / updated, all footprints of "a person stepped in" or "the deployment reset". Their reason for skipping policy is the same as the takeover's: a rule that can block the help channel is worse than anything it is trying to prevent.

    The timing of rows on these paths is also placed by the point of no return: resetComputer's audit row is written after provider.reset completes and before the local snapshot is cleared (gateway.ts:890-920), and the comment calls that the point of no return: once the reset happens, the row must already be there. Even a small thing like "stop writes a row whether or not the computer is actually running" has its reasoning: "a trail that only records effective actions cannot tell you what somebody tried" (gateway.ts:843-846).

    Governance rides the protocol: the initiator rides a signed assertion, event types are a closed vocabulary, and even "export" is a protocolized event (audit.exported). The boundary lives in the deployment: append-only lives in database triggers rather than in the application's self-discipline, and "who may delete history" lives not in "who has the admin password" but in a transaction setting that must be declared loudly. The audit trail is the evidence layer of the word "governance": it must be harder to forge, harder to destroy, and harder to exaggerate than the system it governs, or the governance is a show.

    Apply This

    Pattern 1: sink immutability into the database. Problem solved: an application-layer "we never UPDATE this table" is discipline, and discipline fails when the third writer shows up: migration scripts, the psql in an operator's hands, the service added next year; none of them read your code review minutes. How to adapt: give an append-only table a row-level trigger refusing UPDATE/DELETE; give the one legal deleter a window it must declare loudly (in Postgres, a transaction-local set_config(..., true) declaring identity and window); rows inside the window are refused regardless of any setting. Pitfall: row-level triggers do not catch TRUNCATE, so add a statement-level trigger separately; and the operation-type check must come before any comparison that can see NULL, or the fix itself fails open. Have both triggers share one function, so the refusal logic cannot drift into two versions.

    Pattern 2: write the decision row first, and let refusals land as rows. Problem solved: a trail that records only successes lies in two places: refusals are invisible (the policy's effectiveness cannot be proven), and "allowed but did not succeed" gets read as "happened". How to adapt: write the decision row before execution, land refusals as rows before throwing, append a second row for failures in the catch, and record decision and outcome separately; in dry-run mode, use a dedicated field on the row to separate "really blocked" from "rehearsal let-through" (OpenBot's carriedOut). Pitfall: never let "write the audit" become an optional path. OpenBot deliberately throws even "ref failed to resolve", a purely local error, only after the decision row: refusing before the row is written amounts to offering an action path that leaves no trace.

    Pattern 3: answer "who did it" and "who started it" with two columns. Problem solved: in the unattended era, the actor column (whose authority) cannot tell "the owner typing" from "the routine running at midnight", and that is exactly the question compliance most wants to filter. How to adapt: add a second column for the trigger source; pick "person" as the default and keep a "the deployment itself" kind so person never over-reports; then compose filters like Nobody watching out of the "nobody present" kinds, serving the real question "what happened while I was away". Pitfall: the initiator must not be self-reported by the caller; it must be carried by a platform signature, and an unrecognized value degrades to the most conservative reading. With chained delegation, fix the root in place and never let a middle hop rewrite the origin.

    Pattern 4: export is part of the audit surface, not an accessory. Problem solved: once the trail leaves the system as CSV, it escapes all server-side control; it is simultaneously an injection carrier (formula cells) and evidence (which must know whether it is complete and who took it). How to adapt: reuse the list's own query function for export so file and screen agree; hard cap plus an explicit truncation signal (a response header), preferring to send the reviewer back to narrow the range over handing over half the evidence; prefix cells starting with = + - @ with '; and write an audit row for the export itself. Pitfall: do not flatten the payload into columns, since unknown keys get misread by spreadsheets; and conversely, hypothetical operations (policy dry-runs) should not land rows, or every "what if" buries the facts.

    Pattern 5: restraint beats redaction. Problem solved: a secret in an append-only table cannot be taken back out; redaction is probabilistic defense (one miss in the word list and it is in), and append-only amplifies every leak into permanence. How to adapt: grade by "is this the action itself": record the full command text (the command is the action), and do not record typed text, file contents, or command output (record the field, the path, the character count); do not record the person's input during a human takeover, only the takeover's start and end; strip SQL statements and bound values from error messages before they enter the audit. Pitfall: a path that writes no rows loses the trail's cover, so its validation must double (see the /human/<kind> kind allowlist); and "the message of an error object" is not "a message you threw yourself": an ORM's error carries the full SQL and bound values, and the bound values may be the envelope you just encrypted.

    The audit trail answers "what happened, and who started it". The next chapter enters Part III and looks at where these audit rows' target_id points: each Bot's own computer, why one computer per Bot, and how it is fenced.

    ← Chapter 5: The Action Gateway: Decide, Record, Then ActChapter 7: One Computer per Bot →
    Part III: The Bot's Computer

    Every coworker gets a computer. The computer is fenced, and a human can take the wheel at any time.

    Chapter 7: One Computer per Bot

    Chapter 6's audit trail answered "who did it, and what started it", and kept one deliberate restraint: during a human takeover, the person's keystrokes are intentionally not audited. But the actions those audit rows describe, the clicks, the typing, the command runs, have to happen somewhere. This chapter is about that somewhere: the Bot's computer, a service called agent-computer, an HTTP/WS process with a resident Chromium, plus a file volume and a shell.

    The cheapest architecture is all Bots sharing one computer: one browser, one filesystem, one shell, since it is all automation anyway. OpenBot chose the most expensive path instead: one computer per Bot, container-level isolation, a separate browser profile and a separate workspace for each. Once you have seen how the shared design fails, you will accept that this is the only design under which Chapter 5's CEL policy stays enforceable at the browser layer.

    By the end of this chapter you will understand why "one computer each" is a precondition of the grant semantics rather than an optimization; how agent-computer separates "deciding" from "driving a browser" in its code structure; why its boot chain prefers CrashLoopBackOff to coming up sick; and how a person and a Bot take turns holding the same steering wheel without running each other over. This chapter is also the bluntest demonstration of the book's core thesis: governance rides the protocol, and this computer has no policy engine of its own; boundaries live in the deployment, and the strength of the isolation is decided by containers and volumes, not by code.

    The failure shape of a shared computer

    Give the shared design a fair chance first. One computer for every Bot saves memory, saves containers, saves orchestration. Where does it break?

    It breaks at login state. The header comment of profiles.ts says it outright:

    Two Bots sharing a profile share their logins, which makes "this Bot may reach Salesforce" unenforceable. — agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:23-24

    Two Bots sharing one browser profile share every login: the moment the sales Bot signs into Salesforce, the support Bot is signed in too. Chapter 5's policy written in CEL, "only the sales Bot may reach Salesforce", suddenly becomes a dead letter, because the browser layer has no concept of "which Bot"; the cookie jar is one. The failure shape is silent overreach rather than a crash: nothing reports an error, and the audit rows keep reading as if everything were proper.

    The filesystem works the same way. A shared workspace means any Bot can read any Bot's notes, including the personnel material another Bot was told to handle. The shell goes further, and shell.ts admits it itself: "a shell can reach whatever the container can reach". A shared shell in a shared container means every Bot shares the same executing body.

    So OpenBot's answer is one computer per Bot. But there is an honest qualifier, also written at the top of profiles.ts:

    A profile is not a container. Two Bots in this process are isolated from each other's cookies, not from each other's kernel, filesystem or memory. — agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:27-28

    Multiple browser profiles inside one process isolate cookies and storage only; they do not isolate the kernel, the filesystem, or memory. The real "one per Bot" is a deployment shape: the supervisor (the container steward, expanded in Chapter 9) starts one container per Bot and mounts one set of volumes each. Profile isolation in code is the floor; container isolation in the deployment is the wall.

    The chapter's most important sentence is written in the header comment of index.ts: "This process has no policy engine and no audit trail of its own; its direct-port boundary is the computer token" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:73-76). agent-computer judges nothing about whether an action should happen: the judgment lives in the server's gateway, and the audit row is already on disk before this computer is called at all. The computer handles "how", never "whether". That is why it can safely hand out a browser and a shell: what it trusts is not the caller's intent but the deployment fact that every call passed the gateway first.

    The first structural principle: decisions do not live next to the browser

    Open agent-computer/src/ and you see an unusual structure. The entry index.ts runs over sixteen hundred lines, imports Playwright at module scope, and executes serve() at the top level. The other twenty-some files either import no Playwright at all or only import type, which is erased at runtime, so tests importing them need no Chrome. In the whole directory, exactly one file value-imports chromium: profiles.ts (profiles.ts:38). That is a structural principle, enforced to the point of stubbornness: any decision with a wrong answer to pick is stripped out into a pure module that does not depend on the browser.

    The same rationale appears in the header comments of at least six files. The authorisation.ts version is the most complete:

    It lives here rather than in index.ts because that file imports Playwright at module scope, so anything in it needs Chrome merely to be imported by a test. The same reasoning moved the control state machine out: if a decision matters, it does not belong next to chromium.launch(). — agent-computer/src/authorisation.ts:7-9

    index.ts imports Playwright at module scope, so any logic left inside it needs Chrome merely to be imported by a test. bot-id.ts, sessions.ts, viewer.ts, browser-eviction.ts, and profile-listing.ts each carry a synonymous sentence in their headers. The sessions.ts header spells out the type-erasure step as well: "Page comes in as a type only, which is erased at runtime" (agent-computer/src/sessions.ts:4-9, 27). The profile-listing.ts header comes with an incident attached: the rule once lived in both the implementation and the test, and deleting the production-side filter function left the suite fully green, because the test was validating its own copy (agent-computer/src/profile-listing.ts:3-9). The principle's consequence is direct: a decision must be testable without launching a browser.

    Stripped-out module The decision it owns
    authorisation.ts token comparison, which paths count as "actions" (ACTING_PATHS)
    bot-id.ts the Bot id allowlist, the one way to spell a profile path
    browser-eviction.ts whom the LRU evicts, whom the idle sweep reaps
    control.ts / control-store.ts the control state machine, persistence invariant checks
    sessions.ts when a run changes (changing runs is a decision, not bookkeeping)
    viewer.ts the claim protocol for screen ownership
    env.ts strict parsing of environment variables and bounded teardown

    This is the same philosophy as the tenant package pipeline's handwritten validators in Chapter 2: put decisions where they can fail fast, deterministically, and without heavy equipment. The validator does not depend on the database; the control state machine does not depend on Chromium. Testing these files needs no browser image; they run as millisecond pure-function assertions. What remains in index.ts is wiring: routes, serialization, connecting the decision modules' conclusions to Playwright calls. Wiring can be wrong, but wiring errors surface in integration tests. Decision errors must surface in unit tests, because decisions are where a wrong answer is available.

    The boot chain: order is defense

    agent-computer's boot sequence is written at the top level of index.ts, and the order itself is the defense, layer by layer. Every step refuses to boot on failure rather than running degraded. Fail-closed here is the startup order, not a configuration option.

    The first step admits no negotiation: missing COMPUTER_TOKEN means process.exit(1). The comment explains why this is not fussiness: "Refusing to start without a token makes missing authentication a deployment failure, never an open computer" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:104-105). A browser holding real login state that comes up with a default or empty password is an open door, not a usability problem. Refusing to start turns "forgot to configure the secret" from a security hole into a deployment error. The second step, setDefaultAutoSelectFamily(false), has a provenance too: why Bun's multi-address racing must be turned off is the incident history in Chapter 8's egress section.

    The fourth step deserves a line-by-line look, because the failure shape it prevents is so typical:

    typescript
    // agent-computer/src/index.ts:222-236
async function assertWritable(label: string, directory: string) {
  const probe = join(directory, `.openbot-write-probe-${process.pid}`);
  try {
    await mkdir(directory, { recursive: true });
    await writeFile(probe, "");
    await rm(probe, { force: true });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(
      `${label} at ${directory} is not writable by uid ${process.getuid?.() ?? "unknown"}: ${String(error)}. ` +
        "A Bot's files and browser profile live here, and a profile this process cannot write is one Chromium silently replaces with a throwaway, so this refuses to start instead. " +
        "On Kubernetes this usually means the volume's storage class does not apply fsGroup, which hostPath-backed provisioners such as local-path do not: chown it to the pod's uid, or set computers.podSecurityContext to null.",
    );
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

    Write a probe file, then delete it. Why such a fuss? Because Chromium does not report an unwritable profile: launchPersistentContext silently falls back to a throwaway profile, the container health check stays green, and the Bot is logged out of every site. The comment's verdict is painfully precise: "the failure that actually happens in the field is a green pod and an empty profile, which is the worst shape a failure can take: nothing to read, and a week of logins gone" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:209-211). The comment even names the real-world trigger: k3s's default local-path provisioner uses hostPath volumes and does not report fsGroup capability, so uid 1001 gets a directory it cannot even list. The probe turns all of this into a CrashLoopBackOff with a named cause that operations can act on directly.

    The egress filter starts before any browser exists, "so nothing escapes it" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:276-280). Its four modes and its always-deny list are Chapter 8's story; here only the order matters: the filter exists before the browser exists, and the network exit has never had an unwatched moment.

    Managed Chromium: a browser that holds up to scrutiny

    The Bot's browser sits in an awkward spot: many of the sites it deals with run bot detection, and headless Chromium happens to be the browser bot detection is best at recognizing: HeadlessChrome in the UA, no GPU rendering path, a pile of missing traits that windowed browsers have. The comment is blunt: Cloudflare guards sites like ChatGPT and Canva and challenges headless browsers on sight (agent-computer/src/browser-runtime.ts:26-31).

    So on Linux the default is headed mode. Where does the window go? Into an in-process Xvfb: the container starts its own virtual X server, at a display resolution of 1280×800, appearing nowhere, and the live screen's transport is unchanged because of it. The readiness probe for starting Xvfb is a detail worth stealing: Xvfb starts with -displayfd 3, and the spawn sets fd 3 to a private pipe (stdio: ["ignore", "ignore", "inherit", "pipe"], agent-computer/src/virtual-display.ts:46-50). Xvfb writes the display number to this fd only after the display is truly usable: "so a stale socket or another X server can never satisfy our readiness check". A stale socket file or another X server cannot satisfy this readiness check; the ready signal comes from "this Xvfb announcing itself ready", never from "something that looks like a socket sitting in the filesystem".

    The other anti-detection measure needs its boundary stated clearly. The launch arguments include --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:104-115), plus ignoreDefaultArgs:["--enable-automation"] (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:484), removing automation traces like navigator.webdriver. The comment immediately declares the motive and the limit: this exists so that a person taking over can log into Google and other sites that refuse automation; it is no way around governance, "It does not change what the Bot may do". What the Bot may do is decided by the gateway's policy, not by the browser's fingerprint. The distinction matters: the fingerprint solves "will the site let a person log in", not "what is the Bot allowed to do".

    For persistence, OpenBot explicitly rejected Playwright's official export approach, and the original text is worth quoting:

    Persistent context, not a saved storage state. Playwright can export cookies and localStorage as JSON and replay them, and that is the wrong tool here: it captures what the automation knew about, on demand, and misses IndexedDB, service workers, and anything written after the snapshot. — agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:6-9

    storageState exports "what the automation knew about at the time": it misses IndexedDB, misses service workers, misses everything written after the snapshot. launchPersistentContext instead points at a real user-data directory and lets the browser persist itself the way it does on a desktop; the directory hangs on the /profiles volume, so the container can die and the directory remains. The road not taken teaches more than the one taken: state export is the automation keeping the browser's books, a persistent profile is the browser keeping its own books, and the former always loses entries.

    Two more details, both from "tested it, and the docs were wrong":

    WebRTC gets locked into the proxy by editing the Preferences file, not by a command-line switch. Chromium's WebRTC goes over UDP and walks straight past the HTTP proxy unless told otherwise. The official switch --force-webrtc-ip-handling-policy no longer works on current Chromium; the comment records the experiment: "the switch on the command line, packets still sent" (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:122-125). So the implementation edits Default/Preferences under the profile directory directly, writes webrtc.ip_handling_policy=disable_non_proxied_udp, and merges it into the existing Preferences rather than wiping the other preferences the profile remembers (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:127-148).

    The Chromium sandbox is off by default, and that is not a preference. --no-sandbox is the default, because Docker's default seccomp profile blocks the syscalls the Chromium sandbox needs to create user namespaces. A container that does nothing special gets No usable sandbox!, and the browser does not start at all. The comment emphasizes in all caps: "OFF BY DEFAULT, AND THAT IS NOT A PREFERENCE" (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:82-84). Where the host allows it, turn it on (COMPUTER_SANDBOX=on); serverless platforms like Fargate cannot, and the compensating control is "non-root user, plus the gVisor underneath". The key point: whatever the switch's state, the boot log says it out loud, "An operator should not have to read this file to find out whether the browser rendering the open internet is sandboxed" (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:96-97). The security posture must be observable, not buried in source.

    Last, capacity discipline. Each resident Chromium costs a few hundred MB, and a "one Bot per employee" deployment drifts toward "one resident browser per employee" until the container is killed for memory (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:226-233). The countermeasures: COMPUTER_MAX_BROWSERS caps at 8 by default with LRU eviction; COMPUTER_BROWSER_IDLE_MS sweeps browsers idle for 30 minutes by default, with 0 meaning resident forever; a sweep runs every 60 seconds. LRU eviction deliberately runs after a new launch, "so the Bot that just asked is never the one closed" (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:361-363). Closing a browser loses nothing: the profile is on disk, and the next launch picks up where the last left off.

    Deep Dive: The thirty-second insurance for session cookies

    A persistent profile has the same hole as a desktop browser: Chromium discards session cookies with no expires on exit. On the desktop this hardly matters, because the browser hardly exits. Here, "exit" means the pod suspended for idleness, the node drained, the image updated and the container deleted, so "every site that signs in with only a session cookie asks the Bot to log in again after each of these events" (agent-computer/src/session-cookies.ts:4-9).

    The compensating mechanism is a keeper: every 30 seconds it serializes session cookies to openbot-session-cookies.json in the profile directory (a temp file plus an atomic rename, 0600 permissions), and before the next launch's first navigation it puts them back with context.addCookies: "the first request a site sees from this launch is already signed in" (agent-computer/src/profiles.ts:498-501). Only session cookies are written, because the ones with expires are already in the profile, and writing both would make one cookie with two sources of truth (agent-computer/src/session-cookies.ts:11-13). The file lives in the Bot's profile directory, so it shares the profile's volume and lifetime: no other Bot's browser can read it, and reset deletes it along with the profile. The logging discipline is just as strict: only counts and reasons get logged, "A cookie's value is a credential and never reaches a log" (agent-computer/src/session-cookies.ts:83).

    ARIA snapshots: address by reference, not by pixel

    How does a Bot "see" a page? OpenBot's answer is written in the header of index.ts:

    Elements are addressed by reference, not by pixel. …That is the accessibility-tree-first driver this is built on, and it is why filling in a form needs no vision model at all: the Bot reads a list of fields rather than squinting at a picture and guessing coordinates. — agent-computer/src/index.ts:82-86

    Say first what was not built: there is no vision model here. No screenshot sent to a multimodal model to guess coordinates, no "click (412, 300)". POST /snapshot calls Playwright's ariaSnapshot({mode:"ai"}), gets the page's accessibility tree as YAML, and parses it into a flat element list: every interactive element carries a ref, a role, an accessible name, its current value, and its checked state, capped at 200 elements. The Bot reads a list of fields, not a picture. Pixels are the fallback, kept for canvas-style pages that expose no elements. The reasons for choosing the accessibility tree over stamping attributes into the DOM are also written in the comments: refs stay outside the page, survive framework re-renders, resolve accessible names, and can reach into iframes (agent-computer/src/index.ts:431-433).

    Incidentally, /snapshot is a POST rather than a GET, out of HTTP semantic hygiene: "it mutates the page, stamping every element it describes, and a GET that changes the document is a lie that caches and prefetchers eventually punish" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:1350-1352).

    Snapshots go stale by nature: the page changes, and a ref points at something that no longer exists or has changed. The staleness defense is two-dimensional, and each dimension handles one kind of "old".

    The first dimension is generation: each session holds a snapshotId counter, and taking a snapshot increments it first; navigation, switching to a new window, login submission, and reset all increment it too, invalidating every old ref. The action endpoints (/click, /type, /key, /scroll) carry the snapshotId the caller claims, and a mismatch throws StaleSnapshotError: a 409 with an instruction for the model, "take a new snapshot and use the refs from it". Chapter 5 covered how this 409 means the opposite of HumanHasControlError (one says "re-snapshot", the other says "hands off"); here you see the mechanism that produces it.

    The second dimension is the run: a uuid for one browser incarnation. Generation alone is not enough: "this process mints one at zero for every session that is new, so a restart, a redeploy, an eviction…all produce a page at generation one that looks older than the page the server still has" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:1050-1056). A restart, a redeploy, an idle eviction all produce a brand-new page at generation 1 that looks older than the page the server still holds. The server orders snapshots by the (run, generation) pair, so snapshots from an old run go stale on their own. After a reset you must explicitly renewRun, otherwise "the late save inserts the wiped page straight back, and every ref on it goes on resolving" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:1104-1113): an in-flight old snapshot would insert the just-wiped page back as-is. Note that renewRun deliberately leaves the generation counter untouched: zeroing it would fake a restart on a counter that never restarted (agent-computer/src/sessions.ts:175-177).

    Below generation there is runtime enforcement: Playwright's aria-ref selector engine (the same one its MCP server uses) resolves refs only against the latest snapshot; an element that leaves the document fails to resolve, a changed role or accessible name mints a new ref, and a recycled DOM node inherits no old ref (agent-computer/src/index.ts:163-171). The caller-side generation check is a clear error for humans to read; the engine's rules are the real wall.

    Finally, a defense so cheap it is nearly free:

    typescript
    // agent-computer/src/index.ts:504-517
async function resolveRef(
  session: BotSession,
  target: Page,
  ref: string,
  expectedSnapshotId: number | undefined,
) {
  const locator = locateRef(session, target, ref, expectedSnapshotId);
  if ((await locator.count()) === 0) {
    throw new StaleSnapshotError(
      `Nothing on this page has the ref ${ref}. Take a new snapshot and use the refs it returns.`,
    );
  }
  return locator;
}

    "A generation check is not an existence check" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:493-495). The model can perfectly well invent a ref that has the right generation but does not exist on the page: it comes from the current snapshot, passes locateRef, and then Playwright dumbly waits out the whole action timeout before reporting an internal call log nobody can use. count() returns immediately and turns an "invented ref" into an actionable hint within milliseconds. The check costs one selector count; the payoff is turning model hallucination from a timeout black hole into a self-correcting signal.

    Control mutual exclusion: there is only one steering wheel

    Chapter 5 covered the approval gate, and Chapter 6 covered the audit restraint during human takeover. Here is the mechanism of the takeover itself: one computer, one steering wheel, and the person and the Bot cannot both hold it.

    The state machine's core is a 48-line primitive, action-barrier.ts: synchronous admission, asynchronous draining, "No work is queued or replayed". enter() throws while the barrier is closed; close() rejects new actions; drain() waits for every admitted action to exit, with a 30-second deadline, and on timeout throws "An admitted action is still finishing; human control has not been granted. Try taking control again." The handoff order is etched into take():

    typescript
    // agent-computer/src/control.ts:379-393
barrier.close();
// Never await here from requestHelp: a navigation detector still owns its action lease.
await barrier.drain(options.drainTimeoutMs);
const after = intended(requestId);
if (after.status === "taken" && data.holder === "human") return get();
if (after.status !== "waiting")
  throw new ControlRequestError(
    "That request is no longer waiting for control.",
    409,
  );
after.status = "taken";
after.updatedAt = now();
delete after.expiresAt;
data.holder = "human";

    Close the gate first, wait for the floor to empty, then re-validate that the request is still waiting (during drain's 30 seconds it may have expired or been cancelled), and only then hand over. The world changed between two awaits, so validation runs twice. One easily missed fact: the barrier closes the instant requestHelp is called, "Before any persistence or awaited browser operation" (agent-computer/src/control.ts:342). Once a Bot asks for help, its action admission closes immediately, without waiting for the person to arrive. A Bot that asks for help cannot keep acting while it waits.

    Which paths count as "actions" is answered by one single list at the dispatcher layer, rather than each handler remembering to check on its own:

    typescript
    // agent-computer/src/authorisation.ts:68-83
const ACTING_PATHS = new Set([
  "/navigate",
  "/click",
  "/type",
  "/key",
  "/scroll",
  "/exec",
  "/files/write",
  // Typing a person's login into the page. Refused while they hold the wheel, like any other typing.
  "/sign-in/fill",
  "/sign-in/code",
]);

export function actsOnTheComputer(pathname: string): boolean {
  return ACTING_PATHS.has(pathname);
}

    This list grew out of an incident. The comment records it plainly: "The handler that forgets is the whole defect: the shell shipped without this check and ran commands underneath a person who had taken the browser at a login wall" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:780-784). Checks scattered across handlers are exactly the thing the next endpoint will forget; the list lives in the dispatcher, and a new endpoint comes under control only by being added to the list. The direction of forgetting is reversed.

    What is outside the list carries meaning too: reads are not actions. /files/read and /files/list stay open, "so a Bot that has been stopped can still read its own notes and explain what it was doing" (agent-computer/src/authorisation.ts:64-66). A Bot whose wheel has been taken can still read its own notes and explain to the person what it was doing, which is usually exactly the answer the person who took the wheel wants.

    The human side has an easily forgotten check of its own. humanMayDrive() is defined as holder==="human" && barrier.pending()===0 (agent-computer/src/control.ts:463-465): nominally holding the wheel is not enough; every remaining admitted action must have exited too. A connected live-screen socket is not permission, and owning the screen is not permission either: in index.ts, input messages pass two gates, and the two gates reject different things (agent-computer/src/index.ts:671-679). The socket is a transport-layer fact; permission is a state-machine fact. Using the former in place of the latter mistakes "can see" for "may act".

    Returning control is not a simple switch flip. release() sets resumeSnapshotRequired=true: while the person held the wheel, the person changed the page, and the Bot's snapshot is void; its next browser-mutating action must take a new snapshot first, or it receives SnapshotRequiredError (409). Pure reads are unaffected. The design's subtext is respect for the person: it does not assume the person changed nothing, and it does not punish the Bot for reading the page the person left behind.

    Finally, this state machine is persisted at /profiles/.control/<botId>.json, with invariants validated in both directions on load and save, "Never salvage corrupt data as success" (agent-computer/src/control-store.ts:120); once persistence fails, all further writes are blocked and the barrier closes: with storage broken, every action on the computer stops until storage is repaired (agent-computer/src/control.ts:107-117). On process restart, recovered active requests and human-hold state are immediately marked interrupted: "A persisted active request names a page in a previous process. Never call that completion" (agent-computer/src/control.ts:267-272). An active request from a previous process must never be declared complete by this one. This is the same philosophy as the audit trail: state may lose people, but it must not invent them.

    The shell: hands, not judgment

    /exec gives the Bot a real shell: it can apt-get install, run pipelines, write files. Its self-positioning is written at the top of the file and worth quoting in full:

    Nothing here decides whether a command may run. The gateway decides, against the deployment's policy, and writes the audit row before this is called at all, the same as it does for a click. This file is the hands, not the judgement. — agent-computer/src/shell.ts:11-13

    Judgment lives in Chapter 5's gateway, the audit row lands before the call, and this file only governs the shape of the call: it cannot run forever (default 120 seconds, clamped to 1–600), it cannot output without bound, cwd is the workspace, and it does not inherit the process environment.

    Environment inheritance uses an allowlist, and one sentence sentences the deny-list approach to death:

    A deny list is the secrets that existed on the day it was written; the next variable added to a deployment is not on it. — agent-computer/src/shell.ts:54-56

    So only these get copied: PATH, locale (LANG/LANGUAGE/LC_*), the terminal trio, ten proxy variables (userinfo stripped first, "Proxy URLs routinely carry a password"), plus variables explicitly named by COMPUTER_SHELL_ENV. HOME points at the workspace: a command writing to ~ should write where the Bot's files already live.

    Beyond the allowlist there is a second list of "not passed even when named": NEVER_PASSED enumerates twelve names: BASH_ENV, ENV, BASH_XTRACEFD, BASHOPTS, SHELLOPTS, CDPATH, GLOBIGNORE, IFS, LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, LD_AUDIT, PS4 (agent-computer/src/shell.ts:137-150).

    These twelve differ in kind from something like GITHUB_TOKEN: "They do not give a command information, they give it a hook that runs before every later command, which is the .bash_profile hole arriving through the front door" (agent-computer/src/shell.ts:124-127). BASH_ENV is the one that survives under -c: bash expands it for non-interactive shells and sources the file it names. The handling is deliberate too: refuse with a warning, rather than silently dropping. An operator who sets such a variable had a purpose in mind and deserves to be told it did not happen.

    The same thinking explains bash -c over bash -lc. A login shell sources $HOME/.bash_profile, and HOME is the workspace, the very place the Bot can write with computer_write_file. There was a time when the Bot could leave behind a .bash_profile that ran before every later command: rank its own apt-get ahead in PATH while the audit row still says apt-get --version. The comment's verdict is worth remembering:

    A permissive shell is a decision a deployment can make. A trail that describes something other than what ran is not. — agent-computer/src/shell.ts:255-256

    Note that this is no longer a security argument but an audit-integrity argument, and it connects directly to Chapter 6: an audit row's value depends on the reality it describes.

    Pipes, redirection, and && are deliberately kept. "Refusing them would leave something that runs one binary and calls itself a shell…there is no safe way to read a command's intent from its text, so nothing here tries" (agent-computer/src/shell.ts:240-248). Not parsing command text for intent is an honest boundary statement: that is the container's job ("ISOLATION IS THE CONTAINER'S JOB"), and it is why a deployment with a shared container should not give Bots a shell.

    Output discipline is one more lesson made permanent: a 64KB cap, trimmed while collecting (once twice the threshold has arrived, cut to the last 64KB and set truncated), rather than a one-time clamp at the end. The incident being fixed: cat on a large file dragged the process down along with every Bot's browser it held. Why keep the tail? "A command that fails says why in its last lines". Why must truncation be conveyed? "Output that quietly ends is output a model reads as the whole answer" (agent-computer/src/shell.ts:288-289). On stop, kill the whole process group (kill(-pid, "SIGKILL")), because bash -c "sleep 600 | cat" leaves sleep and cat holding inherited pipes, and close never fires.

    Constraint Value What it prevents
    Timeout default 120s, clamped to [1s, 600s] a hung command means a hung Bot
    Output 64KB, trimmed while collecting, tail kept, truncated always set large output dragging the process down; silent truncation misleading the model
    cwd workspace commands and file tools see the same directory
    Environment allowlist plus COMPUTER_SHELL_ENV naming env cannot print the deployment's secrets
    Process group detached + kill(-pid) pipeline background processes die with the command

    Storage topology: the two volumes' division of labor

    The computer's persistence ultimately lands on two volumes, and those volumes are deployment artifacts: the supervisor derives their names and mounts them when creating the container:

    typescript
    // supervisor/src/docker.ts:422-429
Binds: [
  `${names.profileVolume}:/profiles`,
  `${names.workspaceVolume}:/workspace`,
  // Read-only: a computer asks the agent what it is and has nothing to tell it.
  ...(options.spireSocketVolume
    ? [`${options.spireSocketVolume}:/tmp/spire-agent/public:ro`]
    : []),
],

    The comment points out the semantic weight of the mounts: "This is what turns the path confinement inside the computer from a boundary between a Bot and the host into a boundary between one Bot and another" (supervisor/src/docker.ts:420-421).

    The two volumes' lifecycles differ on purpose. stop gives the container a 30-second grace period, enough for Chromium to flush its profile and matching compose's grace period, while storage stays untouched and login state survives (supervisor/src/docker.ts:607-620). reset deletes the container and the profile volume but keeps the workspace, for a one-sentence reason: "files a Bot was asked to produce are work, not browser state" (supervisor/src/docker.ts:625-626). Reset is unrecoverable, so it is its own endpoint rather than a parameter of stop: "a person clicking 'stop' must not be able to discard a login by mistyping a parameter" (agent-computer/src/index.ts:1095-1097).

    The control state file also lives on the profile volume (/profiles/.control/), and the session-cookie keeper file lives in the profile directory too. Location is isolation; location is reset semantics: these files live and die with the state they describe, and reset takes everything it should take and leaves everything it should leave. This is "boundaries live in the deployment" at the storage layer: isolation strength and reset semantics are not written in an application-level if; they are written in the mount table and the volume lifecycles.

    Apply This

    The five patterns in this chapter each port into any system where an automation holds real state.

    Pattern one: strip decisions out of the heavy-side-effect entry point. What problem it solves: the entry file imports a browser, a database, or some other heavy client, so business rules left inside it cannot be tested lightly, and untested rules get tested by nobody. How to adapt: set a rule for your entry point: it does wiring only. Every judgment with a wrong answer available moves into a pure module, with the reason written in the file header (the authorisation.ts wording can be copied verbatim). The pitfall: the rules will crawl back into the entry point. OpenBot's defense is writing the reason into at least six file headers, so every latecomer reads the predecessors' verdict before taking the shortcut.

    Pattern two: probe real capabilities at boot; do not trust the mount. What problem it solves: a depended-upon runtime (a volume, a secret, a display service) silently degrades while the process stays healthy and runs the wrong thing, the "green pod with an empty profile". How to adapt: at startup, perform one real operation against each critical dependency (write a probe file and delete it), fail-closed, with the error message naming which directory, which uid, and how to fix it. The pitfall: the probe result must decide the process's life and death, not print a warning and continue. An observable failure is fail-closed; an ignored failure is a postponed disaster.

    Pattern three: two-dimensional staleness tokens. What problem it solves: a single counter (generation or version) restarts from zero after a process restart, making old snapshots look newer than new ones while stale references keep resolving. How to adapt: for any design where a client holds a reference to server-side state, order and invalidate by the (run uuid, generation) pair; when minting a new run, do not zero the generation along the way, because that fakes a restart on a counter that never restarted. The pitfall: a generation check is not an existence check. A client can perfectly well invent a reference with the right generation; one cheap count() turns the hallucination into an actionable error in milliseconds.

    Pattern four: barrier-style handover. What problem it solves: when two controllers (a person and an automation, a primary and a standby) switch, in-flight operations crush the new holder. How to adapt: hand over in three steps: close the gate against new actions first, then drain admitted actions with a deadline, then re-validate after the drain that the request is still valid, and only then transfer. Close the gate the moment help is requested, before the other party arrives. The pitfall: do not take transport-layer facts as permission. A connected socket or a visible screen is not authorization to act; permission comes only from the state machine. Also, after the handover completes, remember to invalidate the old holder's context (OpenBot forces re-observation with resumeSnapshotRequired).

    Pattern five: a subprocess environment allowlist plus a "never pass" list. What problem it solves: a subprocess inheriting the parent's environment means env prints every secret in the deployment, and a deny list never catches up with new variables. How to adapt: copy an allowlist of clearly needed categories (PATH, locale, terminal, proxy, remembering to strip userinfo), add an operator naming channel (COMPUTER_SHELL_ENV), and stack a layer of hook-type variables refused even when named (BASH_ENV, LD_PRELOAD, and other things that "install a hook before every later command"), refusing with a warning rather than a silent drop. The pitfall: the shell's startup files. The difference between bash -c and bash -lc is whether .bash_profile executes, and when HOME is a directory the automation can write, that difference is the life or death of audit integrity.

    This chapter looked inside the computer: how it boots, how it drives the browser, how the wheel passes between a person and a Bot. The next chapter steps out of the chassis to look at this computer's boundaries: how egress traffic gets filtered, how secrets are kept out of every read-back, and how a Bot asks for help with dignity when it hits a CAPTCHA.

    ← Chapter 6: The Audit Trail: Who Did It, and What Started ItChapter 8: The Computer's Boundaries: Egress, Secrets, and Asking for Help →

    Chapter 8: The Computer's Boundaries: Egress, Secrets, and Asking for Help

    Chapter 7 took agent-computer itself apart: resident Chromium, persistent profiles, ARIA snapshots and refs, control mutual exclusion, an allowlist shell. A fenced computer, where the fence is the container, and everything inside the fence has been said. But a fence is not an island. The browser has to reach the network, login forms need passwords filled in, and websites will keep automated traffic out. A computer that connects to nothing, touches no secrets, and dies in front of every wall is a computer no company would hire.

    This chapter answers the question of three doors in the wall. The first faces outward: who decides what traffic may leave. A filtering proxy living on loopback, plus a rare honest statement: what it cannot stop, it says so. The second faces inward: how secrets never reach the model. A password exists only on the two-point path from form to browser, and three read-back channels each have their checkpoint. The third faces upward: what to do with a wall you cannot get through. CAPTCHAs are never solved; the Bot only says "I am stuck, and why", then hands the scene to a person as-is. Along the way there is a proposition in the reverse direction: should the Bot proactively identify itself to every website.

    The three doors share one shape: no decision is made inside the computer process. Egress policy is pushed by the server, and the computer and the server share one rules engine. The password-handling rules are written in one module's constitution, not scattered across call sites. The authority over a help request always belongs to the person. The computer is hands, not judgement: this is "boundaries live in the deployment, not the model" landing once more at the process level. By the end of this chapter you will know how far an agent system's egress narrowing, secret hygiene, and human-machine handoff can go, and the reason for each thing that was not built.

    Egress: a filtering proxy living on loopback

    Get the threat model straight first. The Bot's computer stores real login state. This is the capability Chapter 7 insisted on persistent profiles to buy, and it is also the price: for a Bot led astray by prompt injection, the most valuable action in its hands is not deleting files but POSTing the Salesforce cookies to the attacker's server. Files are written to volumes, and volumes have boundaries; traffic leaves the machine, and the network has none. So egress must be narrowed, and narrowed inside the process: network policy outside the container cannot handle granularity like "this Bot may reach GitHub, that Bot may not".

    OpenBot's answer is an HTTP filtering proxy running inside the agent-computer process on a random 127.0.0.1 port, started before any browser. The browser does not reach the network directly: Playwright's launch arguments point it at this filter, and, the first elegant move here, the Bot's identity is encoded in the proxy credentials:

    typescript
    if (filter) {
  return {
    server: `http://127.0.0.1:${filter.port}`,
    username: botId,
    password: filter.secret,
  };
}

    — agent-computer/src/egress.ts:57-63. The username is the Bot id; the password is a random secret generated at process start. This is a routing mechanism rather than an authentication mechanism: one computer may have several Bots' browsers alive at once, and every CONNECT tunnel each browser opens carries its identity, so one filter can hold multi-Bot policy and decide per connection. The filter validates the identity itself (it issued the secret); a Bot cannot impersonate anyone, because it has no idea what to fill in. The shell goes through the same filter: HTTP(S)_PROXY is injected into the subprocess environment, with userinfo stripped before copying. Why strip it was covered in Chapter 7's shell section: proxy URLs routinely carry a password. The filter then chains to the upstream configured by EGRESS_PROXY_<BOT>, a residential proxy or the like, keeping a different exit address for each Bot in the peer's eyes. Three layers each own one thing: the filter owns permission, the upstream owns the identity address, and the container network owns the backstop.

    Boot order is part of the defense too: the filter starts before any browser, "so nothing escapes it" (index.ts:280), and the first browser connection already has no unexamined path. The same process carries a reverse discipline: the filter's own address does not enter this process's environment variables; it is only passed to shell subprocesses. The reason is a live experiment: Bun's http.request follows HTTP_PROXY and ignores options like agent:false, so requests the filter forwarded out turned around and came back to the filter itself, an infinite loop, "a page waiting behind one never loaded" (egress.ts:777-783). Identity credentials, loop avoidance, shell injection: three things revolve around the same loopback port.

    Four modes, one always-deny list

    The policy itself is simple: one table per computer, hot-pushed by the server (PUT /egress-policy), effective on the next connection, with nothing to restart. Four modes:

    Mode Meaning Typical use
    allow_all allow everything (except the always-deny list) default; trust the Bot to browse freely
    defaults_plus_allowlist eighteen development registries and source hosts plus a custom list development Bots: can install packages, cannot wander
    allowlist_only only the custom list business Bots: may touch only the designated SaaS
    deny_all deny everything a Bot with cloud network access turned off

    "Defaults" is a hardcoded list: GitHub, npm, PyPI, crates, Go, Debian/Ubuntu, Docker Hub, "the package registries and source hosts a development computer needs to install anything at all" (egress.ts:201-224). The decision order is fixed: always-deny list, then allow_all allows, then deny_all denies, then domain rules (suffix match), then CIDR+port rules (a hit only when all resolved addresses fall inside the same rule), then default deny. Connections without Bot credentials (the shell, for instance) follow another set of rules: if the machine has exactly one policy, use it; if it has several, judge under all policies simultaneously and the strictest wins; if nothing has been pushed yet, deny: "No network policy has reached this computer yet, so nothing may leave it" (egress.ts:544-546). This is fail-closed: no policy does not mean "not configured yet, so allow"; it means "nothing may pass". The one remaining gap is EGRESS_POLICY_REQUIRED=0, for a computer running standalone without the server: a switch that must be explicitly declared as "I know no policy will come", not a silent default.

    The always-deny list deserves its own look, because it holds things that must not be allowed in any mode, allow_all included:

    typescript
    const ALWAYS_DENIED: readonly [string, number, "ipv4" | "ipv6"][] = [
  ["169.254.0.0", 16, "ipv4"],
  ["100.100.100.200", 32, "ipv4"],
  ["fe80::", 10, "ipv6"],
  ["fd00:ec2::254", 128, "ipv6"],
  ["fd20:ce::254", 128, "ipv6"],
];
