    — agent-computer/src/egress.ts:363-369. 169.254.169.254 is the shared metadata endpoint of AWS, Azure, GCP, and Oracle, where a cloud machine's temporary credentials are issued; Alibaba Cloud's counterpart and two IPv6 variants are also listed. Why make it a separate layer instead of a built-in rule in the policy table? Because policy is written by the deployer: it gets changed, it gets wrong, it has allow_all. "No Bot should ever get the host cloud's credentials" is a platform-level fact and should not depend on anyone remembering to configure it. The list also recognizes encoded variants: IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:169.254.169.254) and NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) are manually expanded and re-checked; a list that blocks only dotted decimal is decoration on an IPv6 network. The source comment adds a stinger: the Helm chart's NetworkPolicy also blocks 169.254/16, but it is off by default and never mentions IPv6, "so this is the guard a default install actually has" (egress.ts:358-362).

    Rule parsing itself treats input as hostile. A CIDR rule written as 10.0.0.5/ is rejected: Number("") yields 0, and accepting it equals "allow every address". Addresses with a zone id are rejected: they pass isIP but blow up on the rule's first use (egress.ts:241-245). Domain and port each have a handwritten regex guarding them. Better to reject a rule at push time than to allow a misunderstanding at connection time. Refusal is not silent either: a refused connection gets a 403 with an x-openbot-egress: refused header and a readable reason (egress.ts:724-728), so troubleshooting does not have to guess where the traffic went. When the admin UI displays egress configuration, it returns hostnames only: "A proxy URL routinely carries a password, and this string is rendered in a browser" (egress.ts:143-147). The egress policy's read-out channel obeys the same discipline as the secrets' read-back channels.

    Two more user-input tolerances at the configuration entry, both incidents made permanent. First, splitProxyCredentials accepts bare host:port spelling: an operator writing a proxy is not thinking of a URL, and new URL reads proxy.internal:8080 as scheme proxy.internal: plus path 8080, throwing nothing and returning empty strings for username and password. So the bot:s3cret@proxy.internal:8080 spelling would leave the password inside the server string handed out. The implementation re-parses with a synthetic scheme and strips it after splitting, so both spellings split correctly while the server string still reads the way it was written (egress.ts:83-89).

    Second, decodeUserinfo falls back to the original text on an illegal %: a % not followed by two hex digits is a character someone typed into a password, not an escape, and decodeURIComponent throws URIError at it. That exception type escaped every caller here, which only catches TypeError, and since the shell strips credentials from proxy variables before every command, "one such password made every /exec fail" (egress.ts:130-141). Pass it through as written, because the way it was written is the intent.

    DNS pinning and a runtime landmine

    Domain judgement has a classic time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) hole: judging resolves the name and gets A; connecting resolves it again and gets B, and B is not on the list. OpenBot's approach is pinning: a name is resolved once, every resolved address is checked, "a name that resolves partly outside is refused rather than connected to whichever address came first" (egress.ts:415-418), and then connections dial only those checked addresses. The same name is never resolved a second time.

    Pinning needs a per-address dialing loop, and a runtime incident history is buried here. The first version used the runtime's autoSelectFamily (the Happy Eyeballs algorithm, racing IPv4/IPv6 concurrently), and ran into a Bun bug: node:net's multi-address connect timer can fire after the connection it belongs to is destroyed, throwing a TypeError nobody can catch, and the whole computer process exits outright. The trigger conditions are exactly a Bot system's daily routine: sites behind Cloudflare resolve to several addresses at once, and challenge pages open and abandon many connections simultaneously, "opening one in a Bot's browser restarted the computer and lost the page the person was being asked to solve" (egress.ts:605-618, the comment cites oven-sh/bun#25633). A browser helping a person solve a challenge restarted the whole machine by opening one connection, and the page in front of the person was gone. Upstream later fixed the bug and the repo has long been running the fixed version, but the manual dialing loop stayed, for the reason written in the comment: walking the checked list one by one is exactly the shape of pinning itself, "it is the right shape regardless of the runtime bug". Dodging the bug was expediency; getting the correctness right along the way was the harvest:

    typescript
    // Pseudocode — illustrates the pattern
async function connectPinned(name: string, port: number): Promise<Socket> {
  const candidates = await resolveAll(name);          // resolve only this once
  for (const addr of candidates) assertEgressOk(addr); // check every address
  for (const addr of v4First(candidates)) {            // IPv4 first
    try {
      return await dialOne(addr, port, ATTEMPT_BUDGET); // dial checked addresses only
    } catch { /* try the next one */ }
  }
  throw new Error("no checked address accepted");
}

    The pattern's weight sits in the words "resolve only once": there is no second trust between check and use. IPv4 first comes from measurement, not preference: container networks often have no IPv6 route, and trying AAAA answers first costs every connection a full wasted timeout (egress.ts:582-592).

    An honest boundary statement

    The module's header comment contains a paragraph most security code does not write:

    WHAT THIS CANNOT STOP: a process that ignores proxy variables and opens a raw socket. That is the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy's job, which this narrows rather than replaces.

    — agent-computer/src/egress.ts:177-178

    The filter works only on traffic that respects proxy variables: Chromium and shell subprocesses are both pointed at it, but any process that opens a raw socket walks right past. So it narrows the boundary rather than constituting it; the real network boundary is at the deployment layer, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, or the container topology Chapter 9 will cover. What makes this statement valuable is its accuracy, not its modesty: a platform engineer who read this comment knows to also configure NetworkPolicy; code that did not write this sentence lets a reviewer believe egress is already solved. A boundary statement is an engineering deliverable, the same as the boundary itself.

    The same rules engine is also imported directly by the server for pre-navigation refusal, "so the two ends cannot disagree" (egress.ts:170-171): when a Bot initiates navigation the server judges once, and when the connection happens the filter judges again, and with the same code at both ends the answers must agree. This is a small specimen of "governance rides the protocol": there is one copy of the rules, riding the push channel to reach both ends. That the rules engine can be shared by both ends still relies on Chapter 7's first structural principle: egress.ts does not import Playwright, and the module header states "proxy parsing tests can run outside the browser image" (egress.ts:13). Decisions must be pure to leave the browser, be tested, and be reused.

    One more form removes the deployment layer entirely: COMPUTER_BROWSER_BACKEND=local-chrome makes the computer drive the local Chrome on a developer's machine, with no container to lean on. The compensation is written into the boot decision: headed is forced (a window on the local desktop is there for the person to watch), the HTTP service binds only 127.0.0.1, and /exec is not exposed at all (browser-runtime.ts:38-49). Where no container backstops, the shell hand does not exist.

    The file boundary: the workspace's three-layer path confinement

    The egress section opened by saying files are written to volumes and volumes have boundaries. In code, that sentence takes the shape of workspace.ts. Chapter 7 covered the volume lifecycle: stop keeps it, reset takes the profile but keeps the workspace. This section covers enforcement inside the volume. The three doors govern what comes in and out; this section guards the last place inside the wall: the filesystem.

    All four of the Bot's file verbs (read, write, list, download) pass through workspace.ts's resolvePath first, and the header comment states the threat model without euphemism: the process is root in the container, write_file("../../etc/passwd") is the obvious first move, and read_file("../../root/.ssh/id_rsa") is the second (workspace.ts:1-7). A persistent writable directory is attack surface by itself.

    The confinement has three layers, also written in the header comment (workspace.ts:9-19):

    Layer Check What it prevents
    One absolute paths refused outright a Bot names files relative to its own workspace; a legitimate request does not start with /
    Two explicit refusal of .. segments lets the error message say exactly what the Bot did wrong, instead of a generic refusal it would retry unchanged
    Three re-check after symlink resolution text paths can lie: a link passes the text checks, then points anywhere in the filesystem

    The first two layers are text judgements, a few lines each. About the second layer, only the motive is worth noting separately: .. could have been left for the containment check to catch along the way, but refusing it explicitly tells the Bot what it did wrong so it can correct itself, rather than handing it a generic refusal it would retry as-is (workspace.ts:124-130).

    The third layer is the one people miss. Where does a symlink come from? Left behind by some earlier write, or carried in by something the Bot downloaded from a page (workspace.ts:14-16). It lies in the workspace, passes every text check, and then points anywhere on the filesystem.

    So the read side resolves the file itself and checks again; on the write side the file may not exist yet, so it resolves the "deepest existing ancestor": walk up to the first directory that really exists and verify it, so writing into a new subdirectory is allowed but aiming through a symlink is not (workspace.ts:136-150, 414-433).

    The containment comparison itself has a trap: startsWith on raw strings lets /workspace-evil impersonate /workspace. The implementation judges by the result of path.relative instead: returning "" means the root itself; starting with .. or crossing roots means outside the wall (workspace.ts:359-373).

    The write side has a second asymmetry, hidden in the last path segment. Proving dirname(target) is inside the wall proves only where a new file would be created; about an already-existing name it proves nothing, because writeFile follows a symlink in the last segment just like readFile does (workspace.ts:154-158).

    So a notes.txt pointing at /root/.ssh/authorized_keys passes all the checks above: no .., not absolute, sitting right in the workspace, while the bytes land outside the volume. The read side refused the same link long ago; the write side is the asymmetric one (workspace.ts:159-162).

    So the write side walks the lstat/readlink chain by hand on the last segment rather than calling realpath: the latter throws on a dangling link, while writeFile happily creates the file where the link points. "A link aimed at a name that does not exist yet would otherwise escape through the failure path rather than the success one, which is the harder version of the bug to notice" (workspace.ts:389-392).

    The chain walks at most 32 hops and treats anything longer as a loop: the kernel gives up at 40, and a chain approaching that number is either circular or deliberately making traversal expensive, neither of which is a file a Bot needs to write (workspace.ts:375-412).

    The stance is confinement, not prohibition: links pointing back inside the workspace work as usual. "refusing every link would be easier and would break legitimate use" (workspace.ts:394-395).

    Why plug this hole for a Bot that already has a shell? The comment's reason is not escape prevention: a Bot holding run_command can write outside the wall directly anyway. It is audit fidelity: decisions and audit rows are made against the path the Bot gave, so a policy written for credentials/ or *.env is evaluated against notes.txt and never sees the file actually being written; the audit row names a file nobody touched (workspace.ts:164-172).

    "A permissive workspace is a decision a deployment can make. A trail that describes a different file from the one on disk is not." (workspace.ts:171-172) This is Chapter 7's shell-section constitution replicated onto the filesystem: behavior may be permissive; description must be true.

    Beyond confinement there are quotas and decoding discipline (workspace.ts:93-98):

    Verb Quota Incidental rule
    read 64,000 bytes always decoded as UTF-8; binary comes back as replacement characters, not base64, "pretending otherwise would invite it to try images"
    write 1MB per call the route does not echo content back: the Bot may be storing something entrusted to it (docs/architecture.md:159)
    list 500 entries recursive files and folders only; other types skipped
    download 100MB streamed back via Bun.file, bytes as-is, does not consume the text read quota

    The four verbs share the same resolvePath, symlink resolution included (workspace.ts:217, 267, 304, 346). A read path over quota sets truncated, saying outright it gave less than the whole thing: "Bounded, and it says when it gave you less than the whole thing" (workspace.ts:260); listing includes folders, "so a Bot can see the shape, not just the leaves" (workspace.ts:79).

    The error-to-status mapping is interface design too: out of bounds 403, missing 404, oversize 413, everything else 400. "Collapsing these into 500 would tell the caller the computer is broken and invite a retry of the same request" (index.ts:1641-1650). Kept apart, the Bot knows which class of error is worth a different approach.

    Two structural decisions deserve naming. First, WorkspaceEntry and the server's public contract (server/src/computer/schema.ts) are deliberately duplicated rather than shared: "this process is a separate deployable with no code in common with the server; the two must be changed together" (workspace.ts:80-85). Between separately deployed artifacts, contracts are synchronized by discipline, not by import.

    Second, the confinement logic lives in a factory parameterized by the root directory and reads no environment variables, so it can be tested against a temp directory rather than by faith (workspace.ts:21-22): Chapter 7's first structural principle, cashed once more on the file boundary.

    The file boundary governs where bytes may land. The next section governs a more slippery class of thing: secrets that have already legally landed in the page, and how they never get read back out.

    Secrets: three lines of defense on the read-back channels

    Egress governs where traffic goes; secrets govern something else: how sensitive values that have entered the page never come back out. The problem is sharper than intuition suggests. A password box shows dots on screen, but Playwright's ARIA snapshot plays no such game: it reports the textbox's current value, which for <input type=password> is the plaintext. The source comment keeps the experimental evidence: "checked against Playwright 1.62: textbox [ref=e4]: hunter2" (secret-masking.ts:5-8). The moment a person finishes typing a password through a private form, the Bot's next snapshot hands the password to the model on a plate; and everything the model reads goes on into the transcript, the audit, the logs, the model provider. Plain text boxes are worse: tokens and one-time codes typed in get not even dots; they sit bare on screenshots and the live screen.

    The defense's shape: do not block the write; mask the read-back. Secrets must be written into the page (otherwise login does not exist); what can be done is to have every "read" channel replace it:

    Read-back channel Defense Mechanism
    ARIA snapshot (for the model) value replaced with [hidden: sensitive field] for filled fields, query the page for sensitive selectors (password, one-time-code, current/new-password, credit-card number, the data-openbot-secret attribute)
    Screenshot (for the model) Playwright's official mask option regions hitting sensitive selectors are blacked out
    Live screen (for the watching person) -webkit-text-security: disc fields a secret has landed in get tagged and drawn as dots even when they are not password fields

    Two companion disciplines tighten the gaps. First, a failed determination is treated as sensitive: the act of querying the page about whether a field is sensitive can itself fail (the element happens to be unloaded), and then the field is treated as sensitive: "hiding an ordinary value is a small cost, and showing a password is not" (secret-masking.ts:82-87). Fail-closed here protects privacy, the same philosophy as egress's deny-all-without-policy. Second, the responses of /type and the human input endpoint return only the character count, never the text: "this response is read by the model and logged by the server, and a value typed into a form is exactly where a password or a card number lives" (index.ts:1593-1595).

    And the most fundamental line of defense is the path itself: the keyboard of a person who has taken over the computer connects the browser directly to the page, never passing the model.

    Nothing a person types here reaches the model. It goes from their keyboard to this browser and stops. That is what makes a password or a one-time code safe to enter during a takeover: not a filter that strips it out afterwards, but a path the model is not on.

    — agent-computer/src/index.ts:1487-1490

    That last line is the first principle of secret-hygiene design: filters leak, break, and get bypassed by newly added read-back channels; where the path does not exist, nothing exists. For the concrete practice of enumerating read-back channels, see pattern three in this chapter's Apply This.

    The password constitution

    Private sign-in has a dedicated passwords/ module on the server side, and its header comment reads like a constitution:

    The rule the whole module is built around: a credential goes from the person's form to the Bot's browser and nowhere else. It is never a tool argument, never a tool result, never a transcript row, never an AG-UI event, never an audit payload and never a log line. The model is told only whether the sign-in worked.

    — server/src/passwords/types.ts:4-7

    Six "never"s name and veto every place a credential might appear. The only thing the model gets to see is whether the sign-in worked, plus an explicit line: "You were not told the credentials and must never ask for them another way" (passwords/service.ts:90-105). The password's lifecycle is compressed to the shortest: it lives only in fill()'s argument and one call to the computer; what lands in the database is not the password itself but an AES-GCM envelope (Chapter 17 covers the encryption division of labor); error strings pass through scrub() before entering storage or display, replacing any occurrence of the secret with [hidden]. Belt and suspenders, because "an error message from a page or a browser is not something this module wrote".

    The module has one more state-machine discipline worth mentioning in passing: the fill lease is 120 seconds, so if the server dies mid-fill the request hangs there and only that long; a request's total lifetime is 15 minutes, and an expiry transition writes the model a custom prompt, roughly: do not ask for the password again in some new disguise. The state machine's details belong to the principle "secrets need a lifecycle too": a login request pending forever is a password entrance open forever.

    The fill's execution side lives in agent-computer's sign-in.ts, which refuses three kinds of pages before typing: the page must still be on the exact origin the person was asked to log in on, because a login must not be carried to a page after a redirect or to one the Bot later navigated to; a login form must actually be detectable on the page; a two-step login that crosses origins (hopping to an identity provider) is not followed, and a person is asked to take over (sign-in.ts:14-19). Stored password vault entries bind to the exact origin: a login stored for https://example.com is never offered to or filled into example.com.evil.test, an http downgrade, or a subdomain, "the way a browser's password manager scopes one" (passwords/types.ts:128-134). Verification codes are never saved: "a verification code is good once". Right after filling, the field is tagged with data-openbot-secret, and the three lines of defense take effect on it immediately.

    Secret requests: fill only, never submit

    There is a second secret channel, solving a subtler situation: the Bot has already focused a field and needs a value it must not know, say the token field in a form. It initiates requestSecret{label, ref, snapshotId}, and the person provides the value via POST /human/secret. This channel's discipline has four clauses (index.ts:878-934): the scope narrows to the pending request, cleared as soon as answered, so it "cannot be used as a general back door to type into the page"; fill only, never submit, because "Committing a form is a separate action through the gateway and audit trail", and submission still goes through the action gateway and audit as its own action; the value is typed and forgotten, not stored, not echoed, not logged, and the response carries only the character count; if the field has already vanished it is treated as non-retryable, closing the request outright so the Bot asks again against a fresh snapshot, otherwise "the person would retype their password into the same dead ref for ever". Note the fourth clause's converse also holds: when typing fails, the request stays, letting the person retry. "Close or keep on failure" is divided by "which failures are retryable", not by one size fits all.

    Error messages are an exit too

    The most covert read-back channel is one nobody built on purpose: the error message. When Playwright errors, it quotes the call it was making, and a selector call's arguments may be sitting on a password. When a database driver errors, it quotes the statement it was running, and the statement's bound parameters may be sitting on ciphertext. So both places set the same rule: the error handler only speaks sentences the module wrote itself.

    Every failure is one of this module's own sentences. A Playwright error can quote the call it was making, and this call's arguments are a password.

    — agent-computer/src/sign-in.ts:21-22

    THE ERROR HANDLER NEVER RELAYS AN UNEXPECTED MESSAGE. A body on these routes carries a password, and an error this module did not write (a database driver's, say) can quote the statement it was running.

    — server/src/passwords/routes.ts:53-56

    The practice is to split errors into two classes: the module's own thrown SignInRefusedError, whose messages are all sentences the module wrote and which may pass through; and everything else, which the route layer collapses into one fixed 500. Chapter 6 covered the same redaction for credential-rotation refusal reasons, where it hurts more because the audit table is append-only and ciphertext that lands there never comes back out: "a secret landing there is not one anybody can take back out" (credentials.ts:633-635). Auditing error messages as a data exit is an intuition this codebase cashes repeatedly; most systems think of it only at the log layer, while error messages go to far more places than logs: response bodies, frontend toasts, model context, audit rows.

    Asking for help: detect, never solve

    The third boundary problem is the least technical-looking: a website pulls out a CAPTCHA; what does the Bot do? The industry has no shortage of answers: solving services, vision models, behavior simulation. OpenBot uses none of them and etches the stance into the module comment: "Does not solve, click, or reload a challenge" (challenge.ts:32). This is a boundary statement, not a capability statement. Solving a captcha equals lying to the website about being human, and that is the dividing line between Chapter 7's headed-Chromium anti-detection and this chapter's Web Bot Auth: removing automation traces lets a person use Google and other automation-refusing sites during takeover, and does not change what the Bot is allowed to do; solving the challenge kicks the person, the final arbiter, out of the loop. The Bot's correct move is raising its hand: "It does not take control: it says it is stuck and why, and a person decides. A Bot that could hand itself to a human could also hand a human a page they never asked to see" (index.ts:832-834).

    So challenge.ts only detects, on three signals: cf-mitigated: challenge in the navigation response headers (Cloudflare says so outright); a visible challenge iframe in the page (reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, challenges.cloudflare.com) or a visible checkbox or button whose text matches human|not a robot|verify|captcha; and six classes of sentence regexes in the body's first twenty thousand characters ("verify you are human" and the like). Generic access-denial pages and pure score blocks are not classified: "Generic access denial and score-only blocks offer no actionable human challenge" (challenge.ts:10). With no actionable challenge, no help request is manufactured. On detection it calls control.requestHelp(reason, toolCallId, kind, page.url()). Note the last parameter: the page URL gets recorded along. This detail supports the recovery logic in the Deep Dive below.

    A help request has a 10-minute TTL, expiring rather than hanging there forever; a model re-sending help for the same toolCall does not stack requests (alias idempotency, handled by Chapter 7's control module). The means to lower trigger frequency live in the configuration layer, not the detection layer: headed Chromium, Web Bot Auth, and residential proxies are all "get stopped less", not "solve it once stopped".

    Recording the URL brings a hygiene problem of its own: a page address may carry a one-time token, a login code, a reset link, a magic link, and the help record stays on disk for a month. So before persisting, pageWorthKeeping keeps only http(s) addresses no longer than 2048 characters and strips Cloudflare's __cf_chl_* parameters: those are one-time challenge tokens, long dead after a restart, and "the page kept is the one the Bot was opening" (control.ts:53-65). When the request ends, the URL is deleted in full by default; only the newest request in the "interrupted by a restart and still within TTL" case keeps its page for recovery (control.ts:121-125). Record the scene, but do not collect secrets along the way: the same discipline as the masking in the previous section.

    Deep Dive: After the handoff, open the page back up

    The reason for recording the URL is a real incident shape: the browser restarting during the help wait happens more often than you would think. A Chromium crash, an idle sweep, a whole-container restart each bring the page back to about:blank. Without recovery logic, the person clicks take control and sees a blank browser, while the Bot still waits for them to solve a challenge that no longer exists. So when takeover happens, the computer first reopens the page that asked for help, then hands over.

    The recovery action is heavily guarded; the core lines:

    typescript
    const target = await currentPage(botId);
if (!isBlankPage(target.url())) return;
if (
  session.humanInputs !== inputsBefore ||
  session.control.pageToRestore() !== want
)
  return;
await navigateWebPage(target, want, RUNTIME.backend, NAVIGATION_TIMEOUT_MS);

    — agent-computer/src/index.ts:361-368. Three gates: if the page is not blank, do nothing (the person or the site moved the page elsewhere, on purpose); if the humanInputs count changed while the browser was starting, do nothing, because the person has already started typing in the blank page, and the page must never be swapped out from under their feet; if the page the request now points at changed, do nothing. Before the gates there is one more gate: only one recovery runs at a time per Bot, deduplicated by a restoringPages set. Both the help call and the "Take control" button trigger recovery, and without the block the second would navigate the page again while the first is still loading (index.ts:348-351). Recovery navigation deliberately goes through the same navigateWebPage the Bot uses, so the egress filter and page admission rules judge this jump as always: recovery is not a privileged channel. Failure is only logged, and the handoff proceeds as usual: "a person in front of a blank browser can still type the address, and a refused handoff helps nobody" (index.ts:334-346). This is the correct spot for fail-open: when blocking is worse than letting through, let through, and write the reason in the comment.

    Identifying yourself: Web Bot Auth

    The previous three sections were all about "blocking"; the last is about an active "showing". Websites block robots, and a Bot has two roads. One is looking more like a person: change the UA, hide the webdriver flag, hang a residential proxy; Chapter 7's headed Chromium walks the compliant part of this road. The other is honesty: use cryptography to tell the website who I am and whom I browse for. Web Bot Auth is the latter, Cloudflare's signed-agents scheme, built on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, called by the source comment "the honest alternative to looking like a person" (server/src/web-bot-auth.ts:20). OpenAI's agent identifies itself this way; a site behind Cloudflare can choose to let a signed request pass rather than challenge it. Without directory registration, signing earns nothing, and joining Cloudflare's verification directory is a manual step for the operator.

    The mechanism: one Ed25519 key per deployment. The public key is published at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory, and the directory response itself is signed with the private key, so the verifier knows this key was published by the key holder, not by whoever placed it on the host. The private key can be configured explicitly (WEB_BOT_AUTH_KEY); more often it is derived one-way from the deployment's encryption master key:

    typescript
    function derivedSeed(keyEncryptionKey: string): Buffer {
  return Buffer.from(
    hkdfSync(
      "sha256",
      Buffer.from(keyEncryptionKey, "base64"),
      Buffer.alloc(0),
      Buffer.from("openbot web-bot-auth ed25519 v1"),
      32,
    ),
  );
}

    — server/src/web-bot-auth.ts:46-57. The point of HKDF one-way derivation is isolation: this key is issued to every Bot's computer, meaning "the computer can sign in the deployment's name", which is exactly its purpose; and one-wayness guarantees you cannot derive any other secret the deployment holds from it (Chapter 17 covers the full picture of deployment encryption). Every replica and every restart signs with the same key, and the deployment does not fret over one more secret. One more detail when parsing an explicitly configured JWK: re-derive the public key from the private key and compare it against the declared public key; if the halves do not match, refuse to boot: "Refuse a pair whose halves do not match, which would publish a key nothing signs with" (server/src/web-bot-auth.ts:84-90).

    How does the key reach the computer? By riding the egress policy push: the PUT /egress-policy body carries an extra webBotAuth member. This design has an explicit priority ordering: in the same push body, the network policy is a security control and signing is an enhancement; when the webBotAuth member is malformed, signing is turned off and a warning is logged, but the whole push is not rejected: "the network policy in the same body has to land whatever happens here" (agent-computer/src/web-bot-auth.ts:120-121). The security policy must land; the enhancement may yield to it but must not take it down with it.

    Three signature headers, injected in the browser

    Every outbound request carries three headers, formatted after the Cloudflare verifier's documentation rather than the newer draft: Signature-Agent uses a bare string rather than the new draft's dictionary, "because that is what Cloudflare documents and what it verifies" (agent-computer/src/web-bot-auth.ts:11-20). The signature lives 60 seconds: short, because the signature covers only the host, not the request itself, so within its validity everything to that host holds. Any Signature-* headers the page set itself are stripped before signing: "a request never carries two Signature-Agent values for a verifier to choose between" (web-bot-auth.ts:146-147).

    The choice of injection point is the most telling stroke of the whole design: CDP's Fetch domain, chosen over Playwright's route(). The reason is written in page-network.ts's header comment: route interception turns off the entire browser context's HTTP cache, every static asset re-fetched on every page, visible to the site and felt by the waiting person; and routes cannot see requests made by service workers. The Fetch domain is enabled on the browser target and pauses everything the whole browser emits: pages, cross-site iframe processes, dedicated workers, service workers and their script fetches. The interception point sits after the page has decided to send and before the network stack actually sends, so cookies attach as usual, no CORS preflight is triggered, TLS stays Chromium's own, and the request goes on through the egress filter as always (page-network.ts:12-19). One interception layer inserted in the right place fights with no other layer.

    Fail-open and "the switch is a stance"

    When signature injection itself fails, the request goes out unsigned: "Sent unsigned rather than held: a request that never continues is a page that never loads" (page-network.ts:147-148), and the warning prints once. Put this fail-open next to egress's fail-closed and you see the system's grading logic: egress without policy denies everything, because the filter is a boundary and a boundary failing cannot be pretended away; signature failure lets through, because signing is an enhancement, an unsigned request is equivalent to "this feature is off", and that state is legitimate to begin with. The consequence of failure decides the grade, not the importance of the feature.

    The switch itself is also a stance. Web Bot Auth is off by default; WEB_BOT_AUTH accepts only on/off, and any other spelling refuses to boot; turning it on requires an https, non-localhost public address. The reason: signing broadcasts the deployment's URL to every website the Bot visits, and an OpenBot deployment is private by default: "signing is the operator's deliberate choice, never inferred from the address" (server/src/web-bot-auth.ts:125-133). A feature that changes the deployment's visibility to the world can only be a switch the operator presses by hand, never a default inferred from configuration. This is Chapter 2's "configuration is the boundary" echoing at the feature level.

    Apply This

    Encode identity into transport credentials. What problem it solves: in a multi-tenant computer, several tenants' traffic shares one egress filter; how does the filter know whose connection this is? OpenBot puts the Bot id in the proxy credential's username, and the filter issues and validates the secret itself: identity lives at the connection layer, and the caller cannot forge it. How to adapt: anywhere "one proxy or gateway serves many tenants", you can pin the tenant label at the transport layer with a credential field, a client-certificate SAN, or an mTLS identity, instead of trusting a self-reported field in the request. The pitfall: this holds only while "the filter and the caller are in the same trust domain": the secret is issued by the filter and travels loopback; across trust boundaries the credential must be upgraded to real authentication.

    An always-deny list independent of policy. What problem it solves: some things "the most permissive configuration must not allow": the cloud metadata endpoint is denied in every egress mode, allow_all included. It does not enter the policy table, because policy gets misconfigured by people; it is a platform fact, not a configuration. How to adapt: reserve a hardcoded layer in your policy engine that always runs first, holding the "no tenant and no mode may allow" items, and make the layer visible to reviewers at a glance. The pitfall: two of them. One, encoding variants: IPv4-mapped, NAT64, case, zero compression; a list that blocks only one spelling is decoration. Two, time-of-check/time-of-use: after judging, pin the resolution result and connect only to checked addresses, or DNS's second answer replaces the first.

    Mask the read-back, do not filter the write. What problem it solves: secrets must be written into the page to be useful (no password filled, no login), so the only side that can be defended is "read": the snapshot replaces with placeholders, the screenshot blacks out, the live screen draws dots; three channels, one rule. How to adapt: enumerate every channel in your system that "reads the page or state back" and ask each what it would leak; when a new read-back channel is added, the masking list must update in step. The pitfall: when the masking determination itself fails, treat the field as sensitive: "the query failed" must not equal "not sensitive". Also, stronger than masking is the path: any channel that can avoid passing through the model should avoid it.

    Error messages are a data exit. What problem it solves: errors thrown by libraries quote the call site: Playwright's error carries the selector call's arguments (a password), and a database driver's error carries the statement and bound values (ciphertext). Relaying them sends the secret to every reader of the error: response bodies, toasts, model context, the append-only audit table. OpenBot's rule is that the error handler speaks only sentences the module wrote itself, and unexpected errors collapse into one fixed sentence. How to adapt: define your own error type for secret-touching modules; pass-through is limited to that type; everything else gets rewritten. The pitfall: matching error types by message text is fragile (Chapter 4-style string matching gets shattered by dependency upgrades); use error classes. And remember the audit table may be irrevocable: treat every line that lands in it as a permanent archive.

    Hand over the scene along with the request for help. What problem it solves: a Bot saying "I am stuck" is easy; the hard part is the scene still being there when the person arrives. OpenBot's help request carries the page URL, and after a browser restart the page is reopened before control is handed over; the recovery action has three gates preventing the page from being moved out from under a person who already started operating. How to adapt: at any "machine asks for help, person takes over" junction, the request should carry the full context needed to restore the scene rather than a single sentence of description; before completing the handoff, first verify the scene was not altered by a third party (the person included). The pitfall: recovery must be fail-open: a failed recovery must not block the handoff itself, "a refused handoff helps nobody"; and do not let recovery become a privileged channel, because recovery navigation goes through the same admission and filtering.

    The computer's wall now has three doors standing: egress narrowed and honest, secrets living only a two-point life, help requests carrying the scene to find the person. But so far we have assumed this computer exists: who builds it, starts one per Bot, watches its upgrades and its life and death, and guards the Docker socket from meddling hands? Next chapter, meet the supervisor, the container steward.

    ← Chapter 7: One Computer per BotChapter 9: The Supervisor and the Deployment Topology →

    Chapter 9: The Supervisor and the Deployment Topology

    Chapter 8 drew the boundary at the computer's exit: the egress proxy decides where each of a Bot's connections may go, secrets exist only on the short path between form and browser, and CAPTCHAs are left to the person sitting in front of the screen. But we deliberately skipped a row of earlier questions. Who builds this computer? Who may start it, stop it, wipe its browser profile? If the answer is "the API server does it on the side", then every boundary Chapters 7 and 8 drew is built on sand, because whoever holds the power to create containers holds the host itself.

    The Docker socket is a root equivalent of the host: if you can start a container, you can mount the host filesystem into it. Putting it inside the API server would place every request-handler bug, every prompt injection arriving through a Bot's output, and every package in the dependency tree one step away from owning the machine. OpenBot's answer is to lock the socket into a process with only four verbs: the supervisor, the container steward. ensure, stop, reset, list. All four take a Bot as their subject; none is a Docker primitive.

    The supervisor is only the first half of this chapter. The second half is the deployment topology behind it: how the same governance semantics land in three shapes, Compose on a laptop, an all-in-one single-container image, a Helm chart on Kubernetes, plus an optional SPIRE identity layer. The chapter barely mentions models. It is the literal unfolding of the second half of this book's thesis: boundaries live in the deployment.

    The only process that holds the socket

    The whole supervisor service is about a thousand lines of TypeScript and depends on just two libraries, dockerode and Hono. The size is itself design: the attack surface is small enough to review in one sitting. Its header comment lays out the threat model (supervisor/src/index.ts:20-48): the Docker socket is host root, so putting it in the API server is unacceptable; but a process that hides the socket while forwarding any Docker call hands root straight back through a politer door:

    The shared secret is not the boundary; the vocabulary is.

    — supervisor/src/index.ts:35

    The token only blocks other processes on the same network. The real boundary is the set of expressible operations. The worst thing a compromised API server can do is restart a computer some Bot already owns; nothing else can be expressed, so nothing else can be done. This is a clean specimen of capability security: instead of exposing a dangerous capability behind permission checks, give the dangerous operations no name in the protocol.

    The boot discipline continues Chapter 2's refusal list, with its own entry in this process: a missing SUPERVISOR_TOKEN refuses to start (supervisor/src/index.ts:56-62), and the error says why: "This process holds the Docker socket and will not start without the secret its caller must present." A process holding a root equivalent and running without authentication is a deployment accident, not a configuration option.

    The HTTP surface is correspondingly minimal: /health is open to the orchestrator, and everything else requires the Bearer token, compared in constant time (supervisor/src/authorisation.ts:13-19). The error mapping is semantic too. A held name is 409, because the conflict is with something that already exists, not with a broken daemon. Unreachable Docker and an unanswering computer are both 503, because the caller's next step is the same, wait and retry; what differs is the message a human reads (supervisor/src/index.ts:119-133). Status codes here are operational language, not HTTP etiquette.

    The listen parameters pass through the same gate: PORT is strictly parsed and an illegal value exits the process; an empty string counts as unset rather than 0, because Bun.serve handed NaN binds an ephemeral port while compose still publishes 4300 (details in this chapter's Deep Dive). idleTimeout is set to 120 seconds (supervisor/src/index.ts:176), covering ensure's longest 60-second readiness wait; the server-side client timeout is likewise 120 seconds (server/src/computer/supervisor.ts:50). The alignment is no coincidence: the waiter must be more patient than the waited-on, or the slowest legal cold start gets killed by its own most patient caller.

    Ownership twice over: derived names, checked labels

    For the "four verbs" promise to hold, this process must never be able to touch a container that is not its own. OpenBot adds two locks, each against one specific accident.

    The first lock: names come not from the caller but from a validated Bot id. The Bot id passes an allowlist first: letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, 64 characters at most (supervisor/src/names.ts:16-18). The comment accounts for each banned character: a slash would let the name escape into another segment in the socket API's paths, a dot evokes .., a colon is image-tag syntax. Once validated, every name derives from the id:

    typescript
      return {
    ok: true,
    names: {
      botId,
      container: `${NAMESPACE}-computer-${botId}`,
      profileVolume: `${NAMESPACE}-profile-${botId}`,
      workspaceVolume: `${NAMESPACE}-workspace-${botId}`,
    },
  };

    — supervisor/src/names.ts:85-93. What this code shows is "derive, don't accept": the caller says which Bot, and never says which container. NAMESPACE solves a different problem: container names are globally unique on a Docker host, so two OpenBot deployments sharing one host would derive the same container name from the same Bot id; fold the namespace into every name and the two deployments become invisible to each other. The namespace itself is validated at module load, and an illegal value throws (supervisor/src/names.ts:30-39): fail-closed at import time, long before the first request arrives.

    The second lock: label checking, concentrated in one function. Everything the supervisor creates is stamped with three labels, openbot.supervisor=true, openbot.bot-id, openbot.namespace (supervisor/src/names.ts:59-65), and the ownership check has exactly one entry point:

    typescript
    /**
 * One computer, if this supervisor owns it.
 *
 * Ownership is checked here rather than at the call sites, so no verb can skip it by accident.
 */
async function inspectOwned(names: ComputerNames): Promise<{
  status: string;
  port?: number;
  image?: string;
  startedAt?: string;
  token?: string;
} | null> {
  try {
    const info = await docker.getContainer(names.container).inspect();
    if (!ours(info.Config?.Labels)) return null;

    — supervisor/src/docker.ts:210-224. The check lives in inspectOwned rather than at the call sites, "so no verb can skip it by accident". A container whose name happens to match but lacks the labels is treated as nonexistent. ours() also hides a kindness toward old deployments: the namespace label was added later, and containers without it are claimed under the default namespace (supervisor/src/docker.ts:167-176). After an upgrade, an old deployment's computers are still recognized instead of all becoming "nonexistent" overnight. Tightening a boundary should not orphan the existing stock.

    The real test of this rule comes when ensure hits a 409 while creating a container. A 409 has two possible meanings: usually a concurrent request created the same computer first (idempotent; use it), but it could also be a squatting container this supervisor did not create: hand-built, left over from another namespace, or placed by someone who guessed the name. The only path that ever "adopted" a foreign container was start-by-name, and that path would send this deployment's computer token to whatever is listening inside the container. So after a 409 the code passes through inspectOwned once more, and if the check fails it throws NameHeldError, turning ambiguity into an error a human can read (supervisor/src/docker.ts:537-552).

    The server side shows the same restraint. When the server goes through the supervisor via COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL, it answers "which computer is this run on" with list, not ensure (server/src/computer/supervisor.ts:183-203), because ensure starts any computer that is not running. Using it to answer a query would mean "anything that asks about a sleeping computer wakes it up", and a deployment that suspends idle computers would never get to suspend any. Verb-surface discipline binds the caller too.

    ensure: idempotence, replacement on upgrade, and the race budget

    ensure is the only one of the four verbs with internal structure, and its state machine earns a diagram:

    First, the idempotence budget. ensure's caller is a request handler and can race itself: two messages sent to the same Bot at the same moment must never produce two containers. So ensure is reentrant as a whole: a volume create that hits 409 means "already exists" and counts as success for a restarted supervisor; a start that hits 304 "already running" is success too. The retry cap is just 2 (supervisor/src/docker.ts:73), and the comment explains why not more: retries cover exactly one race, losing to a concurrent request for the same Bot; losing a second time means something else is deleting containers, and infinite retries would hide that behind a hanging request. A start that hits 404 (the name not yet published after create) pauses 250 milliseconds before spending its last attempt: an immediate retry would see the same unpublished state within a millisecond and burn the budget for nothing, with the symptom that "the first browser action a Bot is ever asked for fails, and the second one, seconds later, works" (supervisor/src/docker.ts:560-575).

    Second, replacement on upgrade, the most underestimated half of ensure's job. The old behavior was "reuse if the name matches", so after the image was rebuilt, old computers ran old code indefinitely: docker compose down does not touch supervisor-created containers because compose did not create them. The comment says this is worse than stale code: the agent-computer is the browser, the workspace and the isolation, and any fix to them would silently never take effect (supervisor/src/docker.ts:253-264). Now ensure compares two things on every call, and either one drifting deletes the container and rebuilds:

    • The image is compared by resolved id, not by tag: both sides are the same tag, and the whole question is whether it moved (supervisor/src/docker.ts:266-267).
    • The token is compared against the value injected at creation. A computer holds its creation-time COMPUTER_TOKEN for life; reinstalling from scratch mints a new token, and compose recreates everything it owns except the computers. The result: the gateway lets the call through, the audit records it as executed, the computer refuses, and the screen says only "Not authorised" without naming anything. This failure shape was caught on the first real reinstall from scratch, and is now blocked by holdsCurrentToken (supervisor/src/docker.ts:296-326).

    Replacement deletes only the container and leaves the volumes: profile and workspace are named volumes, so when the Bot wakes, its login state and files are still there; what is lost is the in-memory state, open pages and pending takeover requests, which belonged to the run the upgrade just ended (supervisor/src/docker.ts:475-486). Compare reset: that verb runs only when a person explicitly asks, deletes the profile volume along with the container, but keeps the workspace, because "files a Bot was asked to produce are work, not browser state" (supervisor/src/docker.ts:625-626). Both are "delete"; ensure's delete preserves data and reset's delete clears identity, and the line between them is the nature of the data.

    The return value keeps up the pretense that the caller knows no topology: on a shared network the URL is http://{container}:4100, otherwise http://127.0.0.1:{port} (supervisor/src/docker.ts:592-598). The server uses whatever it gets and does not need to know whether it runs on the host or inside a compose network. Topology knowledge lives in the one process that actually knows the answer.

    There is one deliberate fail-open in this function worth a separate look. runsCurrentImage returns true when the image cannot be inspected, never pulled, registry unreachable, and keeps the existing computer (supervisor/src/docker.ts:269-272):

    Unanswerable is not stale... Destroying a Bot's working browser over a failed inspect is a worse answer than running an image that may be a version behind.

    The whole book stresses fail-closed, and here the code explicitly books a pass. The difference is the asymmetry of consequences: a false refusal destroys real state, while a false pass costs "maybe one version behind" and can be asked again next time. Fail-open here is not laziness; it is a weighed decision with a comment written down.

    The readiness wait: a wait that cannot fail is a sleep

    A started container does not mean an answering Chromium. "'Started' and 'ready' are not the same thing, and the gap is seconds": Docker reports running the moment the process exists, while the computer is still booting. So ensure waits, but it asks Docker's health status rather than fetching the computer directly: which address works depends on the deployment shape (direct from the host versus container name on a shared network), and the supervisor can always reach the socket, or it could not have created the container at all (supervisor/src/docker.ts:331-345).

    A cross-engine pit is buried here. The healthcheck is delivered explicitly at create time instead of being inherited from the image, because the OCI image config has no healthcheck field: Podman drops it at build and at pull, and podman inspect of the same image reports no healthcheck. That drops you silently into the one branch that cannot tell the difference: with no health to read, the wait logic can only accept Running, and a running container is not an answering Chromium; every cold start races the first request. Delivered explicitly, both Docker and Podman accept it (supervisor/src/docker.ts:36-53).

    The wait's deadline is 60 seconds, and on expiry it does not return; it throws:

    typescript
      /*
   * The deadline is a failure, not an answer.
   *
   * Returning here reported every computer that never came up as ready, which is the exact thing
   * this function exists to prevent: the caller is handed an address, sends the deployment's
   * computer token to it, and gets a transport error it cannot tell from a computer that is broken
   * in some other way. A wait that cannot fail is a sleep.
   */
  throw new ComputerNotAnsweringError(container, timeoutMs);

    — supervisor/src/docker.ts:369-377. What this code shows is "the deadline is a failure". The old behavior returned at the deadline, reporting every computer that never came up as ready: the caller walked off with an address and a token, hit a transport error, and could not tell it apart from "the computer is broken". "A wait that cannot fail is a sleep" deserves copying onto the wall of every codebase with a polling loop.

    Deep Dive: Three small functions where parsing is the defense

    The supervisor holds three parse functions that total under a hundred lines; each has an incident behind it, and together they teach one lesson: environment variables and daemon return values are untrusted input, to be schema-checked before use.

    • parseHostPort (supervisor/src/docker.ts:160-165): the daemon returns an empty string before port assignment finishes, and arbitrary values on error; a bare parseInt turns "abc" into NaN and "0" into a port nobody can dial. It accepts only pure digits between 1 and 65535.
    • listenPort (supervisor/src/listen-port.ts:9-29): an empty PORT= counts as unset rather than 0, because Bun.serve({port:NaN}) binds an ephemeral port while compose still publishes 4300, and the service comes up with nobody able to reach it. Prefix parsing was another pit: a typo like 30o0 was read by parseInt as 30, and the process silently came up on port 30.
    • computerMemoryBytes (supervisor/src/computer-memory-bytes.ts): parseInt("512m") yields 512 bytes. Docker accepts the number and Chromium cannot live on it. Pure digits only.

    None of the three exceeds thirty lines, but each moves a class of "misconfigured yet looks alive" failures forward into "die loudly at boot". It is Chapter 2's boot-refusal philosophy continued inside a process.

    The hardening list on every computer

    A container is not a boundary by nature. "A container is a boundary only if it is configured as one" (supervisor/src/docker.ts:414-415). hostConfig is that configuration's checklist, and each entry defends one specific route:

    typescript
        // No path from inside to more privilege than it started with, whatever it manages to run.
    SecurityOpt: ["no-new-privileges:true"],
    // Chromium needs none of these, and each is a documented container escape route.
    CapDrop: ["ALL"],
    // A runaway Bot is a resource problem for itself, not for every other Bot on the host.
    ...(options.memoryBytes ? { Memory: options.memoryBytes } : {}),
    PidsLimit: options.pidsLimit ?? 512,
    // Chromium's sandbox wants shared memory and will crash on the 64MB default.
    ShmSize: 1_073_741_824,

    — supervisor/src/docker.ts:449-457. The itemized ledger:

    Setting Value What it defends against
    SecurityOpt no-new-privileges:true Whatever manages to run inside, no path from inside to more privilege
    CapDrop ALL Every capability is a documented container escape route; Chromium needs none
    PidsLimit 512 A runaway Bot's fork bomb is its own problem, not the whole host's
    ShmSize 1 GiB Chromium's sandbox wants shared memory; the 64MB default crashes it
    Memory optional OOM isolation when Bots share a host
    Runtime optional, e.g. runsc gVisor intercepts syscalls in user space; for more, point to a microVM runtime
    RestartPolicy unless-stopped Crashes self-heal; explicit stops stay stopped

    One more line in the list is easy to mistake for an ordinary mount: Binds mounts the profile and workspace volumes at /profiles and /workspace (supervisor/src/docker.ts:420-424). Chapter 7 already quoted the comment for its boundary semantics: these two named volumes turn the path constraint inside the computer from "a boundary between the Bot and the host" into "a boundary between one Bot and another". The optional SPIRE socket volume mounts read-only: the computer asks and does not answer.

    Port handling forks by topology (supervisor/src/docker.ts:430-444). When the server and the computers share a Docker network, no ports are published and the server reaches computers by container name, because a remote host should not accumulate an open port per Bot. On a laptop the server runs on the host, so an ephemeral port is published, pinned to 127.0.0.1. The comment gives the reason: "Loopback, not the world". The token is one lock and loopback is the second; the browser holds other people's login states, and two locks is the right number.

    The stop grace is 30 seconds (supervisor/src/docker.ts:612), and not picked at random: it is enough for Chromium to flush the profile to disk, and it aligns with compose's stop_grace_period. Chapter 8's defense of login state has its last fortification in this grace value.

    Network topology: the database never enters the Bot's network

    Look first at the line the diagram does not have: there is no edge between the default network and the data network. This is the most important negative sentence in docker-compose.yml (docker-compose.yml:390-398): the data network carries only postgres and migrate, and everything else lands in default. The motive is in the file header (docker-compose.yml:4-15): "Off the network the Bots are on, because a Bot's computer is on it and a Bot has a shell." Without the split, compose puts every service in one network with DNS by service name, so the agent-computer can open postgres:5432 directly, and the password sits in the same file: the audit trail, the policy store and the agent tables, reachable from the one container whose job is executing Bot requests. A deployment that puts the server into compose joins both networks; the comment calls that the only place the two sides are designed to meet.

    Splitting networks is not enough; published ports are a second pit with three layers (docker-compose.yml:20-35). A publish without an interface qualifier is reachable on every interface, and the container's default gateway is the host: measured from inside the agent-computer, :5432 answered and began authenticating as openbot/openbot. So bind only loopback. But loopback is not one address: localhost resolves to ::1 and 127.0.0.1 in an order the platform decides, and Bun and Node do not fall back once they have ::1. Binding only one leaves localhost unreachable on half the machines, with an error message that never mentions why.

    So every port is bound twice: 127.0.0.1:${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432}:5432 and [::1]:${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432}:5432, one publish record each (docker-compose.yml:34-35), and the supervisor's 4500 and the computer's 4100 are double-bound the same way. The server-side client code keeps the same discipline: it connects to the supervisor with the literal 127.0.0.1 and never writes localhost (server/src/computer/supervisor.ts:51-57): "Node prefers ::1, bun prefers 127.0.0.1"; one name resolves to different interfaces in different processes. Every line of this discipline was paid for by an "unreachable on half the machines" incident.

    The supervisor's own compose definition is decisions all the way down (docker-compose.yml:183-257). The Docker socket mounts read-only: read-only because it only needs to ask, and it is still a root equivalent, which is exactly why nothing else here gets it. The socket path is configurable (ENGINE_SOCKET), because rootless Podman on Linux either has no socket at the default path or has a symlink to the rootful socket there, and the supervisor would hold a dead socket and report "cannot reach Docker". The two tokens carry development defaults, so a manual docker compose up -d builds the same stack as start.sh rather than a silently unauthenticated one. The computer's egress proxy config travels in a separate egress.env rather than .env: .env holds the deployment's secrets, and this container drives a browser and runs the Bot's shell, so it gets what it needs and not the rest. The principle of minimal credential exposure reaches all the way into field selection in a compose file.

    How images are sourced is written in the same file, with a pit's epitaph attached. Services like migrate, supervisor and agent-computer carry both a build section and an explicit image: name: a release pushes images under those names, and a machine that can name an image does not need a toolchain to build one. But a service with a build section builds no matter what by default; IMAGE_PULL_POLICY=missing switches it to pulling. pull_policy is the arbiter between the two paths (docker-compose.yml:50-61). The comment then admits this is not a guarantee:

    Not a guarantee that nothing is built: a pull that fails falls back to building, silently, which is right for a developer and wrong for an installed OpenBot, where there is no toolchain and the honest answer is that the image could not be fetched.

    — docker-compose.yml:55-58

    A failed pull falls back to building, silently. So when images are shipped to machines that cannot build, the release process overrides the build section outright rather than entrusting fate to this variable. The file's only exception is agent-harness: it has no build: section, and its pull_policy: missing applies unconditionally, because "this image is only ever published, never built from this tree" (docker-compose.yml:300-305).

    Three shapes: the same semantics, three ways to land them

    The supervisor is one answer to "where do computers come from": with a Docker socket present, per-Bot containers exist. But there are three deployment shapes, and each answers the same questions: who supplies the computers, where the database lives, who notices when a process dies. The server-side choice is a fork on one environment variable (server/src/computer/provider.ts): if COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL is set, go through the supervisor with one computer per Bot; if not, shared mode: "No supervisor is configured, so every Bot uses the same browser. Sessions, files and logins are shared between them." On clusters, COMPUTER_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE selects the sandbox provider. Isolation strength is a deployment decision; the code path is single. The comparison table first:

    Shape Computer supply Database Process orchestration Fits
    Laptop Compose supervisor, one per Bot (optional) postgres container compose restart policy development, small teams on one machine
    all-in-one single container built-in shared browser external hosted (DATABASE_URL) s6-overlay one-container-one-port platforms
    Helm shared StatefulSet ×1, shared by all Bots bundled or hosted K8s probes + restart first install, no CRD needed
    Helm sandbox one Sandbox per Bot, suspended when idle bundled or hosted agent-sandbox controller clusters with the Sandbox CRD

    all-in-one: the one-line case for s6

    The all-in-one image's header comment starts with "WHAT IS NOT HERE" (Dockerfile:7-15), and both exclusions are boundary decisions. PostgreSQL is not inside, because the container filesystem does not survive a redeploy and the audit trail is the product. The supervisor is not inside, because per-Bot containers need the Docker socket and no serverless container platform allows that; without it, every Bot shares the built-in browser, exactly as on a laptop with no supervisor configured. Note how the exclusions are phrased: not "not done", but "cannot be here, and why".

    Multi-process inside one container uses s6-overlay rather than the more common supervisord, for a one-line but decisive reason (Dockerfile:97-99): when a supervised process exits, s6 brings the container down with it so the platform restarts it; supervisord stays alive, and the container keeps reporting healthy after the API inside is dead. "Looks healthy but cannot answer" is the worst failure shape this book names again and again, so the selection criterion for a process orchestrator is exactly one: a process's death must equal the container's death. s6's service graph also encodes boot order as dependencies: migrate before api, computer before api, "Started after the browser so a Bot's first action does not race a computer that is still coming up" (docker/s6/s6-rc.d/api/run).

    The single container accounts for "sharing one computer" in finer detail. When COMPUTER_TOKEN is unset, computer-token.sh mints a 32-byte random value into the s6 environment directory: "Generated rather than required", because operations should not have to invent a shared secret for two processes that cannot be addressed separately. The scenario it defends is stated concretely: "What this defends is somebody publishing 4100 anyway" (docker/s6/scripts/computer-token.sh). If embedded PostgreSQL is enabled, initialization uses scram-sha-256 instead of trust authentication, with a randomly generated password living on the same volume as the data. The motive is the same: the Bot's shell runs in this very container, and under trust it could psql without a password straight into the audit trail, the policy store and the credential vault (docker/s6/scripts/postgres-init.sh).

    The permission topology is explicit too: s6 stays root (the only way to drop different services to different users), the browser and shell run as pwuser (uid 1001), the API and migrations as apiuser (uid 1002). The uids are pinned with --uid, because the Helm chart's podSecurityContext hardcodes 1001, and the day the base image ships one more user, every number shifts: "Pinning makes it a contract" (Dockerfile:39-45). sudo used to be NOPASSWD: ALL; now it covers only the package-manager commands, because a shared computer plus an installable library means root can read other Bots' workspaces, the API's environment and the audit store. The comment locates it precisely: "It is a floor, not a boundary"; the real boundary is the per-Bot computer and gVisor (Dockerfile:181-195). And the shell and package manager themselves are deliberately kept: a Bot being able to open a shell and install what a task needs is a required feature, and deleting them "hardens the image by deleting the product" (Dockerfile:205-211). Security comes from Chapter 5's gateway, resolve, decide, audit, act, not from deleting features. That comment is the product's security philosophy in concentrate.

    start.sh: converge every round, probe for identity

    The laptop stack's boot script (scripts/start.sh, four hundred-odd lines) makes two counterintuitive decisions, both born from incidents.

    The first: every selected service gets compose up -d --build every round, even if it is already answering (scripts/start.sh:229-243). "answering says the process is alive, not that its environment still matches the deployment's". Skipping "already answering" services once left Bot containers calling tools with a replaced token; every call was refused, and it was "a false negative delivered as an answer". compose is declarative: if the configuration has not changed, up costs one comparison; if it has, compose converges it for you. Run it unconditionally and hand the "should I update" judgment to the declarative tool instead of the script's memory.

    The second: probes answer "it is OpenBot", not "something is listening" (scripts/start.sh:142-173). Any single-page app answers its own index.html to paths it does not know, so an unrelated service squatting on the default port also answers 200 to /api/capabilities. The boot script once parsed that HTML as JSON, and a JSON parse error stood in for "that port belongs to someone else". The identity probe now greps the response for characteristic fields; stop.sh reuses the same probe in reverse and kills only processes confirmed to be its own. When a port is held by something that is not OpenBot, the script names it in red and suggests changing the port; it never shuts down someone else's service.

    The cleverest probe is the 401/404 reading of the server. Every worker dispatch is a POST to the server's /internal/routines/run; a server older than this route answers 404, and a server holding last round's secret answers 401. Both are "alive but wrong", and neither cures silent routines. The script's solution is to ask once and look:

    bash
    # Pseudocode — illustrates the pattern
code=$(post_json "/internal/routines/run" "{}" --header "Authorization: Bearer $THIS_ROUND_SECRET")
case "$code" in
  400) keep ;;     # secret checked before the body is read: 400 is a healthy refusal
  401) restart ;;  # it holds last round's secret
  404) restart ;;  # it predates this route
  *)   keep ;;     # the probe itself got no answer: leave an answering process alone
esac

    The real implementation is at scripts/start.sh:324-354. It exploits the server's order of "check the secret first, parse the body second": a server holding the same secret answers 400 to an empty body, so 400 is the healthy answer here. Using a known-bad request to tell apart three kinds of "alive" is the limit of what a black-box probe can do.

    The worker process cannot use this HTTP probe: it has no endpoint to ask, and the rerun script's only signal is "is a process with a matching command line running". So the guard is pgrep, the same idea as the restart guard above that uses pkill -f on the server's own command line. And pgrep on Linux can see container processes, which once buried an incident:

    The old pattern matched those containers, the guard false-positived, and the worker silently never started.

    — scripts/start.sh:385-386

    The server, agent-computer and supervisor containers all happen to have bun src/index.ts as their argv, and the old pgrep pattern mistook them for the worker: the guard falsely reported "already running", and the worker was silently absent forever. The fix now starts the worker from the repository root as bun worker/src/index.ts: that string is unique in the whole repo's process table, and relative imports resolve from the importing file rather than the process cwd, so starting from the root is safe (scripts/start.sh:382-387). The identity probe asks "is it OpenBot", the 401/404 probe asks "is it this round's server", the pgrep pattern asks "is it the worker": three guards all asking for identity, with lower and lower questioning budgets.

    Helm: move the refusal to install time

    The Helm chart moves Chapter 2's boot-refusal philosophy one step earlier: from boot-time refusal to install-time refusal. templates/validation.yaml runs about four hundred lines, and the creed is in the file header (charts/openbot/templates/validation.yaml:1-9): "Refused at install time, not discovered in a crash loop". A chart that installs successfully and then crash-loops in place is worse than one that refuses with a reason, because the latter names the value to change. The refusal list shows shadows of the book's other chapters: a bundled database must be given a reproducible password (otherwise the failure arrives on the second deploy, the worst possible time); non-external mode must be given a computerToken; and the chart refuses at install time the public sample encryption key from .env.example, checked by shape rather than by a copied value, because writing a key-shaped literal into a template to forbid key-shaped literals is self-referential absurdity (validation.yaml:175-185).

    The shared-mode computer uses a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment, with the reason in the template comment (charts/openbot/templates/computer/statefulset.yaml:6-9): the profile directory holds real login state, and a Deployment's pod has no stable volume of its own. Two replicas would fight over the same ReadWriteOnce claim, and one rolling update would hand an empty profile to the new pod, which reads like every Bot being logged out of everything at once. persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy's whenScaled: Retain is written out explicitly rather than inherited, because the default, "the first scale-down wipes every Bot's login", would lead a later reader to think the field was missing and helpfully clean it up (statefulset.yaml:33-42). The same file carries a "STORAGE HAS GRAVITY" reminder: RWO block volumes are zone-scoped on all three clouds, so the pod is pinned to the zone where its profile lives. Acceptable, but worth writing down rather than being discovered.

    The rest of the pod configuration keeps the honest-ledger style. automountServiceAccountToken: false (statefulset.yaml:69-77): the container that opens pages a person named and executes commands a model chose is the last pod in the deployment that should be able to address the API server, and Kubernetes' default is exactly the reverse. The Service is headless (clusterIP: None), because a StatefulSet wants stable per-pod names, not a load-balanced address. The podSecurityContext comment uncommonly lists what it buys and what it does not (charts/openbot/values.yaml:346-391): bought are that organizational admission policies stop refusing, root-owned files stop accumulating in volumes, and exploit primitives land on uid 1001; not bought is containment of the Bot's shell, because the image by design gives pwuser package-manager sudo. And precisely for that reason, proposals to capability-drop the computer pod were deliberately refused: apt needs CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE and FOWNER, and allowPrivilegeEscalation:false would kill the setuid that sudo depends on. The supervisor path can set no-new-privileges for computers exactly because that image ships no sudo. The two configurations corroborate each other: the hardening list must be designed together with the product's features, or hardening deletes the product.

    The probe configuration is equally counterintuitive: only readiness and startupProbe, and deliberately no liveness (statefulset.yaml:171-184). A browser under load can answer slowly without being broken, and one liveness restart takes away all of its login state. readiness holds traffic off until it can answer; nothing kills it for being busy. This mirrors the all-in-one's reason for choosing s6: there the principle is "death must be noticed", here it is "not dead must not be killed", and the shared criterion on both sides is the value of login state.

    The rarest refusal is warmPool. The template and RBAC both render, but validation refuses to enable it at install time (validation.yaml:118-137): the server has no code that creates a SandboxClaim, so the pool runs, reports healthy and bills for browsers nobody is ever handed, while every first action waits exactly as long. The comment's honesty deserves quoting: "Remove this block when the provider claims from the pool. It is a note that the wiring is unfinished, not a judgement that the feature is unwanted." Unfinished wiring said so at install time is more honest than a "Coming Soon" in the docs, because nobody reads the docs, while a refusal speaks the moment you turn the feature on.

    The sandbox mode's RBAC is the supervisor idea projected onto Kubernetes: the Docker route does not exist on a cluster, and the equivalent is a Role (not a ClusterRole) granting create, delete and get on Sandboxes within the computer namespace only (charts/openbot/templates/computer/sandbox-rbac.yaml:1-30). The comment makes the comparison itself: "Compare the Docker supervisor, which holds the host's Docker socket and is therefore root-equivalent on that host: this is a smaller blast radius, granted by the cluster rather than by a shared environment variable." This is the vocabulary-as-boundary principle, kept intact under a different granting mechanism.

    A few more chart decisions are worth taking away. The server defaults to two replicas, and the comment explains why not one: "Everything that has to survive a replica is in PostgreSQL, and one replica hides every bug that is not" (values.yaml:26-29). Migrations are a pre-upgrade hook Job rather than a start step, "so a rollout never puts a new replica in front of a schema it has not seen" (values.yaml:104-105); the same creed is compressed into one Dockerfile line in the server image: "Migrations are a release step, not a start step" (server/Dockerfile:75-76). Two replicas starting together would race, and a failed migration should stop the deploy rather than leave a half-migrated database serving.
