The ConfigMap checksum is made a Deployment annotation so a content change rolls the pods: otherwise a config-only helm upgrade leaves every replica running old values, "the deployment looks upgraded while behaving exactly as it did" (charts/openbot/templates/server/deployment.yaml:42-45). Sandbox-mode suspension culling uses a CronJob rather than a timer inside the API, because a timer fires once in every replica and five replicas would each independently decide to suspend the same computer. Deleting old audit rows twice is the same as deleting them once; suspending a browser somebody just started using is not. On top of concurrencyPolicy: Forbid there is a deadline, because a wedged sweep holds the concurrency lock forever: "culling simply ceases: no error, no restart, no alert", and the first sign is a cloud bill for a fleet of browsers nobody used (charts/openbot/templates/computer/culler-cronjob.yaml:3-50).

    The bundled PostgreSQL packaging is pinned decisions throughout. The subchart version is pinned to 16.7.27 rather than ~16, with the reason in Chart.yaml's dependency comment (charts/openbot/Chart.yaml:23-30): a subchart patch version carries a new PostgreSQL image tag, and Bitnami's frozen bitnamilegacy repository accepts no new tags, so the next patch is an image that cannot be pulled. CI only renders the chart and never pulls, so nothing on this path would speak early: "the first sign would have been somebody's install sitting in ImagePullBackOff". The image tag 17.6.0-debian-12-r4 is explicitly named for the same reason (values.yaml:580).

    Its NetworkPolicy is taken over explicitly too. The subchart renders its own whether or not this chart enables NetworkPolicy, and its default allowExternal: true means the ingress rule carries no from:

    any pod in any namespace may open 5432. That includes a Bot's computer, the one pod running a browser on pages a person named and a shell on commands a model chose.

    — charts/openbot/values.yaml:584-587

    So the chart pins allowExternal: false and lets through only pods carrying the <release>-postgresql-client label (values.yaml:582-594). The comment writes the motive as a cross-shape echo: "Compose has kept the database off the Bot's network since the beginning; this is the same boundary in the other deployment's words". Compose's two networks are this boundary phrased for a laptop; here it is phrased for a cluster.

    SPIRE: identity that falls out of labels

    The last layer is optional: SPIRE gives every computer a SPIFFE identity (spiffe://{domain}/bot/{botId}), making "which Bot" something the workload holds and can be challenged on, rather than a claim in a request header. The design's cleverness is the registration: the selector is the very two labels the supervisor stamps when it creates the container (supervisor/src/identity.ts:51-54). The docker workload attestor selects by container label, so identity falls out of the same fact that created the container, and an unregistered container gets nothing. Registration happens inside ensure, before the computer is handed out, so it can prove which Bot it is from its first request (supervisor/src/index.ts:101-103).

    Equally notable are its failure semantics: a registration failure is not fatal (supervisor/src/identity.ts:38-42). A computer without an SVID works as usual; it just cannot prove which Bot it is. Refusing to issue computers would turn the identity system's failure into the product's failure, the wrong trade for a deployment that may not run SPIRE at all. The failure is written into the response, keeping "identity not configured" and "identity broken" visibly distinct. This is Chapter 7's structure-first principle applied once more: decisions that have a wrong answer available get peeled into explicit branches rather than sunk into the silence of a try/catch.

    SPIRE's own configuration keeps the deployment philosophy: a single-level CA with no upstream, because "nothing has to reach a CA outside this deployment", which makes the whole thing usable in air-gapped environments, exactly the deployments this product targets (spire/server.conf:6-8); the SVID TTL is one hour, and "a stolen SVID stops working on its own" (spire/server.conf:18-19). Registration is implemented as Bun.spawn calling the spire-server entry create CLI rather than a hand-written registration client: the CLI is a supported surface, ships in the same image as the server, entry semantics are idempotent anyway, and "similar entry already exists" counts as success (supervisor/src/identity.ts:57-81). The agent config's insecure_bootstrap is explicitly marked as local bootstrap only: a real deployment should issue trust through a hardware attestor, not trust on first contact (spire/agent.conf). But start.sh does not start the SPIRE services: it is an optional layer, and the default deployment does not pay for this complexity.

    It also has an unfinished gap of the same kind, except that no install-time refusal speaks for this one: the supervisor only creates entries and never deletes them; supervisor/src/identity.ts:57-81 has only the entry create path. reset wipes the container and the profile volume, but the registration row in the SPIRE server stays behind. With the container gone the label selector matches nothing, so the leftover row can attest nothing and is harmless, but the registry slowly grows fat with every Bot id ever ensured. Put it next to warmPool and you see two forms of unfinished wiring: one refuses loudly at install time, the other quietly waits for a cleanup path that has not been wired.

    The identity layer's existence does not hold the product hostage. This section and the previous one together are the two correct postures toward optional infrastructure: what is unwired (warmPool) refuses to be enabled; what is wired (SPIRE) degrades on failure.

    Numbers at a glance

    Item Value Source
    supervisor container port / host publish 4300 / 4500 (dual loopback) supervisor/src/index.ts:50; docker-compose.yml:234-235
    computer port 4100 supervisor/src/docker.ts:33
    ensure readiness deadline / poll interval 60s / 250ms supervisor/src/docker.ts:329,366
    ensure race budget 2 attempts supervisor/src/docker.ts:73
    stop grace 30s (aligned with compose stop_grace_period) supervisor/src/docker.ts:612
    supervisor idleTimeout / server client timeout 120s each supervisor/src/index.ts:176; server/src/computer/supervisor.ts:50
    Bot id limit 64 characters supervisor/src/names.ts:16

    Apply This

    The vocabulary is the boundary. The problem it solves: you must expose a high-risk capability (a root equivalent, payment, deletion) to a large and untrusted caller, and no amount of permission checking lets you sleep. How to adapt it: do not forward primitives behind an ACL; build a small service that knows only domain verbs, so the high-risk operations have no name in the protocol. OpenBot's API server cannot even say "start a container by name". The pitfall: the verb surface grows back toward generic forwarding under demand pressure, and every new verb must answer "what is the worst operation a compromised caller could express with it".

    Derived naming plus a centralized ownership check. The problem it solves: your system operates on external resources by name (containers, queues, buckets), and the namespace mixes in things it did not create. How to adapt it: derive names from a validated id so the caller never gets naming rights; collect the ownership mark check (labels, tags) into one function so no verb can physically skip it; on a create conflict, re-check ownership before deciding between reuse and error. The pitfall: checking names without checking ownership means the moment you "adopt" a foreign object you send secrets to whoever guessed the name, and the post-409 inspectOwned exists for exactly this; also leave a claim path for existing stock, where a missing namespace label counts as the default, because tightening a boundary should not create orphans.

    A wait that can fail. The problem it solves: polling-for-ready code returns silently at the deadline, and the caller takes the "ready" answer into an undiagnosable transport error. How to adapt it: the deadline is a failure, not an answer, so throw a named error on timeout; ask the orchestrator (Docker, K8s) for health rather than the network, because which network path works depends on the deployment shape. The pitfall: healthcheck inheritance chains are more fragile than you think; the OCI image spec has no healthcheck field and Podman silently drops it, and only explicit delivery is accepted by both engines.

    Declarative convergence, not "alive means correct". The problem it solves: long-running processes hold the configuration of their boot moment, and after secret rotation or an image rebuild the old process is alive, answering, and wrong. How to adapt it: like start.sh, run compose up unconditionally every round (a declarative tool makes "no change" cost one comparison); like ensure, compare "what is running" with "what should be running" on every call, the image by resolved id because tags move, the token by its creation-time value because the computer holds it for life. The pitfall: drift correction needs a destruction ceiling. OpenBot replaces the container but keeps the volumes, losing in-memory state and keeping login state; and a fail-open on "unanswerable" must be explicitly booked, because a failed inspect is not staleness.

    Install-time refusal. The problem it solves: configuration errors surface at runtime as crash loops, idle billing and silent failure, three alert layers away from the person who could change the config. How to adapt it: turn every error provable at template time into an install-time fail. OpenBot's chart uses four hundred lines of validation to refuse missing passwords, missing tokens and missing CRDs, and even refuses a feature the template renders but no code consumes. The pitfall: check only what template time can judge, and where it cannot, prefer missing the case to guessing (the chart's egress cross-check explicitly gives up on private DNS names); and the refusal must name the value to change, or you have only traded a crash loop for a support ticket.

    The supervisor's four verbs, compose's two networks, Helm's install-time refusals and SPIRE's optional identity together are the literal unfolding of the second half of this book's thesis: boundaries do not live in the model; they live in the deployment, in who holds the socket, who can open 5432, and what gets refused at install time. Part III closes here: Chapter 7 fenced the computer, Chapter 8 governed its exits, and this chapter governed where the computer comes from.

    The next chapter enters Part IV and answers a quieter question: when nobody is watching, how does work happen exactly once, and on what grounds is it not twice.

    ← Chapter 8: The Computer's Boundaries: Egress, Secrets, and Asking for HelpChapter 10: Unattended Work: One Queue and the Routines →
    Part IV: Autonomy and Collaboration

    When nobody is watching, work still happens — and we can still answer who asked for it.

    Chapter 10: Unattended Work: One Queue and the Routines

    Chapter 9 showed how the supervisor, the container steward, governs every computer with the four verbs ensure/stop/reset, and how the deployment topology draws boundaries into networks and namespaces. But well-fenced computers with nobody bringing them work are just warm containers. The most valuable actions in real use happen exactly when nobody is watching: standup notes at nine every morning, a follow-up triggered when a GitHub issue updates, an idle computer suspending itself. The question this chapter answers: when nobody is watching, how does work happen exactly once.

    In a single-replica deployment the question is not worth asking; a setInterval or a system cron is enough. But OpenBot's server runs multiple replicas, and any "timer every replica runs" means one thing done N times. The source says it plainly: "fired by every replica it happens N times, and on a cluster that is Tuesday" (the header comment of server/src/db/schema/work.ts). A timer on a cluster is not occasionally wrong; it is wrong every Tuesday. Two morning briefings sent, the same computer suspended twice, the same handoff delivered to the same Bot twice: all waypoints on that road.

    OpenBot's answer is the plainest and most disciplined piece of infrastructure in the book: one PostgreSQL table work_items, plus a set of claim, lease and idempotence conventions around it. Routines, Responsibilities, Bot-to-Bot handoffs, computer suspension, proactive research, self-wakeups, message delivery: seven kinds of "work to be done later, exactly once across replicas" share this single mechanism. By the end of the chapter you will understand why this table replaces an entire queue middleware, how many gates a routine passes from one sentence to daily firing, and why the system would rather mark a run failed than replay an action that may already have spent money.

    One table, seven consumers

    The schema header comment of work_items is a design manifesto (server/src/db/schema/work.ts:16-33):

    "ONE MECHANISM, THREE FEATURES… POSTGRES, NOT A QUEUE. It is already the thing every replica shares, and for update skip locked is exactly this problem: each replica takes rows nobody else holds, no coordinator, no leader election, no single point of failure, and adding a replica adds throughput rather than contention… NOT setInterval. The audit-retention sweep uses one and is safe only because deleting old rows twice is the same as deleting them once."

    — header comment of server/src/db/schema/work.ts

    Three sentences each cut one class of alternative: no per-feature scheduling, because "the parts that are easy to get wrong are the same every time"; no Redis or SQS, because Postgres is already what every replica shares and for update skip locked is exactly this problem; no in-process timers carrying side-effecting work, because the only sanctioned setInterval is the audit-retention sweep, where deleting twice equals deleting once.

    The table itself holds few surprises; the surprises are all in the conventions:

    Column Role Key convention
    kind, key primary key idempotence lives in the primary key; each consumer composes its own key
    run_at effective moment the claim query never sees rows before their moment
    claimed_by, lease_until lease all computed on the database clock; replica clocks do not participate
    attempts dispatch count a number, not a state: 1 means "certainly never ran", more than 1 means "may have run halfway"
    finished_at completion moment kept, not deleted; a finished row is the wall a late offer hits
    last_error why it was last given up capped rows stay in the table; a terminal state to query, not a silence
    payload the rest of the work data only what cannot go in the key: a routine row carries just routineId and scheduledFor; a handoff row packs the whole envelope (from/to, conversation, depth)

    The seven consumers share this table, differing only in kind:

    The seventh kind not drawn is the delivery kinds (the sweep that delivers notifications); the mechanism is identical. This table is the scheduling-layer reflection of "boundaries live in the deployment": introducing no new infrastructure means the queue's backup, restore and transactional consistency come free from Postgres. It sits in the same pg_dump as the production data, sharing a fate with Chapter 2's tenant seed and Chapter 6's audit trail. Adding Redis would not save complexity; it would split the truth of "was the work done" into two halves.

    The table also has a cheap accelerator: offer executes pg_notify('openbot_work_offered', kind) in the same transaction (queue.ts:33-34), emitted only with the commit. A consumer that wants to start immediately, handoff delivery for instance, listens on this channel and kicks its own sweep when one arrives. But the comment nails its status down: "A notification is a latency optimisation, never a delivery mechanism — one lost in transit costs up to one poll interval, not the work" (queue.ts:27-29). Exceptions in the listen callback are swallowed outright, because polling remains correct: the fast path may fail and the slow path must be correct, a posture recurring through this book. The pg_notify implementation carries the posture too: LISTEN runs on a dedicated connection (pool configured max: 1) rather than one borrowed from the pool, because LISTEN occupies the connection for its whole subscription (queue.ts:44-64); borrowing a pooled connection would starve a resident subscription in the waiting queue.

    The table has a second face: it is the data source of the "pending work" page. The Bot's todo aggregation (forBot) computes the states of handoffs and wakeups live from work_items. There is no redundant status column; the state is computed from the four columns finished_at/claimed_by/lease_until/attempts. Queue rows are both the execution mechanism and the display model, which means the UI can never drift from the queue: the "in progress" on the page is a lease some replica holds at this moment.

    One more thing deliberately not built: the routines table never grows lease columns. The store's header comment says it absolutely: "NO CLAIM OR LEASE MACHINERY, EVER" (server/src/routines/store.ts:17-22). Growing a second set of claimed_by/locked_until on the routines table means growing a second, half-right firing mechanism: "two half-right implementations of the same hard thing, one of which nobody tests". Scheduling state exists in one copy, in work_items; the routines table only manages "what this standing instruction is and when it should next run". This dividing line recurs through the chapter.

    Claim: skip locked turns correct into concurrent

    The heart of the queue is claim. Its SQL is short enough to quote in full (server/src/work/queue.ts:281-292):

    sql
    select "kind", "key"
from "work_items"
where "kind" = $1
  and "finished_at" is null
  and "attempts" < $2
  and "run_at" <= now()
  and ("lease_until" is null or "lease_until" <= now())
order by "run_at" asc
limit $3
for update skip locked

    The claim conditions take one sentence: due, unfinished, under the attempt cap, either unheld or lease-expired, oldest first. The real trick is the last line, for update skip locked. Without it, a second replica blocks on the rows the first replica locked, serializing the whole queue: correct, but not concurrent. The source comment's judgment is precise: "skip locked is what makes this concurrent rather than merely correct" (queue.ts:276-280). With it, every replica walks around the rows others hold and takes the next free batch, so "no leader election, no single point of failure, and a replica added is throughput added rather than contention added" (queue.ts:4-6).

    After selection, the same transaction UPDATEs each row with claimed_by, the new lease and attempts + 1, with returning: the whole claim is atomic, and there is no "saw it but did not get it" window. This is not paper reasoning: an integration test is named "ten replicas racing for ten items take each of them exactly once" (server/tests/work-queue.integration.test.ts:73), ten items, ten racing replicas, each item taken exactly once. Companion tests pin two more semantics: a second replica cannot take what the first is holding, and a lease that stops being renewed comes back on its own.

    The operational meaning: no coordinator means no coordinator to defend. A dead replica needs no death-detection process: "one that stops being renewed is free again the moment anything looks, so recovery needs no process to notice a death, only the next claim to read the clock" (queue.ts:8-10). Recovery semantics compressed into an ordinary claim query.

    The write side has one more concurrency gate: offer's atMost fan-out cap (at most three handoffs out of one turn, say) puts the count and the write in the same transaction and serializes the prefix with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(kind:prefix)) (queue.ts:229-265). Why not count first and write second at the caller? The comment gives the counterexample: "a model that emits five tool calls in one turn runs all five at once, each reads a count taken before any of the others had written, and all five pass a cap of three" (queue.ts:111-116). An advisory lock rather than a higher isolation level, because what is guarded is "rows other transactions have not committed yet", and there is no row to FOR UPDATE. The companion test is named "five at once cannot get past a cap of three". One one-line detail: when atMost counts rows by prefix, % and _ in keys are escaped first (queue.ts:178-180): keys can carry underscores, an unescaped LIKE would count other people's rows, and a wrongly counted cap is a wrongly refused handoff. This technique, an advisory lock guarding a counting invariant, reappears unchanged on the routine enable cap later in the chapter.

    Connecting claim, renew, backoff and reclaim, the full lifecycle of a work_items row is this state machine:

    Note there is no "failed" state in the diagram: failure is not an attribute of the row, only a postponed release and one line of last_error. A row has only two ontologies, "still to do" and "done". This is deliberate: fewer terminal states, fewer recovery paths.

    work_items two-replica claim simulatorSELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED · exactly once
    ● Replica A ● Replica B
    kindkeyrun_atclaimed_bylease_untilattemptsfinished
    routine.firert:daily#10-2009:00:00——0—
    bot.messagemsg:fin→ops09:00:01——0—
    computer.suspendcull:bot_4209:00:02——0—
    responsibility.runresp:escrow#8809:00:03——0—
    proactive.runpro:research#1209:00:04——0—
    A
    B
    to B: SKIP LOCKED ↷
    offer (bot.message, msg:fin→ops) · hits the primary key → already

    The lease: the database's clock, not the replica's

    The lease is the easiest thing on this table to get wrong, and OpenBot's way of getting it wrong is carved into the file header (queue.ts:12-16): leases were once computed on the replica as Date.now() + leaseMs and then compared in Postgres against now(), two clocks pretending to be one. "a node ninety seconds behind wrote a sixty-second lease that Postgres considered expired on arrival, and the next replica to look took the item straight out from under the first. Both then ran it."

    After the incident the rule is one sentence: "Every time this file names a moment it names it in SQL." The function implementing it is three lines (queue.ts:183-185):

    typescript
    /** A moment `ms` from now, named in SQL so it is the database's clock and not the caller's. */
function fromNow(ms: number) {
  return sql`now() + make_interval(secs => ${ms / 1000})`;
}

    Every lease and every deadline is generated as a SQL expression, evaluated by Postgres at execution time. The replica's system clock is allowed exactly one job from then on: measuring minute-scale human windows (how often this sweep runs), never any correctness judgment. The sweep contains a passage arguing why process clock skew cannot cause double-firing: "the key and the CAS are both the database's" (server/src/routines/sweep.ts:126-134). Idempotence keys are rendered from database timestamps; clock advancement is adjudicated by database conditional updates; a replica's fast or slow clock only affects when it comes to look at the table, not the truth in it.

    This is my favorite "what was not built" of the chapter: no clock-sync facility, no NTP dependency, only one discipline, moments may be named only by the database, written into a three-line function and a team rule. Cheap discipline beats expensive infrastructure, provided it is actually enforced: not one Date.now() has been written into a lease moment in this file since.

    Idempotence lives in the key

    The primary key of work_items is (kind, key), and key is not a random id: it carries business time. The culler uses the Bot id as key (a computer needs suspending only once at a time); handoffs use in-run numbering; a routine's key is routineId:due-minute. The function rendering that "due minute" is the other half of the system's idempotence story (sweep.ts:117-120):

    typescript
    function minuteKey(due: Date): string {
  // "2026-08-26T09:30:00.000Z" -> "2026-08-26T09:30" -> back with the zone it never left.
  return `${due.toISOString().slice(0, 16)}Z`;
}

    ISO format, truncated to the minute, always UTC. Truncation rather than rounding, so a moment is never rendered into a minute it is not in; toISOString has no local-timezone component, so a replica in another timezone cannot give the same moment a different name. The comment states the consequence plainly: "THE FORMAT IS THE IDEMPOTENCE" (sweep.ts:108-110). Change this format once and every existing key in work_items becomes an orphan, so the test asserts the format string literally instead of recomputing it and comparing. A routine due at 09:00, three replicas waking at the same time, produces the same key, one insert conflict, one firing.

    Conflict detection sits on the write side: offer uses insert ... onConflictDoNothing().returning(key); a conflict means duplicate, and an empty returning means "already". Note the return value is tri-state, not boolean: "queued" | "already" | "refused" (queue.ts:102-118). Two states once caused an incident: a handoff whose key already existed was reported to the model as handed off, while the handoff that row named had been delivered long ago. "Nothing was queued and nobody was ever going to run it." Three states separate "queued", "was already there" and "refused by the fan-out cap", and a caller can no longer report the second as the first.

    Completion semantics serve idempotence too: finish marks rather than deletes. The schema comment records the old implementation's incident: in the delete-on-finish era, a routine that ran at 07:00 would be cleanly re-offered by the next late-waking replica and run again: "the insert that was supposed to collide had nothing left to collide with. A finished row is the collision." (work.ts:68-75). Finished rows must stay, so a late offer with the same key has a wall to hit.

    The rows that stay are eventually reclaimed by purge, and the reclaim window comes in two; this double window was also bought by an incident. Abandoned rows (at the attempt cap, never finishing) were once outside the reclaim condition: "An item at its attempt cap is not finished, so it was reaped by nothing… five failed suspends meant that Bot never scaled to zero again, silently and for ever" (queue.ts:400-412). Five failed suspends wedged the key computer.suspend:someBot forever, and that computer could never scale to zero automatically again. Now purge uses two independent windows: one for finished rows (the collision target for late offers, it must outlive one sweep) and one for abandoned rows (doubling as retry backoff, better long). The culler script even sets the finished-row window to the idle threshold of 30 minutes rather than 24 hours, or the row left by a suspend would swallow the next offer and the computer would stay awake until the row dies of old age.

    Finally, the count. DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5 (queue.ts:88). At the cap the row stops being dispatched, but stays in the table with its count and last_error: "a terminal state a person can query rather than a silence". attempts is deliberately a number, not a state folded into failure: "ONE MEANS IT HAS CERTAINLY NOT RUN. More than one means a previous owner stopped renewing, and may already have called a tool or spent money" (queue.ts:70-78). "Never ran" and "may have run halfway" must be distinguishable. This distinction will save your life in the Responsibility engine later.

    Two clocks for loops: repeatAfterEach and CronJob

    With a queue, someone still has to look at the table periodically. Here is another "not built": no periodic task in the repo carries side-effecting work on setInterval. The reason is in loop.ts's header (loop.ts:1-14): setInterval fires on the clock regardless of whether the last run finished; a sweep claims a batch at a time, one delivery can run out its whole timeout, and a two-second interval would start a hundred and fifty more sweeps while it does, each claiming another batch, each starting a set of agent turns: "The concurrency has no bound but the backlog."

    The replacement is the 64-line repeatAfterEach: the next schedule happens after the previous run ends, and the interval counts from the end. The core is a self-recursive scheduling closure (loop.ts:33-52, one explanatory comment elided):

    typescript
      let stopped = false;
  const next = () => {
    if (stopped) return;
    const timer = schedule(() => {
      if (stopped) return;
      /* ... */
      void work().then(next, next);
    }, everyMs);
    timer.unref?.();
  };

    The elided comment carries the weight of the line void work().then(next, next): success and failure both schedule the next run, and failure is swallowed inside the loop rather than routed through finally, because finally would rethrow the exception and Bun kills the process on an unhandled rejection by default, "turning a blink into a crash loop". A two-second database wobble should not buy a crash loop. The timer is also unref'd, so a pod that should exit is not held back by a loop timer. The Responsibility sweep, the proactive-research sweep, the wakeup sweep, the delivery sweep: ten-plus periodic tasks in the server process all go through this one primitive.

    "Firing routines" itself has two deployment shapes, running the same sweep function. On Kubernetes, a CronJob */5 * * * * runs fire-routines.ts, one round and exit, with activeDeadlineSeconds: 240 (cadence in the charts' values.yaml:483-488, deadline in templates/routines/cronjob.yaml:40). On a laptop, start.sh starts a worker process ticking every 30 seconds forever (worker/src/index.ts:89). The worker does not spawn the script; it imports the same sweep: "the two shapes are the same code doing the same thing on two different clocks" (worker/src/index.ts:8-9). Claimants go to work with names: workOwner("routines") expands to routines/<HOSTNAME>-<uuid8>, so a stuck claim can be traced back to a pod. Dispatch HTTP requests carry a 30-second timeout: "a wedged server must not stall the only thing firing routines" (worker/src/index.ts:77). Even the reclaim cadence is designed for "a laptop can close its lid at any time": purge runs every 120 ticks (about an hour), and always on tick 1: "a laptop restarted every 40 minutes would otherwise never survive to tick 120" (worker/src/index.ts:145). The worker's own configuration is validated with the same paranoia: three environment variables, missing any one is fatal, and a whitespace-only string counts as unset; the old if (!value) guard once let ' ' through (worker/src/env.ts:20-26).

    The two shapes side by side:

    K8s CronJob Laptop worker
    Cadence */5 * * * *, one round then exit 30s per tick, infinite loop
    Deadline activeDeadlineSeconds: 240 none (resident process)
    Concurrency concurrencyPolicy: Forbid single process, naturally serial
    Failure philosophy exceptions bubble up; let K8s mark failed and alert each phase has its own try/catch and swallows the wobble itself
    purge along with each round every 120 ticks + always on tick 1

    The same sweep function, two clocks. The fork in failure philosophy is deliberate: on the CronJob side, "a failing CronJob that pages somebody at 3am should mean something worse than that" (scripts/fire-routines.ts:10-13), an alert should be worth what it costs. On the laptop side, a worker that exits because Postgres wobbled for two seconds needs a human to notice and restart it, and no human is there.

    The door between worker and server is built fail-closed: POST /internal/routines/run is not under /api and does not pass user sessions; the credential is a constant-time comparison of the whole Authorization header; an unconfigured secret and a wrong secret get byte-identical 401s: "A deployment with no worker must not answer a guess any differently" (app.ts:1284-1288). And the endpoint is mounted only on deployments that built a runner: a deployment without a worker "has no door for this at all, rather than one that is mounted and permanently refuses" (app.ts:323-327).

    The last part exists to fight silent failure: if a deployment never started a worker and configured no CronJob, routines never fire, and a deployment with no worker looks exactly like a healthy one, "right up until nobody's standup notes ever arrive" (docs/routines.md). The fix is a heartbeat row: every sweep first writes one routine_sweeps row, and the routines page compares it against a 15-minute window. "No worker" turns from a silent failure into a state visible on the page. The pattern is nearly free and worth copying into every system with background jobs.

    Routines: standing instructions that only grow out of conversation

    Queue and loop are the foundation; routines are the first full tenant on it. First, what was deliberately not built: the REST routes have no create and no edit (server/src/routines/routes.ts:20-24): "THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO CREATE AND NO EDIT ENDPOINT HERE". The page API has only list, toggle, delete, run history and Run now. The reason is hard: "the hard part of both is turning a sentence into a cron expression and a channel, which is exactly what a conversation is for". Translating "give me a morning briefing every weekday" into 0 9 * * 1-5 plus some channel is naturally conversation work; building a form to receive that sentence pushes the hardest step back onto the human.

    So creation goes through four chat tools (create/list/update/delete_routine), mounted in the plugin catalog on the builtin transport and requiring an admin grant per Bot. The tool implementation states a principle outright (server/src/plugins/builtin-routines.ts:29-31): "the ACTOR is not context, it is the authorization". ownerUserId and agentId are read from the connection; the model's parameters have no owner field at all: "a model that could name another owner could schedule work as another person, into a channel it was never in, on a timer nobody else can see". Identity is not context; identity is authorization. An identity the model can fill into a parameter is not authorization.

    Tool descriptions are product too. The instruction field is required to be written as the work one firing should do, imperative, without restating the schedule. A lesson paid in blood: a model reads "Every run, append…" as a schedule-management problem, calls list_routines first to confirm the routine exists, then does nothing, producing "a routine telling somebody it is working while doing nothing at all, which is worse than one that breaks" (shared/routine-firing.ts:22-27). After writing, the tool reads the summary back before wording the confirmation; a failed read-back is not reported as a failed write, so the model does not retry and create duplicates. Channel resolution uses one join to validate at once that the channel exists, is not deleted, the owner is a member and the Bot is in it; if any fails, the refusal is the same sentence, because telling them apart equals telling the caller which channel ids exist (store.ts:360-428).

    Tool descriptions are only half of that file. The other half of shared/routine-firing.ts is a three-sentence text frame, FIRING_FRAME. On every firing, the stored instruction is wrapped in it and written into the transcript as the turn's user message, telling the turn "you are a firing":

    One of your routines is firing right now, on its schedule, and this is that firing. Carry out the instruction below in this turn: do the work now, then say what happened. Do not create, list or change any routine unless the instruction itself asks you to.

    — shared/routine-firing.ts:8-12

    Why does a constant live alone in the shared package? The server writes this text into the transcript, and the browser must recognize it again to draw the message as a firing rather than as something a person typed: "ONE DECLARATION, READ FROM BOTH SIDES". The comment volunteers that this shares its reason with the handoff markers handoff-markers.ts: "Two copies of a sentence is a contract with two authors, and the first rewording breaks the renderer silently" (shared/routine-firing.ts:1-7). The third sentence continues the incident above: without forbidding schedule management, the model reads a firing as an invitation to manage routines. The reading side is readFiring: strip the frame by PREFIX (the frame plus the blank line below it), hand back the original instruction, return null when the frame is not recognized (shared/routine-firing.ts:15-16, 76-78).

    Both numeric gates are designed around "a model can be talked into things". The 15-minute floor (MINIMUM_INTERVAL_MS, schedule.ts:4) has a one-line comment: "A model can be talked into anything; the floor cannot." And the floor is enforced by two independent checks, making acceptance a property of the expression rather than of the moment of asking: the validator scans 200 occurrences from a fixed start and refuses on any adjacent gap under 15 minutes (schedule.ts:72-131); at runtime the actual adjacent pair of firings is pair-checked once more, catching daylight-saving compressions far from the scan window (schedule.ts:171-173). The runtime check throws, which is exactly the entry the sweep uses to switch the routine off automatically. The 20-per-person enable cap (store.ts:66) defends a different shape: "a conversation is an easy place to accumulate standing work without noticing, and 20 is where a person's own list stops being something they can hold in their head". The cap's implementation had a concurrency bug fixed: count and write now live in the same transaction guarded by pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('routine-cap-'+owner)). It was once a bare count-then-write, and "two concurrent creates that both counted 19 both inserted — the person held 21" (store.ts:459-469). An advisory lock rather than a row lock, because what is guarded is a COUNT: "there is no one row whose for update covers 'how many are enabled'". hashtext collisions are harmless: two owners sharing a hash just take turns, slower but not wronger.

    The design here is the scan itself; the number 200 is only its visible part. The start is fixed at 2024-01-01 rather than "now": asked at 08:50, 45,55 8 * * * fires next at 08:55 and then tomorrow at 08:45, a 23-hour-50-minute gap, so a check sampling from "now" would accept the same expression at some times of day and refuse it at others. A fixed start makes acceptance a property of the expression itself, and a leap-year start lets expressions pinned to February 29 be scanned on the days they actually fire (schedule.ts:62-72). 200 is not picked at random either: a five-field cron's intraday pattern is the same on every firing day, the densest day the floor allows is 96 firings, and 200 covers such a day plus the rollover into the next firing day. But the comment admits this is not exhaustive: sub-floor gaps that exist only in a daylight-saving compression more than 200 occurrences from the scan start still slip through, which is exactly why the runtime pair-check stays as the backstop (schedule.ts:74-96). Results are memo-cached with a cap of 1000 entries: validation runs on the sweep's hot path (every due routine passes through it every round), and cache keys come from caller-supplied strings; an unbounded cache with caller-controlled keys is a slow leak a malicious caller can inflate forever (schedule.ts:27-33).

    Timezone validation is solved in-house too: the only reliable way to validate an IANA timezone name in pure JS/TS is to have Intl.DateTimeFormat try constructing one and see whether it throws. cron-parser, via luxon, silently accepts an illegal zone at parse time and explodes much later with an "unhandled timestamp: Invalid Date" that never mentions timezones, so checking early here buys a meaningful refusal (schedule.ts:36-61).

    The read and maintenance sides keep the discipline. Cron expressions never appear raw on the page: describeCron translates them into English sentences ("Weekdays at 09:00"), and the DTO carries text, not cron: "there is no second implementation of cron-to-English anywhere to drift out of step" (routes.ts:145-151). The whole formatter is wrapped in try/catch, because "a formatter that throws on a weird expression would take a page down". Re-enabling a routine recomputes next_run_at (store.ts:518-520): a routine switched off in June does not wake up with a stale June stamp; the next run counts from now. Enabling also writes enabledAt = now(), and the fatigue rule counts only failures since this enabling. Deletion is hard delete, runs cascading: "nothing reads a routine that was deleted". The page's Run now goes through the same runner on the same track, with one debounce before entry: startManualRun takes an advisory lock per routine and refuses if a run is still open within ten minutes: "a double click is one run" (store.ts:675-708).

    One detail worth naming: refusal sentences pass through verbatim to the model (store.ts:308-323). "a model that gets 'Routines may run at most every 15 minutes' can propose a schedule that works, and a model that gets 'invalid cron' cannot". Refusal copy is executable input in this system: a refusal written for a model and a refusal written for a human share one copy budget.

    The store file itself draws the same dividing line with a banner comment, "THE SWEEP'S HALF STARTS HERE":

    One store, because there is one table and one owner-guarding discipline to keep straight about it; but the two halves read nothing alike. Above, every method takes an owner and every failure is one person's… Below, nobody asks a question: a sweep on a clock reads the ledger, and every method has to be read as a race between replicas.

    — server/src/routines/store.ts:733-745

    Above the line, every failure is one person's: a bad cron, a channel they are not in. Below the line, every method has to be read as a race between replicas. The comment names the clock too: every moment comparison below the line uses the database's clock, "now() in SQL, never Date.now()", the same discipline as the queue.ts header, from the same cause. The next section unfolds below this line.

    The two-phase sweep: deciding what should fire is not firing it

    The routine sweep splits into two halves, and the dividing line quotes the culler's precedent: "deciding what should fire is not the same act as firing it" (sweep.ts:1-23). The replica that finds a due routine need not be the one that fires it; a dispatch that dies halfway is taken over by the next claimant, not lost with the process that found it.

    Phase one, offerDueRoutines, has a carefully chosen order: offer before advancing the clock. A crash between the two leaves the next scan reading the same timestamp, rendering the same key, colliding: firing exactly once. Reversed, advance first and offer second, a crash loses the firing permanently. The advance itself is a CAS: where next_run_at = from (store.ts:808-813). Exactly one replica's UPDATE moves the clock; the rest affect zero rows and exit naturally. There is a pit textbooks miss here: the column is microsecond precision and the driver binds milliseconds, so if any writer writes next_run_at with SQL now(), the CAS equality comparison mismatches "silently, for ever" (store.ts:800-807). The clock's advancing authority is the database, but the stamp's read and write formats must round-trip.

    An overdue stamp is not a backlog to repay. A routine a month behind does not catch up; it computes the next run from NOW and one pass sets the clock right. The old implementation advanced one step per pass: "a fifteen-minute routine idle a month stayed silent another fortnight" (store.ts:213-216). The docs put it as "A routine's next run is a stamp, not a queue", and "catching up is a silent drain, not a burst" (docs/routines.md:52-56). Read it together with the 10-minute grace window (DEFAULT_GRACE_MS, sweep.ts:58): the window is "comfortably under the fifteen-minute floor", so it can never treat two adjacent firings of the same routine as both current. A firing that misses its window is skipped, not reissued: a nine-o'clock briefing sent in the afternoon is worse than none.

    Phase two, dispatchClaimedRoutines, renews each claim before acting: "Renewed before acting, because the batch is many and the lease is one" (sweep.ts:329-334), and the comment quotes the culler's lesson verbatim: "A lease nobody renews is a timer, and a timer is what this queue exists not to be." Then comes the discipline this chapter keeps returning to: re-read the world before acting. A claimed row is another replica's judgment at another moment, and in between the routine may have been deleted or switched off. If the routine is gone, finish (not release), because "no number of retries will make a deleted routine exist". The grace window is checked again before acting too, because a queue redelivery can outlive the window at offer time: after five one-minute backoffs, the work is claimed long past the minute it names.

    Dispatch itself is POST /internal/routines/run, returning 202: "accepted, not finished". A dispatch timeout does not close the run row, because a timeout is not a failure: the server may already have accepted and detached, "a turn that will come back minutes later and finish this very row" (sweep.ts:418-429). Truly abandoned run rows are reaped by age: closed only when status stays null beyond twice the turn timeout (2×5 minutes). "Age is the only signal the sweep has that no server is coming back for a row": reaping by identity would kill live turns still running in someone else's hands; reaping by age does not.

    finish/release/renew share one ownership predicate: all three WHERE clauses carry claimed_by = owner and finished_at is null (queue.ts:195-201). The history lesson: they once matched by key alone, and "a replica whose lease had quietly expired could delete or reschedule an item another replica was in the middle of executing". A false return means "it is someone else's now", and the only correct reaction is to stop, not to raise an error.

    The last layer is failure stratification. One routine's error does not sink the whole sweep, but errors split into two grades by "will it heal": queue errors and database errors heal and get retried next round; an unadvanceable schedule (RoutineRefusedError, for instance the runtime pair-check finding adjacent firings violating the floor) does not, because "Deterministic refusals do not heal" (sweep.ts:217-221). Those go straight to markUnschedulable, which switches the routine off and writes a skipped run row as notice, so a person can see in the history why it stopped. One sentinel lives only in the logs: dispatch succeeded but finish returned false (the lease changed hands midway, and another replica may be running the same firing), logging routine-fire-redelivery-possible: "it is the shape of a duplicate run and nothing else in the system will mention it" (sweep.ts:438-453). In this system an unmentioned duplicate is more dangerous than any error.

    The fatigue rule: is this routine still worth firing

    The runner is one turn of an unattended browser: it runs a headless turn as the owner (through Chapter 4's turn runtime and Chapter 5's action gateway, with the initiator marked routine; governance does not discount unattended work), and replies land in the channel via recordActivity. Its failure governance deliberately keeps two ledgers (runner.ts:10-23): the queue's attempts bounds "how many times this due was dispatched", while the fatigue rule counts "how many consecutive firings failed", possibly across days. "Conflating them is how a broken routine either spams a channel… or retries for ever." A retry policy answers "did this one attempt make it through"; the fatigue rule answers another question: is this routine still worth firing (docs/routines.md:43-46).

    The rule itself is plain: the first failure posts one "This routine failed: …" to the channel (the reason truncated to 160 code points); failures 2 through 9 are silent, and the run rows carry all the facts; the tenth (FATIGUE_LIMIT, runner.ts:45) flips enabled off and posts a switch-off announcement, asking a human to fix it and switch it back on. Consecutive failures count only since the last enabling (startedAt >= enabledAt): a routine switched off in June does not come back carrying May's old debt. The streak count itself is bounded too: the scan window is fixed at 20 rows (twice the rule's cap, store.ts:954-1003), because an unbounded query gets slower for exactly the routines that fail most. Worst routines paired with slowest queries is a positive feedback loop you cannot keep. skipped counts as neither failure nor streak-breaker: otherwise a routine whose channel keeps flapping would never reach 10 and never reset to zero. The whole fatigue block is wrapped in its own try/catch: "nothing in it is allowed to throw its way out of a firing whose failure is already on the row". The failure ledger is already on the row; the notification's failure must not lose the ledger.

    skipped is itself a complete three-way judgment, all of it before any turn actually runs: a paused routine is skipped ("PAUSED NEVER RUNS"); a missing channel is skipped, which is exactly why channel_id deliberately has no foreign key: after a channel is soft-deleted the routine survives and shows as broken on the page, instead of being taken away by a database cascade (coworker.ts:106-110); a paused Bot is likewise skipped. None of the three is a failure, because nothing broke; the conditions just do not hold. One small priority discipline: saying "I skipped this one" in the channel is courtesy, and a recordActivity failure is logged without retry: "losing the courtesy is not worth losing the ledger" (runner.ts:103-106).

    This is the governance loop closed with nobody watching: firing has idempotence keys, execution has leases, failure has two ledgers, and termination has an announcement a person can see. Every step can answer "who made it happen and why it stopped".

    The queue's other tenants: same mechanism, different parameters

    Routines are the thickest consumer; the other tenants deserve quick naming, because they show how the same queue primitive takes different parameters for different work shapes. Responsibilities have kind responsibility.run, a 15-minute lease and just two attempts; the next section details them. Proactive research is a background read-only research turn with a 10-minute lease and maxAttempts: 1: "a background run is not worth repeating a partial read for", so a failure waits for the next interval; its initiator mark proactive:<runId> is treated the same as routine in the action gateway: "every policy written for unattended work applies to it too". Bot-to-Bot handoffs (bot.message) renew their lease for the run's duration, and the fan-out cap goes through the queue's atMost; why they do not use in-memory callbacks is the next chapter's topic. Self-wakeups (bot.wakeup) have their own pending and daily-quota caps, likewise guarded by advisory locks. Computer suspension (computer.suspend) is the table's first consumer, and the "re-read the world before acting" discipline comes from its lesson: dialing a computer to ask whether it is idle would wake the computer, "everything works, nothing ever suspends", so it reads only the audit trail and never touches the browser.

    The parameter table persuades better than an inheritance hierarchy: lease length follows "how long one execution takes" (a 60-second HTTP dispatch versus a 15-minute full turn); attempt count follows "the cost of a replay" (an idempotent suspend gets 5, an externally side-effecting Responsibility gets 2, read-only research does not get even one extra). One mechanism survives precisely because the shape choices stay in each consumer's hands.

    Deep Dive: Responsibilities would rather mark failed than replay

    A Responsibility is a persistent goal: triggered by external events (seven trigger types, webhook, GitHub, Linear and the like, ingested after signature verification) rather than cron, carrying progress and successCriteria, able to complete. Its concurrency design differs from routines in one place.

    The event entry ingestEvent does three things in one transaction: insert the event row (a unique index on (ownerUserId, source, externalId) dedupes; a conflict is a duplicate delivery), for update-locks the candidate Responsibilities, and for each hit inserts a run row and a work_items row via queueRun (kind=responsibility.run, key=runId). Event, ledger row and queue item live in the same transaction: there is no "event received but work not queued" middle state, and no "work queued but the event ledger has no record" orphan.

    The heavy side is recovery. The Responsibility engine claims with maxAttempts=2 (responsibilities/engine.ts:49-55), two chances only, because the second chance is implemented like this: beginRun reads a run with attempts > 1, marks it recovered, then directly sets it failed with the note "Actions may already have executed; this run was not replayed" (responsibilities/store.ts:333-344). The queue has already distinguished "never ran" from "may have run halfway" for it (remember why attempts is a number and not a state), and the Responsibility's choice is a queryable failure over a replay that might spend money twice. This is fail-closed at the scheduling layer.

    The lease-turn coupling goes all the way: the Responsibility lease is 15 minutes (covering a long turn), renewed every leaseMs/3 during the turn, and a failed renewal is controller.abort(lostLease) (engine.ts:108-113): lease loss translated into the turn's interrupt signal. Without this translation a lease is only a database field; with it, "someone else took over this work" physically stops the current turn's tool calls. Compare routines: a firing is one short HTTP dispatch and a 60-second lease suffices; a Responsibility hugs a whole turn, so lease length, renewal cadence and interrupt propagation all upgrade together. One elegant reuse: a turn suspending midway for approval (waiting) resumes not through a special channel but by re-queueing with a new key (${runId}:resume:…) (store.ts:436-475). A resume is a fresh piece of claimable work, going through the same queue and the same lease discipline, and the approval endpoint calls it only after validating the stored question.

    The same queue primitive, two work shapes, parameters each their own: exactly the precondition for "one mechanism, seven consumers" to hold.

    Unattended does not mean ungoverned

    Connect this chapter back to the book's spine. Governance rides the protocol: unattended work is not an exception to governance but its home ground. Every headless turn driven by a routine, a Responsibility or proactive research goes through Chapter 4's same turn runtime and Chapter 5's same action gateway; the initiator marks on audit rows (routine / responsibility / handoff; proactive booked as routine with the id prefix proactive:<runId>, having no cell of its own in Chapter 6's six kinds) keep "who made it happen" answerable forever after, and the whole reason Chapter 6's "Nobody watching" filter exists is to sieve these initiators out for a person to see. Boundaries live in the deployment: the queue lives in no framework and no process; it lives in the same Postgres as the production data, so backup, restore and transactional consistency travel with the deployment, and firing's two clocks (the K8s CronJob and the laptop worker) are deployment-shape choices, not code forks. When nobody is watching, work still happens; and every work_items row answers: who made it happen, which attempt this is, and why there is no second time.

    Numbers at a glance

    The key thresholds that appeared in this chapter:

    Number Value Location
    queue default attempt cap 5 work/queue.ts:88
    routine minimum interval 15 minutes routines/schedule.ts:4
    per-person enabled routine cap 20 routines/store.ts:66
    fatigue switch-off threshold 10 consecutive failures routines/runner.ts:45
    firing lease / backoff 60s / 60s routines/sweep.ts:40,48
    grace window 10 minutes (always under the 15-minute floor) routines/sweep.ts:58
    abandoned-run reap age 2× turn timeout (10 minutes) sweep.ts:60-70
    CronJob cadence / deadline */5 minutes / 240s charts values.yaml:483-488 (cadence); templates/routines/cronjob.yaml:40 (deadline)
    worker tick / purge 30s / about 1 hour worker/src/index.ts:89,101
    Responsibility lease / attempts 15 minutes / 2 responsibilities/engine.ts:40,54

    Apply This

    1. The database is the queue; skip the middleware. Solves: exactly-once claiming of timed or asynchronous work across replicas, without introducing new infrastructure. Adapt it: one table, a (kind, key) primary key, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for claiming, a same-transaction UPDATE writing the lease and the count; finished_at marks rather than deletes, left as the wall for late duplicate writes. Watch out: the premise is that Postgres is already the thing every replica shares, so building one just for this inverts the priority; SKIP LOCKED is not every database's dialect, so confirm the equivalent before porting; and once rows pile up, the claim index (kind, run_at) and the purge windows must be designed together, or finished rows grow into the next ownerless big table.

    2. Idempotence lives in the key: let business time into the primary key. Solves: retries, redeliveries and replicas waking at the same time all degrade into primary-key conflicts instead of second executions. Adapt it: the producer renders the key from the business's due moment (a routine is routineId:UTC-due-minute, a suspend is the Bot id), every write is insert on conflict do nothing plus returning to tell the three states apart, and the format is pinned by a literal test. Watch out: never mix inconsistently rendered components into a key; local timezones, millisecond tails and replica ids all grow two keys for one moment. Finished rows must stay until every late offer has expired; delete early and idempotence dies with them. Abandoned rows (at the attempt cap, never finishing) must enter the reclaim condition too, or the key is wedged forever.

    3. The two-phase sweep that separates deciding from acting. Solves: the replica that found the due work dies halfway, or queue backlog makes "the world at claim time" inconsistent with "the world at action time". Adapt it: phase 1 does only idempotent offer plus a CAS advance of the business clock; phase 2 claims, renews first, re-reads the world (does the object still exist? does the window still hold?), then acts; failure backoff goes through the queue's release, not a local retry loop. Watch out: the order cannot flip, offer before advancing the clock, or the crash window becomes a permanently lost firing; the re-read must be a real re-read, and "the offer is another replica's judgment at another moment" deserves posting above every consumer; a renew returning false has exactly one correct reaction, stop, do not raise.

    4. Moments are named only by the database. Solves: replica clock skew makes leases expire on arrival, and work gets torn out of a living replica's hands and executed twice. Adapt it: every lease, deadline and comparison uses SQL now() expressions; write a fromNow-style helper and fold the discipline into three lines of code; process clocks measure only human windows (poll intervals, page hints) and never participate in correctness. Watch out: half compliance equals none; one Date.now() written into a lease column turns the whole discipline into decoration. And mind timestamp precision round-trips: a microsecond-precision column with a millisecond-binding driver makes your CAS equality mismatch forever, silently.

    5. Heartbeat rows: turn "no worker" from a silent failure into page state. Solves: the top failure shape of background systems is not errors but silence; a deployment without a worker looks identical to a healthy one, until someone notices the morning briefing never came again. Adapt it: every sweep first writes a heartbeat row (who, when); the list page compares it with the "longest acceptable gap" and shows overdue ones in the UI; the cost is one INSERT per round. Watch out: anchor the heartbeat window on the business floor (OpenBot uses the 15-minute routine floor as the judgment window); a 60 seconds picked from thin air false-alarms under normally slow sweeps; heartbeat rows themselves go into retention cleanup. The same idea generalizes to every background job where "nobody watching" equals "never happened".

    The next chapter looks at the most social kind of work on this queue: Bot finding Bot, Bot finding human. It explains why a handoff is claimed work rather than a callback, and why the four decisions, who is addressed, where the answer lands, who is asking, and how deep the chain runs, are never left to the model.

    ← Chapter 9: The Supervisor and the Deployment TopologyChapter 11: Bot to Bot, Bot to Human →

    Chapter 11: Bot to Bot, Bot to Human

    The work_items queue from the previous chapter carries seven kinds of work, and six of them are the system talking to itself: suspending computers, triggering routines, delivering notifications. The seventh is the restless one: bot.message, one Bot handing work to another. Chapter 10 covered how this table gets claimed, renewed, and how its keys collide; this chapter covers why collaboration between Bots must take the shape of a hop on a queue, rather than a function call, a message, or worse, a paragraph of free text.

    Picture how a multi-agent system falls apart without this layer. The asking Bot receives a full roster in its prompt, composes "to: the finance Bot" by itself, writes it into a paragraph together with the task, and sends it off; the receiver guesses the intent, the constraints, and the shape the answer should have from that paragraph, and a wrong guess does not error, it confidently answers a different question. Then A asks B, B asks C, and C asks A again: three runs on three pods going in circles, every lap a real, billable model call, and no process holds a variable that can call a stop, because the counter lives in A's memory and stopped counting the moment the third hop landed on C's pod. OpenBot's answer is to take all of these decisions out of the model's hands: who can be addressed, where the answer lands, who is asking, and how deep the chain runs. Four decisions, all made and signed by the deployment; the model is allowed to fill in three typed fields.

    By the end of this chapter you will have the full anatomy of one collaboration chain: message_bot, a tool deliberately unable to improvise; why the decision and the delivery live in separate processes; why chain depth must be signed into the assertion rather than stored in a variable; how the answer relays back to the conversation a person is watching; and the safety exit that never gets a switch, asking a person. The chapter closes with multi-Bot group chat: when two Bots share one channel, how the platform's one-agent-per-thread constraint stretches a group chat into two tables.

    Collaboration is two decisions offered side by side

    When a Bot runs into something it cannot decide, it has three roads: guess, ask another Bot, or ask a person. OpenBot builds the latter two as two tools, offered side by side in the same tool batch, competing for the same decision: message_bot (hand it to another Bot) and ask_person (hand it to the person the deployment believes stands behind the work). The juxtaposition is itself the design, not a listing order. The header comment of escalation.ts says it plainly: if the model has no named "stop and ask" exit in its hands, it will take one of the two roads it does have, either guess confidently, or push the work sideways to a Bot that cannot decide either, spending a whole run to discover the other side cannot decide (escalation.ts:1-8). Giving "ask a person" a name gives "don't guess" an option.

    The two tools share one set of rules, written in the module header of handoff.ts: every refusal is an answer, not an error. The asking Bot is mid-turn with someone waiting for what comes next; a thrown exception ends the whole run saying nothing, which reads to the person as the Bot ignoring them. So both tools' execute translate a refusal into a sentence the model can say out loud and return it, while the audit row is written as usual: the refusal lives in the trail, the dignity lives in the conversation. This rule runs through the whole chapter and is the common shape of every refusal path ahead.

    message_bot: a tool that cannot improvise by design

    The parameter schema of message_bot is this subsystem's first "what was not built": there is no message field. The model must name three things separately:

    Field Required Meaning
    bot yes the target Bot's name, spelled as on the roster
    task yes what you are asking it to do, in a sentence or two
    constraints no boundaries: date ranges, which system to query, rules that must not be broken
    expecting no what a good answer looks like: a list, a number, a recommendation with reasons

    Why not message_bot(target, message) with one free-text field? The header of handoff-tool.ts gives the reason: free text is the most common way multi-agent systems fail quietly, because the receiver has to infer intent from the paragraph, re-derive the constraints, and guess the answer's shape, and a wrong guess does not fail, it confidently returns something else (handoff-tool.ts:8-12). Making the asking model spend a little more effort naming the parts separately removes most of the receiver's guessing. This is reliability bought with a schema, cheaper than any amount of prompt pleading.

    Whether the tool is offered at all is already a boundary. The following decides whether a run can see message_bot (handoff-tool.ts:110-119):

    ts
      if (maxDepth <= 0 || maxPerRun <= 0 || !hasSomebodyToAsk) return null;
  /*
   * Not offered to a run that is already as deep as this deployment allows.
   *
   * The desk refuses it anyway, so this is about what the model is shown rather than about the
   * boundary. A Bot at the cap that can see the tool will reach for it, be told no, and often tell
   * the person it tried and failed, which reads as the deployment being broken rather than as it
   * working.
   */
  if ((from.depth ?? 0) >= maxDepth) return null;

    Note the layering in the comment: the desk refuses anyway, so what this controls is what the model is shown. The offered shape is itself product copy, so "not offered" has to happen at the tool-list layer.

    Grants are the routing table

    Which Bot can address which Bot: the answer is not a roster configured into a prompt, but rows with kind='bot' in the plugin_grants table, the same grant table as MCP tools and skills, where a row's presence is the grant and its absence is refusal (the one-table-three-things design is Chapter 12's main course; here we only use its bot flavor). botsReachableFrom (plugin-store/skills.ts:268-277) is one join: fetch every bot-kind grant this Bot holds, inner join the agents table, and "a grant held by a Bot that no longer exists" automatically stops counting (the skills.ts:266 comment: "keeps a grant held by a Bot that no longer exists from counting").

    Making the address table a grant table has two direct consequences. First, the model never sees a target it was not granted: when handoffTool's hasSomebodyToAsk is zero, the tool is simply not offered. Second, revocation takes effect immediately: the grant check is re-read on every hop and never cached (the handoff.ts:267-268 comment: "so revoking a grant applies to the next hop rather than after a restart"). No snapshot, no TTL cache, because "the hop right after a revocation gets through anyway" is exactly the mistake such a cache would make.

    Four decisions the model is never asked

    docs/architecture.md condenses this section into four items, each mapped to a concrete attack or failure shape:

    Deployment decides Where it comes from Failure shape if done otherwise
    Who gets addressed resolved against the roster visible to the asker, roles looked up live rather than assumed a Bot can reach a Bot its owner cannot see, which bypasses visibility; or the wording distinguishes "does not exist" from "cannot see", and a Bot enumerates the whole deployment's roster by reading refusal copy
    Where the answer lands the threadId in the signed run assertion letting the model name the target conversation means allowing a Bot to drop a turn into a conversation it never joined
    Who is asking the deliverer stamps the attribution from a deployment-written row a Bot that can write its own attribution can impersonate another Bot
    How deep the chain runs the depth in the signed assertion an A→B→C→A loop burns real money with nobody able to call a stop

    The first row hides a detail worth reading line by line: target resolution is done from the asking person's perspective, and the role is looked up live rather than hardcoded to user. handoff.ts:184-193 records why: an administrator's visible roster is larger than a regular user's, and with user hardcoded, an administrator who hands off to a Bot they can see and are actively chatting with gets refused as "there is no such Bot". Visibility is a property of a person, not a constant. The same thinking explains the duplicate-name handling: agents.name has no unique constraint, so deliberately copying a Bot yields two with the same name; an exact id match wins, and a name matching several is refused with every candidate id listed (ambiguous_bot). All of these are things this person can already see, so telling the model is no leak (handoff.ts:206-237).

    The desk and the runner: why decision and delivery live apart

    The division of labor between handoff.ts and handoff-runner.ts is written in the two files' header comments, two halves of one argument: the decision happens inside somebody's run and must be fast and fail-closed; the delivery is another Bot's entire turn and must outlive the pod it departed from. So what separates them is not a function call but a queue. handoff.ts calls itself "the part that decides, not the part that delivers" (handoff.ts:8-12): it resolves the target, refuses, writes the audit row, persists one hop into work_items, and immediately hands a sentence back to the waiting model. Claiming that work item and actually running the asked Bot is another process's job.

    This is exactly the answer to the question Chapter 10 left open: why a hop is claimed work on the same queue rather than an in-memory callback. The runner's header says it in full: claimed, not assigned (handoff-runner.ts:8). Any replica can claim any hop, because the addressed Bot is very likely not on the pod that initiated it; the lease is renewed for the run's whole duration, because a turn is measured in minutes, and a lease expiring mid-delivery hands the same hop to a second replica, paying the model bill twice for one piece of work. Even the delivery wakeup reuses queue primitives: pg_notify is only a latency optimization, with a repeatAfterEach sweep every two seconds as the floor, never overlapping (handoff-wiring.ts:170-185).

    Idempotency lives in the key, and the key's construction is itself an incident postmortem (handoff.ts:303-317):

    ts
          const runPrefix = `hop:${createHash("sha256")
        .update(`${from.actorId}\u0000${from.runId}`)
        .digest("hex")
        .slice(0, 32)}:`;
      const key = `${runPrefix}${createHash("sha256")
        .update(
          JSON.stringify([
            found.id,
            task,
            envelope.constraints ?? "",
            envelope.expecting ?? "",
          ]),
        )
        .digest("hex")
        .slice(0, 32)}`;

    The key has two segments: the prefix is a hash of (actorId, runId), the suffix a hash of the envelope's contents (target, task, constraints, expecting). When the model repeats the same request inside one run, the keys collide and offer idempotently keeps just one hop: "the same request sent twice is one hop; that is the honest reading of a model repeating itself, and the alternative is at-least-once with no cap" (handoff.ts:289-295). And the runId is hashed in, not concatenated: it comes from the request, an ordinary string whose shape the deployment never constrains. There was once a runId called notice, which turned the fanout prefix into notice:, and that is exactly the key prefix of deployment-wide failure notifications, so other people's failed hops spent this run's budget of three slots (handoff.ts:296-302). Hashing moves every character the caller can choose out of the prefix while keeping it stable within the same run, which is all the fanout cap needs.

    The atMost fanout cap is also not checked at the desk first: count-then-write is "a cap that holds only while nobody is writing", and the situation it must hold in is exactly the opposite, with the model issuing several tool calls in one turn that run concurrently and each read the count before the others' writes land. So counting and writing are one step inside the queue, an advisory lock pinning the prefix while counting and inserting (Chapter 10 covered this offer transaction). A cap's correctness cannot depend on the caller's timing.

    The whole chain, walked once end to end:

    The desk's full set of refusal reasons earns a table. Every one of them is a sentence the model can say out loud, and every one also writes an agent.handoff_refused audit row:

    reason Trigger Shape of the answer
    no_task task is empty "a handoff must say clearly what you are asking for"
    no_thread the run is not in a conversation "there is nowhere to put the answer"
    depth_cap depth at the cap "already N layers deep; answer with what you have, or ask a person"
    no_actor the asker's identity cannot be confirmed "could not confirm who you were asking for just now; not sent"
    ambiguous_bot the name matches several visible Bots lists the candidate ids so the model names one
    no_such_bot does not exist or is not visible, the same sentence "there is no Bot by that name that you can reach"
    self the target is itself "do it yourself, or ask a person"
    not_granted no bot-kind grant "an administrator grants it"
    paused the target is paused "a person can restore it from the archive page"
    fanout_cap this run's slots are used up "this turn has already asked N Bots"
    duplicate same run, same request, key collision "wait for that answer; do not ask again"

    The refusal wording shares one escape direction: "answer with what you have, or ask a person." A refusal pushes the decision back toward the two legitimate exits rather than leaving a dead end.

    Lease discipline on the delivery side

    The runner's sweep loop is a mirror of Chapter 10's queue primitives, with three tightenings that exist only for hops. First, batch-wide renewal: one claim leases the whole batch, while delivery is serial one hop at a time, and one delivery takes minutes against a sixty-second lease. Renewing only the hop in hand lets the batch's tail quietly expire while the head is delivering; another replica picks it up and delivers again, and both replicas report success. This bug was reproduced with two replicas against real PostgreSQL: "the one being delivered was fine; everything queued behind it was not" (handoff-runner.ts:261-271). Second, ask the database once more before calling the model: a heartbeat over your own set can only reflect "renewal was tried and refused", while a process stalled past its lease expiry never tried, so the set still says "mine". The renewal is itself both the question and the answer, and it lays down a fresh lease before delivery begins (handoff-runner.ts:340-351). Third, finish returning false means the lease changed hands during delivery and another replica may also have run this hop: the turn really happened and the audit must say so, but it must never say this replica completed it, or a person facing two similar answers cannot tell one duplicate from one ghost (handoff-runner.ts:381-409).

    ts
    // Pseudocode — illustrates the pattern
async function sweepHops(queue, runOne) {
  const batch = await queue.claim({ kind: "bot.message", limit: 5 });
  const heartbeat = renewAll(batch, { every: 20_000 }); // renew the whole batch, not only the one in hand
  try {
    for (const hop of batch) {
      if (!(await queue.renew(hop.key))) continue; // ask the database once more before calling the model
      try {
        await runOne(hop);
        if (!(await queue.finish(hop.key))) flag("lease changed hands; another replica may also have delivered");
      } catch {
        await queue.release(hop.key, { delayMs: 60_000 }); // put back, do not drop
      }
    }
  } finally { heartbeat.stop(); }
}

    This pattern deserves to be spelled out on its own: Chapter 10's "claim, renew, finish" was a safety net for routines, and here it is the front line against double billing. A duplicated hop is not a task run twice; it is another Bot run twice, with two copies of the answer appearing in a person's conversation.

    Why chain depth cannot live in a variable

    Back to the A→B→C→A loop from the opening. To stop it, the counter must travel with the chain, and the chain crosses processes: the A, B, and C runs may sit on three pods. OpenBot puts the answer in a signed run assertion, RunAssertion = { botId, actorId, runId, threadId?, depth?, initiator?, handoff? }, signed by the deployment with KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY and handed to the Bot through AG-UI's forwardedProps (callback-token.ts:75-119). The depth field's comment lays out the argument (callback-token.ts:97-101, paraphrased): a counter kept in a variable stops counting the moment the second hop lands on another pod, which is exactly when the loop starts costing real money; the assertion is signed by the deployment and has already crossed every boundary the run crosses, which makes it the one place a Bot cannot edit.

    The mint, in full at a glance (callback-token.ts:130-143):

    ts
    export function mintRunAssertion(
  run: RunAssertion,
  encryptionKey: string,
  now: number = Date.now(),
): string {
  const payload: SignedRun = {
    ...run,
    depth: run.depth ?? 0,
    initiator: run.initiator ?? PERSON_INITIATOR,
    exp: now + RUN_TTL_MS,
  };
  const value = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload)).toString("base64url");
  return sign(value, encryptionKey, RUN_LABEL);
}

    initiator rides the same vehicle: the process that knows "a routine started this run" is the one that claimed the routine, not the one that writes the audit row; signed in together with the other fields, a Bot cannot relabel its own run as a person's, and the audit's "Nobody watching" filter (Chapter 6) depends on that label being unforgeable. The assertion TTL is ten minutes, long enough for slow tool loops and short enough to bound the value of an intercepted assertion.
