    Chapter 15 ended with learning crossing a process boundary for the first time: RemoteLearnedSkillsMiddleware keeps the reviewed skill snapshot server-side and resumes across the AG-UI boundary for up to ten steps, feeding the agent on the other side. Who stands on that side? This chapter gives the full answer: any one of fifteen harnesses. CrewAI, LangGraph, Google ADK, Claude Agent SDK, Mastra... Different languages, different tool loops, different state models, and OpenBot says the same sentence to all of them.

    The framework ecosystem is the liveliest and most dangerous part of an agent platform. Lively, because a new framework shows up every month. Dangerous, because the textbook approach is "write an adapter per framework", which copies the governance logic N times, and three months later one copy quietly drops a check and nobody knows which. OpenBot bets on the upper half of this book's spine: governance rides the protocol, not the framework. The contract has been shaved down to three clauses, shaved to the point where whether a framework can enter the catalog depends on whether somebody else maintains its integration package.

    This chapter first looks at the three clauses and how they are enforced, then at the catalog as one piece of data consumed by three languages at once, then takes apart the server-side middleware and the dual-credential callback that give every framework the same governance, and finally goes inside the four most representative integrations, closing the other eleven with a table. When you finish you will know why adding a sixteenth framework to this platform does not require changing one line of server code, and which roads were deliberately blocked and why.

    A Bot is a row in the registry

    First pin down the word harness. A harness is the running shell of an agent framework: a standalone process with some framework's agent loop inside and an AG-UI endpoint wrapped outside. The OpenBot repo has 15 such directories in three classes:

    • Hand-written TypeScript protocol (2): agent-bot (the built-in Bot, port 4200) and agent-langgraph (4201). They were written before the rule existed, so they hand-write the protocol.
    • Python with maintainer integration packages (12): CrewAI, ADK, Agno, Pydantic AI, Microsoft Agent Framework, LlamaIndex, AG2, Strands, Langroid, Claude Agent SDK, Antigravity, and agent-langgraph-agui, the LangGraph variant on the official integration. Each is FastAPI plus the AG-UI integration package published by the framework's maintainer.
    • The Mastra special case (1): Mastra ships its own HTTP server and deliberately mounts no AG-UI route; the server dials in through the @ag-ui/mastra bridge.

    To the server, all of this collapses into one thing: a Bot is a row in the registry pointing at an AG-UI endpoint. There are only three registration types (built_in, remote_ag_ui, remote_mastra), plus a fourth, unavailable: the tombstone of a deleted coworker, kept in the registry only so Intelligence can still restore threads, with all runs refused. The comment at agent-langgraph/src/index.ts:34-36 states the design goal flatly: "so adding a framework does not require server changes". The built-in Bot and a customer's bring-your-own Bot share the same registry, the same route, the same governance. There is no insider lane.

    The registration types carry a deliberate clumsiness: remote_ag_ui and remote_mastra are a union of two single-literal variants rather than one type with a type field of "remote_ag_ui" | "remote_mastra", because TypeScript cannot do exclusion narrowing on a type whose discriminant field is itself a union: after excluding both literals the member remains, and the built-in path would silently stop narrowing to the built-in Bot. The comment pins the decision to measurement: "Verified against tsc 5.x; collapsing these two back into one costs that" (copilot.ts:108-118). The shape of the type serves compile-time exhaustiveness checking, ugly but honest; this posture shows up once more later in this chapter, at the zod 3/4 conversion.

    Orchestration obeys the same idea. In docker-compose the harness is one agent-harness service, not twelve branches: "a picked harness is a choice and not twelve branches in this file". Image and port come from .env, and each harness's port is pinned in its own Dockerfile; the whole service sits behind profiles: ["harness"], so a deployment that picked no harness does not pull an empty-string image and drag down the entire up. The injected environment is a full set of provider keys and base_urls plus the OPENBOT_TOOL_URL and AGENT_TOOL_TOKEN the callback needs. The finest attention sits on one bind mount: ./.langchain mounts a directory, not a file, because the subscription access token expires in an hour and the harness has to renew it and write it back, and the provider writes with "temp file + atomic replace", so the mount point must be the directory where the temp file's sibling lives, or the replace cannot land.

    For the "a Bot is a row" claim to hold, the contract must be small enough for any framework to afford. The next section shows how small.

    A three-line contract

    The docstring at agent-crewai/src/main.py:8-9 writes out the contract verbatim:

    "The contract with the rest of OpenBot is the same one the other Bots meet, and it is small: serve AG-UI on a port, answer /health, and refuse anybody who does not carry the server's token."

    Unpacked, that is three obligations:

    1. Serve AG-UI on a port. RunAgentInput in, SSE events out (RUN_STARTED, TEXT_MESSAGE_*, TOOL_CALL_*, RUN_FINISHED/RUN_ERROR; the event stream itself is Chapter 4's home). Which path it hangs on is each harness's own business, and the catalog's runPath field records the shapes: most use the root path, LlamaIndex uses /run, Agno uses /agui.
    2. /health skips auth. This is sequencing, not leniency: Compose polls it before any token exists. "A healthcheck that authenticates is a container that never reports healthy" (agent-crewai/src/main.py:184-188).
    3. Every other route checks the x-openbot-agent-token header. Mind the direction: an unconfigured token is not "open", it is "unconfigured", and everything gets refused.

    The enforcement code looks identical in every Python harness, down to the function name:

    python
    @app.middleware("http")
async def refuse_without_the_server_token(request: Request, call_next):
    if request.url.path != "/health":
        expected = _expected_token()
        offered = (request.headers.get(TOKEN_HEADER) or "").strip()
        # An unset token means unconfigured, not open.
        if not expected or not hmac.compare_digest(offered.encode("utf-8"), expected.encode("utf-8")):
            return JSONResponse({"error": "unauthorised"}, status_code=401)
    return await call_next(request)

    (Quoted from agent-crewai/src/main.py:183-197, docstring omitted.) It shows the minimal implementation of clause three: hmac.compare_digest for constant-time comparison; not expected comes first, so unconfigured refuses first. The TypeScript counterpart is matchesToken in shared/agent-authorisation.ts:1-9: hand-written XOR accumulation with length compared first, twenty lines, semantics aligned across two languages. The two TS Bots go further: a missing MANAGED_AGENT_TOKEN is an immediate process.exit(1), because "This process holds a model credential and will not start without a token" (agent-bot/src/index.ts:32-38). A process holding a model credential, when it cannot verify its caller's identity, has exactly one correct state: not existing.

    Port binding is just as deliberate. The Python images all use uvicorn --host 0.0.0.0 rather than ::, because uvicorn binds :: as IPv6-only, and this was measured, not guessed (the comment at the end of agent-langgraph-agui/Dockerfile: "Measured, not assumed"). The Compose side publishes only to the two loopbacks 127.0.0.1 and [::1]: an attacker who wants to touch a harness must stand on the machine first.

    There is a fourth item that counts as the contract's inverse: who the token gets sent to. x-openbot-agent-token goes only to "addresses this deployment itself runs": MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL, plus PICKED_HARNESS_URL when PICKED_HARNESS_IMAGE exists. Candidates are normalized before comparison (trailing slashes stripped, query/fragment differences kept), and an unparseable candidate address is never treated as managed (managed-endpoint.ts). A concrete bug was fixed here: in the era when only a single address matched, the harness picked at setup got no token: registration succeeded, addressable, routed correctly, and it answered 401 to everything. A customer Bot's credential is resolved per run from the vault: "revoking a credential then takes effect on the next run rather than on the next restart" (runtime-agents.ts:46-47). The boundary lives in the deployment, and in code that sentence reads: who may receive a credential is decided by the deployment topology, not by a string in a config file.

    The configuration side has a symmetric tiering (config.ts:641-666): an address without a token refuses to boot: "A URL with no token would send unauthenticated calls to a Bot that refuses them"; a token without an address is ignored, since that is residue scripts/start.sh writes into .env: "it names nothing and is ignored, so a one-container image can boot from that file". The two directions of half-configuration get two dispositions: what would send misguided requests refuses to boot; what points at nothing is silently let through. The tiering standard is each direction's shape of harm, not symmetry for its beauty.

    The three clauses together can be summed up in one picture: all governance sits server-side, and below the transport are fifteen mutually different implementations.

    Note that byo-url is in the picture too: "an agent you already run yourself" is a row in the catalog, and the contract treats it the same as the in-house fifteen. This is why the contract must be three clauses and not thirty: every clause is a demand made of a stranger.

    The catalog is data

    The list of fifteen harnesses lives not in code but in shared/harnesses.json: 14 rows of data plus a _readme field. Thirteen frameworks with images, plus byo-url. The two hand-written TS harnesses are not in it; they ship with the product and are not install options. A few designs worth learning:

    image is a directory, not an id. The release pipeline publishes openbot-<directory> by Dockerfile path, and four rows have ids that differ from directory names: the langgraph row's image is agent-langgraph-agui, not agent-langgraph. Encoding "built from which directory" into the data saves the release script from maintaining a second mapping.

    Ordering is stars first, downloads as check, "because each misleads alone". And entries marked In Progress on AG-UI's official ecosystem table (OpenAI Agents SDK, AWS Bedrock Agents, Cloudflare Agents) are not admitted at all. The _readme's reason is one of this chapter's creeds: "offering a harness that cannot answer is worse than a shorter list". An option that cannot answer is not neutral; it spends trust.

    mark may be null. The four rows ag2, agno, byo-url, and langroid have no logo image, and a test pins this down. No invented logos for the gaps.

    The four credential values are split by "what can be installed with it". any-provider/anthropic/google/their-endpoint (harnesses.ts:24-28). google stands alone because Antigravity's bundled Go harness takes only a Gemini key wherever base_url points: "any provider the person already has" is precisely the promise it cannot keep, and "a deployment holding only an OpenAI key would install a Bot that never answers"; anthropic stands alone because it is the only row where a subscription can stand in for an API key (the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from claude setup-token, expanded in this chapter's agent-claude-sdk deep dive). This field is not metadata decoration; it is the boundary where the installer asks truthfully. Ask for the wrong credential type and you have sold the deployment a Bot that will never talk once installed.

    Only Mastra has webCreate: false. Dialing in through the bridge needs a roster id to say which agent on the server, and the web creation API cannot send one. Putting it in the dialog would "make a Bot that appears, accepts a grant, and answers nothing" (harnesses.ts:50-57). If it cannot be installed truthfully, better not to display it. The webSummary field exists for the same reason, only where the installer copy does not hold for the web (the byo-url and claude-agent-sdk rows).

    The byo-url row also hides the catalog's only runtime verification: its summary reads "It is proved with a real AG-UI run before it is saved". testAgentConnection (server/src/agents/connection-test.ts) POSTs a minimal real run to the entered address ("Only a POST that produces AG-UI events distinguishes 'an agent' from 'a web server that happens to be reachable'") with a fifteen-second timeout, stopping at the first event it recognizes. It used to read the whole body up to a byte cap, until one agentic harness neither capped nor closed: it opened with a ninety-byte RUN_STARTED and then turned around to call the model. The landing point after redirects passes the endpoint check too, since "checking only what the person typed leaves the redirect as the way around it". Failure copy all addresses the person filling the form, and the function never throws.

    This JSON's key is not its content but its consumption: one piece of data, three languages, each with its own anti-drift mechanism.

    Reader How it reads What it guards against
    Rust desktop include_str! bakes it into the binary at compile time (desktop/src-tauri/src/harness.rs:197-198) no dependable working directory exists when the setup window paints; a catalog that can fail to load is a blank picker on first launch
    Web new-Bot dialog imported through shared/harnesses.ts with a type assertion a JSON import would widen credential/maintainer to string; the assertion turns a typo in the file into a test failure
    Tests pin the full id ordering; verify every named mark file really exists "glob matched nothing" passes silently; only assertions can tell the difference

    Why the tension? The comment at harnesses.ts:3-15 answers: this list carries other companies' trademarks, and "a second copy would drift, which matters more here than for most lists". The catalog is data because data has exactly one editable original; copies do not.

    A second file follows the same thinking: shared/model-providers.json. It is the single source of truth for provider/model specs: three provider rows (key variable, base_url variable, default model for openai/anthropic/google) and a bots section with one default provider and model per harness; API keys never enter the file. Two loaders, model-providers.ts and model_providers.py, mirror each other line by line, each holding its own PROVIDER_IDS list and cross-validating in both directions: anything in the file the list does not know, anything in the list the file lacks a row for, any empty field: all blow up at startup with the key path in the error. The Python file's docstring states the motive in full: if the two loaders answered differently it "would put the languages of one box on different models".

    The spec-parsing rules all live in the shared file too, not scattered across fifteen harnesses: the lookup order is uniformly "env var > bots row > provider default"; an empty string reads as unconfigured (Compose's ${BOT_MODEL:-} passes empty strings); a missing bots row throws outright, since an editing mistake should meet the developer at startup, not leave every deployment mysteriously answering with the same model. A blank provider reads as openai, because that is what the desktop writes when it switches back to OpenAI, and "a Bot that refused that would disagree with the screen that configured it". OpenAI with a custom base_url does not require a key: Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, and llama.cpp all serve the same API keyless, and where the SDK must be handed a string the placeholder "no-key-needed" is used, because "empty is a client that cannot be constructed". Inside there is also a predicate this chapter meets twice: requiresResponsesApi(model) recognizes with a regex the model families that must go through the Responses API, and the comment takes care to say it names a fact, not a use, because agent-bot uses it to refuse a model while agent-langgraph uses it to flip a switch. The same predicate, two opposite actions; that is why it lives in the shared spec file and not in any harness.

    How governance rides the protocol

    The contract guarantees a harness can be called and recognized. But "can be called" is a whole Chapter 5 away from "governed". The bridge is the server-side middleware remoteAgentWithStandingRole (starting at server/src/copilot.ts:1230), which injects three things into the input sent to the remote endpoint on every run:

    First, the standing role, as an ordinary AG-UI system message. Not through forwardedProps, not through any framework-specific state channel, because "the endpoint on the other side may be LangGraph, Mastra, ADK or a hand-written server, and a system message is the only thing all of them already understand" (copilot.ts:156-159). Governance information travels the lowest common denominator channel; this is the chapter's most valuable decision. Same-named copies left in the history are stripped: the endpoint must receive exactly one, at the front, no matter how many times the thread has been replayed. Note one asymmetry: the person's own standing instructions are not sent to remote Bots (copilot.ts:948-953). A remote Bot assembles its own prompt on somebody else's endpoint, and sending one user's prose to a server this deployment does not run means not knowing whether the other side reads it at all, nor whether it ranks ahead of or behind the role.

    Second, the holdings message. Generated from the tools actually granted this turn, telling the model what it holds right now. The comment explains why the remote path needs it more than the built-in one: a Bot without this message is the Bot that browses to drive.google.com, holds four Drive tools, and thinks it has none.

    Third, three openbot keys in forwardedProps: openbotBotId, openbotDeploymentTools (which tools are executed deployment-side and which are drawn interface-side; Chapter 13's narrowing decides what is offered this turn, and this division decides who executes at the other end), and openbotRun, the signed assertion of this run. If the assertion cannot be signed it is simply not sent, and the direction is deliberate: "a Bot that cannot prove whose run it is should not be spending anybody's grants".

    The division standard for openbotDeploymentTools is structural, not name-guessing: anything with execute that is not one of the two coordination tools message_bot/ask_person takes the interface side's real AG-UI client lifecycle, so approvals can grab the provider's toolCallId, messages, and state; coordination tools keep their signed callbacks, and the remaining names go down as deployment-side tools (copilot.ts:1320-1333). Only the server side can produce this list, and the comment records why: tools mixes two indistinguishable kinds of name, and there was a Bot that executed a browser-drawn component as a deployment tool, got told no, and then apologized for "not showing that chart", while the chart sat on the person's screen. "Only this side knows which is which, so only this side can say" (copilot.ts:1336-1342).

    Two more things are done "in the middleware rather than by wrapping an agent": history hygiene (Chapter 4's sanitize) and attachment inlining. The reason hides in an easy-to-miss API detail: AG-UI's run method skips middleware registered with .use(), and when the outer agent delegates to the remote agent it goes exactly through run. Wrap a layer and the standing role, holdings, tools, and signed assertion would all be silently lost, "and every one of those is silent — the Bot simply answers worse" (copilot.ts:1253-1258). Worse answers are the hardest failure shape to alert on.

    Both transports (HttpAgent direct and the Mastra bridge) normalize to the AbstractAgent interface, and the governance code programs against the interface only. The comment at copilot.ts:1119-1122 gives this normalization its reason to exist: "A Mastra Bot is governed by exactly the same code as an AG-UI one and cannot skip a control by being a different kind." Writing one wrapper per transport is the standard path to some control being silently bypassed three months later. The stall guard wraps fetch rather than the AG-UI middleware: a stall is the absence of events, so the response body itself is what to watch.

    The hardest spot inside the normalization is one type conversion when the Mastra bridge is assembled (copilot.ts:1168-1182). The bridge straddles a package-manager reality: the server runs zod 4 while @ag-ui/mastra depends on zod 3, so the package manager resolves two peer variants of @mastra/client-js: "identical code at identical version 1.43.0, but two nominal types to TypeScript". Same code, same version number, yet two classes TypeScript will not mutually assign, because zod's nominal types carry private fields. The code's answer is one as unknown as MastraClientForBridge, and the comment writes the discipline: "The cast crosses that and nothing else. It is deliberately written against the bridge's own parameter type, so the day the two versions really do diverge this stops compiling instead of lying." The rejected alternative is recorded in the same place: forcing zod 4 onto @ag-ui/mastra with an override would make the type error disappear, by betting on a runtime behavior inside somebody else's package. "Not worth it for a private field." This is the book's "the compiler guards the truth" theme appearing inside the bridge: a type assertion is a check with its expiry condition written on it, not hush money thrown at the compiler.

    The same assembly makes one identity decision: Mastra scopes memory by resourceId, and what OpenBot hands over is the Bot id, not the person's id (copilot.ts:1184-1190). The reason shares its bloodline with the earlier "the person's standing instructions are not sent to remote Bots" comment: "History here is ours: it is restored from Intelligence and sanitised before every run, so nothing depends on the endpoint remembering anything. Sending the person's identity would put it on a server this deployment does not run". History is OpenBot's own, rebuilt from Intelligence and sanitized before every run, so whether the endpoint remembers anything is irrelevant; sending a person's identity to a server this deployment does not run, to drive a feature this deployment does not use, is pure leakage. Chapter 15's two tracks win again here: because memory belongs server-side, the endpoint can be treated as a memoryless pure function.

    At the bridge's other end, inside the agent-mastra process, the same discipline holds. Governance content arrives via AG-UI context: buildOpenBotInstructions recognizes only three fixed description names ("OpenBot standing role", "OpenBot granted tools guidance", "OpenBot learned skills"), picks them out of the context and splices them into the instructions, falling back to the baseline instructions when none are present (index.ts:86-90, 113-135).

    Model assembly is equally fail-closed: the provider loads only two SDK modules, and a provider the file has not heard of, or one heard of but with no module, is refused at startup on both halves; they "used to fall through to the OpenAI branch below and answer with a model the deployment never chose" (index.ts:28-37). Even build timing is discipline: the Dockerfile runs bunx mastra build at image time, because "mastra start runs a bundle, and building on every container start would put a build step in front of a person waiting for a Bot" (agent-mastra/Dockerfile:14-16). Building belongs to the image; starting belongs to the person.

    A governed remote run, end to end:

    The only genuinely new step in the picture is the "verify signature, check hash, cross-check" on the callback endpoint. That is the dual credential's business, and it gets its own section.

    Two credentials on the callback: who is speaking, for whom

    When a harness calls back to the deployment to execute a tool, two different questions must be answered, and OpenBot answers them with two different credentials (the comment at server/src/agents/callback-token.ts:6-23 is a textbook):

    The token answers "which agent is calling". obot_agt_ prefix, 32 bytes, issued per agent, only its SHA-256 hash stored in the database: "we issue it and we only ever need to check one, so keeping the token itself would make a database dump a working credential". The prefix is designed to be "recognisable on sight": a token leaked into a log can be swept out.

    The signed assertion (run assertion) answers "for which Bot, for which person". The token cannot answer this: it is issued for months at a time, and this answer changes every run. The assertion is signed under its own label (openbot:agent-run) with a ten-minute TTL, long enough for a slow tool loop to finish and a cap on what an intercepted assertion is worth. The assertion also carries threadId, depth, and initiator. Chapter 11 covered how they travel with hops and why a counter in a variable fails at the second hop, so no repeat here; what needs stressing is the provenance: Bot and initiator used to be read from the request body, which meant "whoever holds the token declares their own identity". The comment's verdict: "The trail is the product; a forgeable trail is worse than no trail."

    The two credentials cross-check: the assertion states which Bot it was issued for, and if the presented token belongs to another agent the answer is 403 "That token is not for this Bot". Otherwise a glimpsed assertion could be replayed by any token-holding agent, borrowing the grants of somebody else's Bot. Signature verification failure and token-not-found both return the same 401, without distinguishing which half went wrong: "A caller learning that its token was accepted but its assertion was stale has learned that its token is good." The granularity of a refusal reason is itself intelligence. The read side is tiered too: readRunAssertion is fail-closed on any doubt ("Nothing on any doubt"), while readApprovedRunAssertion deliberately ignores expiry, because an approval is answered by when the human arrives, usually long past ten minutes.

    The input parsing at the entrance has also been repaired one notch: parseAgentToolCallInput first shapes the request body, then maps mcp__server__tool to server/tool. The order used to be reversed, and a non-string name threw a TypeError in the route, which the catch turned into a 200 tool refusal: "A caller error looked like a tool saying no, with no audit row and no 400." A caller's format error wearing a tool refusal's mask is the lie an audit trail least recognizes.

    Finally, refusals are booked too: every refused callback writes one mcp.callback_refused row. This row's reason to exist is a concrete failure history: a Bot whose token rotation did not line up got every callback refused, returned empty to its own model, and the model turned around and told the user "no results found". A false negative taken as an answer, with the audit trail agreeing nothing happened, is the most confusing failure of all. A refused call is part of the trail just as an approved one is.

    Four representatives, four solutions

    With the contract and governance covered, what remains is "what does each harness look like inside". Four of the fifteen get a deep dive: the two hand-written ones (they explain where the rules came from) and the two with the most personality (one stuffs client tools back into the SDK's original query; one hands the protocol back to the maintainer). Each represents one way of living with a framework.

    Deep Dive: agent-bot, or what handwriting the protocol buys

    agent-bot is the proof of concept: 266 lines, a hand-written streaming loop over OpenAI /v1/chat/completions, no framework anywhere. Its tool loop lives on the client: emit a tool call and end the run; the interface side executes the tool, appends the result, and opens a new run with the fuller conversation: "That keeps the tool running where its effects are visible to the person watching" (index.ts:15-24). It publishes no tools of its own; input.tools is translated verbatim into OpenAI function format. This is AG-UI's earliest form: the loop in the browser, because that was the only place with a person at the time.

    What handwriting the protocol buys is configuration honesty, not performance. This file has four fail-closed gates at startup, all process.exit(1): missing token; a BOT_MODEL belonging to a Responses-API-only model family refused outright (because chat completions refuses their function tools); missing OPENAI_API_KEY with no keyless endpoint; the provider pinned to openai, never reading BOT_PROVIDER: a hand-writer of the protocol cannot be rerouted by one variable. The second gate's comment deserves a full quote: "Silence is the worst failure available here, and it is what a single mistaken BOT_MODEL produced: every tool-using turn stopped dead while the Bot looked healthy." Looking healthy while unable to answer is the worst failure shape this repo repeatedly recognizes: the health check is green while every tool-using turn dies inside. Configuration must fail in front of the deployer, not in front of the asker.

    The streaming translation itself has one passage worth learning: the provider streams one tool call's arguments in fragments divided by index, across many chunks, attributed only by index. This service buffers per index and emits one TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END after the stream ends: "Buffering per index is what turns that back into one call the surface can run." On error it sends RUN_ERROR rather than silently ending the stream: "A stream that simply ends leaves the surface waiting forever with no reason."

    Its most flavorful part is history.ts. In the history read back from the persistent thread, tool results are ordered before their calls (the store's order), the provider refuses such payloads outright, and the model answers refusal with silence: "The model answers that with silence rather than an error, which is the worst of both, so the pairing is rebuilt here instead of trusted." So the pairing is rebuilt locally: first collect the answered set and the results table, then replay each call's result right behind its assistant message.

    typescript
    for (const call of message.toolCalls ?? []) {
  if (!call.id) continue;
  messages.push({
    role: "tool",
    tool_call_id: call.id,
    content: answered.has(call.id)
      ? (resultsByCall.get(call.id) ?? "")
      : NO_ANSWER_CAME,
  });
}

    (Quoted from agent-bot/src/history.ts:95-104.) It shows the concrete writing of "do not trust the input's shape": a real result gets used wherever it drifted in the history; absent one, fill in the NO_ANSWER_CAME placeholder. Without the placeholder OpenAI refuses the whole payload on the next turn: "the conversation was not merely stuck on that request, it was finished". There is also a darker pit: in the AG-UI protocol a call is written {id, type, function:{name, arguments}}, while in the history store it is {id, name, args}: two spellings, the same call. The original "fix" gave the name a default, and every restored call became a parameterless call named tool; the model could not recognize the call it had made, so it made it again, "the exact repetition the fallback was written to prevent". The default is still there, demoted to a true last resort.

    History assembly has one more entrance step: input.context is folded into a system message prefix placed ahead of the history (history.ts:20-27); the component catalog and tool guidance arrive this way, and "omitting them leaves the model guessing component names and action schemas". The shape of context is part of the contract too: if Chapter 14's component catalog gets dropped at this step, the model cannot even guess the component names, and the best-governed tools may as well not exist.

    Deep Dive: agent-langgraph, or pulling the tool loop back into the process

    agent-langgraph is the same Bot moved onto a framework, and its most important change is pulling the tool loop back into the process from the browser, not "it uses StateGraph" (index.ts:321-330). In the old form the harness emitted a call, ended the run, and waited for the interface to execute before opening a new run: "That made a watching browser a requirement for a Bot to do anything, which rules out an embed, a schedule, and anything unattended." A Bot that needs a browser watching to do anything rules out embedding, rules out scheduling, rules out every unattended scenario; that is, it rules out the whole of Part IV. With the loop back in-process, the graph has only two nodes, answer (the model) and tools (execution), joined by one three-way conditional edge:

    typescript
    .addConditionalEdges("answer", (state) => {
  const last = state.messages.at(-1) as AIMessage | undefined;
  const calls = last?.tool_calls ?? [];
  if (calls.length === 0) return END;
  if (callsTheSurface(calls, ours)) return END;
  return "tools";
})

    (Quoted from agent-langgraph/src/index.ts:369-388, the long comment in between omitted; the original reads "A call the surface owns ends the run.") What it shows is tool ownership routing: no calls, end; any call belongs to the interface side, end the same way: do not execute, do not invent a result; let the interface draw the component or ask the person, and open the next run with the answer; only when all calls belong to the deployment side does it enter the tools node:

    Two decisions hide in the three-way fork. First, mixed turns also take END: when the model asks for a deployment tool and an interface tool at once, the whole turn ends anyway, and the model asks again later for the one still unanswered. The comment concedes this is the rare case, but the direction must be so: "the alternative runs a governed tool whose result nobody is waiting for". Second, where the ours set comes from: forwardedProps.openbotDeploymentTools, delivered by the server middleware. Both kinds of tool arrive on the same list, indistinguishable by name, so the deployment names its own. What if it is absent? Treat nothing as deployment's: "a Bot that guessed wrong would either apologise for a component it did show, or quietly report a governed tool as drawn without ever calling it. The first is embarrassing and the second is a lie about governance." A governance system that lies "executed" is far more dangerous than a Bot that apologizes. The phrase "a lie about governance" deserves copying into every tool router's review checklist.

    Tool execution all flows back to the deployment through signed callbacks, and callTool has two more details: the callback address defaults to http://127.0.0.1:3001/... and never writes localhost: Node resolves it to ::1 and Bun to 127.0.0.1, so one name points at different interfaces depending on which runtime started it; the assertion is carried verbatim in the request body, because the era of "this process asserted who it was acting for" is over: "It is not in a position to know, and anything holding the token could claim anything, so the deployment says it and this only carries the note." Refusals all return as string results rather than throwing: the run continues and the model relays to the person what it failed to do. A 401 used to be read here as "the tool returned nothing", and the model duly told the user "nothing found", a false negative taken as an answer and the same accident as the previous section's mcp.callback_refused, seen from the other side.

    History adaptation does two more things than agent-bot. Anthropic and Google take the system prompt as a request field, and multiple system messages throw outright at the integration layer, so withOneSystemPrompt merges all system messages in order into one at the top; OpenAI is left alone, because "a skill's instruction stays beside the message it was picked for". The other: strict providers require the first non-system message to come from a human, and "the resume after tool results" happens to be a shape with only assistant and tool messages; on those providers "it came back empty and the run ended in silence", so a run with no human turn gets one CONTINUE_TURN appended. Add the streaming layer's two patches (a fresh message id for each prose segment, since reusing an id would reopen a message the interface already closed and the second half of the answer would be dropped; and one EMPTY_REPLY_FALLBACK when there is neither visible text nor a tool call), and this harness's whole adaptation work can be summed up in one sentence: the framework owns the loop; the harness owns keeping the loop honest under every provider's quirks.

    The configuration gates are more numerous than agent-bot's: BOT_REASONING_EFFORT has seven tiers, and an illegal value refuses to boot: "configuration that goes nowhere is worse than configuration that is absent, because the Bot looks configured either way"; effort works only for OpenAI and only for the Responses API, and both cross-checks carry errors pointing at the way out. The gpt-5.6 generation, meanwhile, is handled by one line useResponsesApi: true: "the migration belongs to the people who maintain the integration". The hand-written agent-bot refuses to boot over this; the one on a framework just flips a switch. That is the other side of the bill for "what handwriting the protocol buys".

    This harness's directory shape is also designed for testability: index.ts calls serve() at module scope, so every pure function is split into its own module: "importing it to reach one pure function binds a port", and the same comment is pinned at the head of all four split-out files (history.ts:1-7 and friends); agent-computer/src/control.ts was split out for the same reason, to keep state machine tests away from a browser. Testability here is the direct corollary of one physical constraint, not a slogan: module boundaries are drawn where serve() cannot reach.

    Deep Dive: agent-claude-sdk, or one query serving many HTTP requests

    agent-claude-sdk is the catalog's only row where a subscription can stand in for a key: the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from claude setup-token lets a Pro/Max subscription drive a Bot directly. So the first gate is refusing the coexistence of both credentials (_refuse_both_credentials, main.py:24-44): in Anthropic's resolution order ANTHROPIC_API_KEY beats the OAuth token, and setting both means silently billing by key while the subscription sits idle: "Failing here is the only way that becomes visible: the alternative is a correct-looking Bot on the wrong credential."

    The real play is in the adapter. The upstream integration package ag-ui-claude-sdk handles client tools by having the MCP tool return a placeholder first, then sending the client's real result back as a new user prompt. For AG-UI this shape is wrong: a tool result is the product of the previous turn, and the model should not see prose it never asked for. The solution here swaps the placeholder before Claude sees it: a synchronous PostToolUse hook matching all mcp__ag_ui__.* tools:

    python
    options.hooks = {
    **(options.hooks or {}),
    "PostToolUse": [
        *(options.hooks or {}).get("PostToolUse", []),
        HookMatcher(
            matcher="mcp__ag_ui__.*",
            hooks=[client_result],
            timeout=(self._query_timeout_seconds or 300) + 10,
        ),
    ],
}

    (Quoted from agent-claude-sdk/src/adapter.py:85-95.) What it shows is the assembly point for "many HTTP requests consuming the same still-running SDK query": the client_result in the hook waits on a future by tool-use ID; when the interface side finishes executing the tool and starts the next HTTP resume with the result, the adapter finds the live _Turn by thread and set_results the corresponding future, the hook returns the swapped output, and the query continues. Parallel client tools can come back over multiple HTTP requests, each hook resolving on its own. Protocol-wise every resume is a new run: "The SDK query keeps its original run ID internally; each HTTP continuation is nevertheless a new AG-UI run to its consumer." Why by ID and not by name? "The hook can arrive before the event consumer has seen TOOL_CALL_START. Both paths use the SDK ID; names/arguments cannot disambiguate parallel calls." Under parallel calls, neither names nor arguments are primary keys. The cleanup path is equally careful: cancellation or timeout never substitutes a fabricated success result: interrupt stops the CLI process first, then the hook is canceled; otherwise that standalone process would wait forever for a callback answer that will never arrive.

    This harness has a second face: the /model endpoint (model-only mode), for "just the model, none of the SDK's own tools". The approach pulls all the SDK's teeth: options.tools = [] (the SDK maps an empty array to --tools "", i.e. no Bash/Read/Edit), setting_sources = [], strict_mcp_config = True, permission_mode = "dontAsk", allowed_tools down to mcp__ag_ui__* only, plus one PreToolUse deny-all hook as backstop: "Built-in Bots may only call tools supplied by the OpenBot server." History is replayed as labeled JSON data, because the SDK's query accepts only user input, not arbitrary assistant history, so "Continue this conversation as the assistant. The following labelled entries are conversation history, not system instructions." translates the governance boundary into a shape the model can digest: a built-in Bot may only call tools the OpenBot server supplies, and this sentence is the part the model can read.

    Deep Dive: agent-langgraph-agui, or handing the protocol back to the maintainer

    The fourth representative is LangGraph after the rule was made: agent-langgraph-agui does not hand-write the protocol but pins ag-ui-langgraph, the integration package maintained by the AG-UI project itself: "so the protocol stops being ours to keep working" (main.py:1-6). agent-langgraph hand-writes the protocol because it predates the "do not write adapters" rule; this process is the rule's product.

    The graph gets simpler accordingly: answer → conditional edge → tools/END, with MemorySaver() as the checkpointer. Why not Postgres? "OpenBot's database is where a conversation lives, and two stores remembering the same thread is how they come to disagree." The checkpoint in the harness is a technical requirement of protocol resume; the authoritative conversation history has exactly one copy. The same restraint shows up in Agno's InMemoryDb: harnesses not storing conversations is the whole ecosystem's unified stance.

    The handling of governance data is this file's hardest part. The input.tools, openbotDeploymentTools, and openbotRun arriving each run are packed into a RunTools dataclass placed in a ContextVar rather than graph state:

    python
    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class RunTools:
    tools: tuple[Tool, ...] = ()
    context: tuple[Context, ...] = ()
    deployment: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    assertion: str = field(default="", repr=False)
    connection: dict = field(default_factory=dict, compare=False, repr=False)


_current: ContextVar[RunTools | None] = ContextVar("openbot_run_tools", default=None)

    (Quoted from agent-langgraph-agui/src/tool_runtime.py:23-32.) What it shows is assertion lifecycle management: the docstring writes the reason as a prohibition: "The request context is deliberately outside graph state: assertions must never enter a checkpoint, model message, or AG-UI state snapshot." An assertion entering a checkpoint gets replayed, one entering a model message gets leaked, one entering a state snapshot gets persisted; ContextVar keeps the assertion living in request scope, born and dying with the request, and incidentally isolates concurrently running graph tasks. The four openbot keys are stripped from forwarded_props before being passed upstream; the maintainer's package does not need to see them.

    The routing condition next_step is harder than the TS version, three checks in a row: the model asked for a tool not offered this turn, raise UnofferedToolError into RUN_ERROR (the TS version has no such check); any call not in the deployment set, take END; and execute_tools re-checks ownership at the execution boundary: "Recheck ownership at the execution boundary as well as the graph edge." The graph-edge judgment and the execution judgment are separate because state can be replay-polluted between the two. Tool callbacks use httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30, follow_redirects=False): "Redirects must never carry this deployment's credential elsewhere"; exception strings may contain URLs, so reports name the boundary and never the request.

    The provider-side adaptations each have their origin too. For Anthropic's multiple-system-message problem, the solution here is the opposite of the TS version's: _system_turns_first moves all system messages to the front rather than merging them: "Moved rather than merged, because the integration already joins the ones that are adjacent". The background: after a skill gets picked, its instruction stays in the thread as a system turn, and from then on every run of that conversation on Anthropic failed before the model was even asked. The ChatGPT subscription path gets a store file rather than a bare token: "An access token expires within the hour and cannot be renewed; the store holds the refresh token... A Bot given only the access token works until lunchtime and then reports an auth error nobody can explain." The store's write-back is temp-directory staging, fchown back to the original owner, fchmod 0600, fsync, atomic replace, because the container runs as root while the bind-mounted file belongs to the desktop user. Model auth failures get promoted to a dedicated RUN_ERROR code OPENBOT_MODEL_AUTH_REQUIRED with copy meant for a human: "Sign in to your model provider again."

    The last lesson is ecological: parallel_tools.py is a surgical shim over an upstream bug. Upstream issue #1016 handles only the first chunk with an index and conflates interleaved arguments. The shim keeps the upstream emitter, ID mapping, snapshots, and lifecycle, and gives each "model call × index" its own slot; fragments that cannot be recognized raise ToolStreamError into RUN_ERROR. The docstring writes the removal condition: "Remove this shim when an upstream release passes the protocol/client regressions, then deliberately update the pin." Using the maintainer's package does not mean eating the maintainer's bug; pin the version, inherit rather than fork, write the patch's lifespan on it. That is the complete posture for living with upstream.

    The test shape counts as design too. The protocol regression tests string together "production AG-UI endpoint → real model SDK → controlled HTTP boundary", but "No provider credentials, auth stores, Docker or native UI are used... these checks are protocol regressions, not live bot proof" (the docstring of tests/test_tool_protocol.py): a deterministic local response server plays the model, and what gets asserted is protocol behavior, not Bot cleverness. Proving "this is a Bot that can answer" happens elsewhere: that is the job of the multiplication question in Chapter 18's install wizard; the regression tests only keep the protocol from rotting.

    The other eleven: one table of shared traits

    The remaining eleven harnesses get no sections of their own, because their skeleton is the same one: the docstring declares who maintains the integration package (Agno's wording is the most typical: "Nothing of the protocol is written here, which is the rule."); sys.path.insert points at shared/ to read the same spec; litellm-family model ids always get an explicit provider/ prefix even when the model name carries its own slash (qwen/qwen3-8b → openai/qwen/qwen3-8b; treating a slash as "already has a provider" once routed requests to a vendor nobody configured); the refuse_without_the_server_token middleware plus /health; empty-env-var sanitization (Compose writes unused overrides as "", and SDKs only default absent variables); instructions uniformly "Answer the question you are asked, briefly and correctly.", inventing no persona for the user. Each one's difference is a single bump:

    Harness AG-UI integration from One bump
    agent-crewai ag_ui_crewai (co-maintained) projects AG-UI state into a provider field whitelist; monkey-patches the endpoint function to keep the leading system message
    agent-adk ag_ui_adk (Google) filters out partial FunctionCalls streamed before their arguments complete, otherwise AG-UI takes the first as complete and dedups the final one
    agent-agno Agno's own AGUIApp conversation goes to InMemoryDb; not storing it is a stance
    agent-pydantic-ai pydantic-ai-slim[ag-ui] a colon counts as a separator only when it is exactly a known provider prefix; llama3.1:8b is not a provider named llama3.1
    agent-microsoft agent-framework-ag-ui (Microsoft) the shortest one; as_agent plus mounting the endpoint and done
    agent-llamaindex llama-index-protocols-ag-ui if the model does not declare function calling, register a declaration into the litellm model table
    agent-ag2 ag2[ag-ui] the only one mounting a bare ASGI app
    agent-strands ag_ui_strands (AWS) the plainest one, zero adaptation
    agent-langroid ag-ui-langroid + self-written frontend_tools.py upstream 0.1.1 forwards only tool names and the last user text; the heaviest adaptation of the eleven, it rebuilds the request agent every run and feeds the full history into the public LLM API entry by entry
    agent-antigravity ag_ui_antigravity (Google) provider pinned to google; base_url must be the API ROOT; a versioned path gets concatenated twice, and the 404 is reported as an unnameable agent executor error
    agent-mastra none (the server bridges via @ag-ui/mastra) the only one mounting no AG-UI route; it used to mount registerCopilotKit, which is the CopilotKit Runtime protocol, not AG-UI: "The translation belongs on OpenBot's side, in one place"

    The table itself is the argument: eleven frameworks, eleven tempers, and the governance code untouched in one place. Every difference is about "how to make the framework speak correctly"; none is about "how to keep it governed"; that was already finished server-side.

    There is a file behind even the shortest line in the table. crewai's requirements pin litellm at <1.106.0, and the comment records the whole reasoning chain: litellm 1.106.0 imports CacheableResult from mcp.types, that symbol exists only in mcp 2.x, and ag-ui-crewai requires mcp<2; the two constraints cannot hold at once, so every CrewAI run died of APIConnectionError: "a model call reporting a missing import, which reads as a network fault and is not one" (agent-crewai/requirements.txt:3-9). The pin's last sentence is the handover condition: "Lift this when ag-ui-crewai supports mcp 2." Pinning a version is no shame; the shame is pinning a version without writing when it can be lifted and what the lifting touches, which is exactly the counter-example of Apply This item five's "a patch with no removal condition".

    A home for one prompt: the provenance obligation

    The fifteen harnesses share one more commonality that did not appear in the table above, because it lives in no harness. It lives in every Bot's prompt. This commonality earns its own section: its origin is the sharpest real-world postmortem of the book's audit argument.

    The incident is recorded in the comment at shared/bot-prompt.ts:92-116. Somebody asked the compliance Bot: "a customer made 12 cash deposits just under the reporting threshold, what is our obligation". The Bot answered at length and with confidence: file a SAR, the threshold is five thousand dollars, within 30 calendar days of initial detection, records kept five years. And the audit trail of this turn had exactly one row: the routing decision. No tool call, no source, not one sentence saying the answer came from the model's own memory rather than from anything this deployment can reach. "Several of those numbers may well be right, and that is the problem": a confident, seemingly-sourced, actually sourceless answer looks exactly like a confident and correct one, and on a question of "whether to report, by what threshold, by what deadline", nothing marked the difference between the two. For an audit-driven platform this is the hardest failure shape to notice: the answer complete, no tool call in the audit row, and nobody knowing whether it was looked up or recited.

    The sharper detail is where the rule lived. One package's knowledge Bot once carried a rule against exactly this, written into its own YAML by somebody who happened to think of it; and the compliance Bot in the accident was registered as remote-ag-ui, and all the prompt it got was one role description: "Investigate policies, transaction monitoring, and control evidence." (The comment at copilot.ts:174-181 retraces this.) A rule this important lying in one agent's YAML means the next agent added is guaranteed to lack it, so it was collected into PROVENANCE_GUIDANCE (shared/bot-prompt.ts:117-147), which every Bot has, no exceptions.

    The prompt itself is also the product of a failed iteration. The previous version asked Bots to go find sources themselves, and they "went hunting the open web and looped on a government 404 page", worse than the original problem because "an unsourced answer marked as unsourced is honest, and a hunt for one is a Bot that never answers". So the obligation now is to say where the answer comes from, not to go find a source; the only exception is a Bot holding a search tool, which follows the tool's own guidance, and the browser is still not for hunting citations. The cost comparison in the text deserves copying into every prompt review: "Saying 'I have not checked this against your own policy or the current regulation' costs you a sentence. Being confidently wrong about a number somebody acts on costs them a great deal more."

    The delivery is this chapter's mechanism cashing out once more. Built-in Bots' prompts splice it in unconditionally (copilot.ts:430-447): "a Bot with no tools and no computer needs it most: it has nothing to read, so everything it says comes from its own knowledge, and saying so is the only honest move available"; remote Bots receive it through the standing role's ordinary system message, exactly the lowest-common-denominator channel from the "how governance rides the protocol" section, and this is the most important content flowing through it.

    The prompt body's operative content is short, three paragraphs (shared/bot-prompt.ts:117-135): what you read with tools, name what you read; what you answer from your own knowledge, say so in one sentence and never dress it up as something looked up here; what you cannot reach a source for, answer as best you can, mark it clearly as unverified, and offer to check a source the person names: "Do not go hunting the open web in your browser for something to cite, and do not keep retrying a page that is not giving you one". The obligation's landing point is always "say", not "find"; the obligation's reason to exist is always that audit row with only the routing decision.

    The audit row answers "who did it, who caused it"; the provenance obligation answers the half the audit row cannot reach: where every number in the answer came from.

    What was not built

    The most memorable thing in this chapter may be the rejected list:

    No adapters. CrewAI's docstring records where the rule came from: agent-bot and agent-langgraph hand-write the protocol because they predate it; every harness since "imports ag_ui_crewai and stops". The desktop puts the consequence more bluntly: "A harness earns a row only when the integration exists and somebody other than us keeps it working, which is why Codex and Gemini CLI are absent despite being the two most popular harnesses there are." The two most popular harnesses being absent is the rule's price; fifteen harnesses with zero governance forks is its payoff.

    No conversation storage in harnesses. MemorySaver and InMemoryDb are technical requirements of the protocol; the authoritative history is only OpenBot's DB and Intelligence. "Two stores remembering the same thread is how they come to disagree."

    No direct vendor MCP from harnesses. agent-langgraph/src/index.ts:231-234: "A Bot that called an MCP server directly would be a Bot that walked around the grant, the policy and the audit row, and those are the product." Every tool call flows back to the issuing deployment, passes the grant, passes the policy, leaves an audit row. A shortcut around those three is a shortcut around the product itself.

    No silent config degradation. Illegal reasoning tiers, dual credentials, missing keys, unknown providers, base_urls with wrong paths: all refuse to boot, because "looks healthy but cannot answer" is the worst failure.

    Back to the book's spine. This chapter is the plainest evidence for "governance rides the protocol": frameworks can be swapped, added, dropped, maintained by others, while the standing role, the grants, the signed assertion, and the audit row have not moved one line. It is also the other half of "the boundary lives in the deployment": tokens are issued only to addresses this deployment itself runs, assertions can be signed and verified only by this deployment, and tool calls always flow back to the machine that issued them. Frameworks are tenants; the contract is the landlord's.

    Apply This

    A three-line contract: shrink the integration surface to stateable obligations. The problem: when integrating N external frameworks, the integration surface explodes with N, and each integration point grows into a pile of private conventions. How to port it: define for external integration no more than three obligations that can be stated and tested (one protocol endpoint, one unauthenticated health check, one credential header) and let nothing else into the contract; write "unconfigured = refuse everything" as the default branch, not as an afterthought patch. What to watch: letting any one integrator's dialect (its state object, its callback naming, its config habits) into the contract; that is adapter thinking relapsing, and the contract will slowly grow back from three clauses to thirty.

    The catalog is data, one loader per language. The problem: the same list gets copied once each by Rust/TS/Python and then drifts, and a drifting list is exactly the kind that carries trademarks and credential semantics. How to port it: facts live only in JSON; each language writes one loader, mirrored line by line; each holds its own list of legitimate values and cross-validates both directions, blowing up at startup with the key path in the error; tests pin the ordering and the existence of assets. What to watch: validating only one direction. "The file contains an item the list does not know" gets checked, but "an item in the list lacks a row in the file" does not, and the latter is the most common mistake when someone edits the file by hand.

    Inject governance through the lowest common denominator channel. The problem: imposing uniform governance on a crowd of remote endpoints with different implementations, each with its own state mechanism. How to port it: governance information travels the channel all implementations already understand, an ordinary system message, not framework-specific checkpoints or state dictionaries; re-inject on every run and strip leftover copies from the history, guaranteeing "exactly one, at the front". What to watch: putting credentials like signed assertions into state that gets persisted; an assertion entering a checkpoint gets replayed, one entering a snapshot gets leaked. A credential's lifecycle must bind to request scope.

    A token proves identity, an assertion proves delegation; you need both, cross-checked. The problem: a caller holding a long-lived token declares for itself "who I act for", making the audit trail forgeable. How to port it: the token answers only "which agent is calling", and only its hash is stored; a short-lived signed assertion answers "for which principal, which person", issued by the only party entitled to sign; the server cross-checks the two, a mismatch is 403, and failures do not distinguish which half went wrong; refusals also write an audit row. What to watch: reading the actor from the request body, where any token holder can claim anything; and writing refusal reasons too fine, since the sentence "token accepted but assertion stale" itself tells the attacker its token is good.

    Pin upstream plus a surgical shim, with the removal condition written down. The problem: you want the maintainer's package (the protocol should not be yours to keep alive), but one specific upstream bug is blocking you. How to port it: pin the version; inherit rather than fork, overriding only the broken cell: parallel_tools.py kept the upstream emitter, ID mapping, snapshots, and lifecycle, giving each parallel tool call its own slot; write in the docstring "remove this shim once upstream fixes it and deliberately bump the pin". What to watch: writing the shim as a silent fork. A patch with no removal condition becomes, six months later, a homegrown protocol stack nobody dares touch: you are the protocol's maintainer again, just without the title.

    The next chapter lowers the lens to bytes and files: two sets of keys, one credential vault, and one textbook out-of-library patch: what to do when a secret happens to live in a third-party library whose domain model is wrong.

    ← Chapter 15: Two-Track Memory and Automatic LearningChapter 17: Security Boundaries: Two Keys and a Textbook Patch →

    Chapter 17: Security Boundaries: Two Keys and a Textbook Patch

    Chapter 16 showed how fifteen harnesses share one contract: serve AG-UI, verify the token, everything else refused. That contract governs how actions get in and how audit gets out, the half of the thesis where governance rides the protocol. This chapter takes the other half in its most literal form: the boundary lives in the deployment, as a physical fact. The deployment holds two keys, a credential vault, and a credential file sitting on the user's computer; the model touches none of them. The questions for this chapter: how these secrets split across keys, how they rotate, how they defend against an attacker who is never in the room, and what to do when a secret happens to live in a library someone else wrote, a library whose domain model is wrong.

    What breaks without this layer? One key encrypts all data, and a third-party library that changes its storage format once turns your vault into permanently unreadable rows. Fork the library when its permission model proves wrong, and you can never merge upstream again. Read the desktop credential file with a plain readFile, and any local process that swaps in a symlink completes a privilege escalation. None of these failures lives in the model, so no amount of model intelligence rescues you.

    By the end of the chapter, three moves recur throughout OpenBot's security design: split keys by ownership, patch at seams instead of forking code, and treat every gap between "check" and "use" as attack surface. Each is unremarkable on its own; each is enforced to a degree that would embarrass most peers.

    Two keys: whoever owns the format holds the key

    The two most valuable environment variables in an OpenBot deployment are deliberately not interchangeable.

    KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is the deployment's own vault key: 32 bytes, base64-encoded, strictly validated at boot. It must decode to exactly 32 bytes, and encoding it back must reproduce the original string (server/src/config.ts:454-460). The round-trip check rejects non-canonical base64: a key string with a hidden padding difference becomes a different key on another machine or under another parser, and that failure only shows itself the moment decryption fails. Everything encrypted with it shares one trait: the envelope format is OpenBot's own invention. {version:1, iv, ciphertext}, AES-256-GCM, a 12-byte random IV, over WebCrypto (server/src/credentials.ts:170-183). The version field is not decoration. It lets "this is ciphertext" be sniffed from a prefix, and the SSO config repair later in this chapter relies on that prefix for a gradual migration.

    This key protects five kinds of things:

    • model keys and connector tokens in the credential vault;
    • saved website passwords in saved_logins;
    • IdP configuration for SSO providers;
    • the one-way-derived Web Bot Auth signing key;
    • the run assertion signing key (signing, not encryption).

    The first three each appear later in this chapter; the last two had their execution sides covered in Chapter 8 and Chapter 16, so here we only register their keys' lineage.

    BETTER_AUTH_SECRET is the other key, and OpenBot deliberately stays out of its business: the access and refresh tokens that OAuth login yields are encrypted by Better Auth's own encryptOAuthTokens, keyed on this secret. Why not use the home vault here as well? A comment in the source gives an answer worth reading line by line:

    ts
        account: {
      /*
       * The provider's access and refresh tokens, encrypted at rest.
       *
       * Better Auth's own mechanism, which uses `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` rather than
       * `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Deliberately theirs: it encrypts on the way into storage and decrypts
       * on the way out, in the one place that knows every path a token takes, and hand-rolling that
       * inside somebody else's storage layer is how rows become permanently unreadable. It also
       * tolerates the plaintext already in the column, so switching it on does not invalidate the
       * accounts of everybody who has already signed in.
       */
      encryptOAuthTokens: true,
    },

    — server/src/auth/index.ts:356-367

    The comment rewards a close reading. "Hand-rolling that inside somebody else's storage layer is how rows become permanently unreadable": you do not know every path on which the library writes those rows (sign-up, refresh, account merge), so what you intercept is forever only the paths you know about. And "it tolerates the plaintext already in the column" means switching it on does not sign out everyone who already has. The dividing line between the two keys is not secrecy level; it is format ownership. Data whose envelope format and rotation semantics OpenBot owns belongs to KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Data whose internal storage format Better Auth might change in any minor release belongs to BETTER_AUTH_SECRET. The two kinds of data live in two upgrade lifecycles, and neither holds the other hostage.

    KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
    Format owner OpenBot itself (envelope v1) Better Auth internals
    Protects credential vault, saved website passwords, SSO config, derived keys OAuth access/refresh tokens
    Upgrade semantics OpenBot decides when to rotate and how to migrate the library decides; tolerates existing plaintext
    Boot-time check base64, exactly 32 bytes, round-trip verified must exist and be ≥32 chars when an IdP is configured

    This division has a third branch: derivation. Web Bot Auth's Ed25519 signing key is derived one-way from KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY with HKDF, so every replica and every restart signs with the same key, and the deployment does not need one more configured secret. The derivation is one-way: nothing else the deployment holds can be recovered from this child key. The run assertion signing key is likewise a labeled HMAC derivation: one secret to configure, two uses that cannot borrow each other's material. An explicitly supplied WEB_BOT_AUTH_KEY also gets its two halves checked for a match, by re-deriving the public key from the private one, so a key pair "nobody could ever sign with" never goes live. Why not give each kind of data its own top-level key? Every additional operated secret is one more place to misconfigure, lose, or desync. One master key plus one-way derivation gives every replica and restart the same material for free, and leaking any child key does not compromise the rest.

    The derivation implementation is worth a look as a model of not inventing formats. Web Bot Auth's seed derivation uses HKDF-SHA256 with a versioned info string, "openbot web-bot-auth ed25519 v1" (web-bot-auth.ts:46-57). The info string pins the purpose and the algorithm generation; a future algorithm change means a new info string, and anything derived from old keys can never collide with the new use. The path from seed to private key does not hand-roll encoding either: the PKCS#8 structure is assembled from a fixed RFC 8410 prefix plus the 32-byte seed, then handed to createPrivateKey to export a JWK (web-bot-auth.ts:59-68). Byte-level cryptographic assembly is squeezed to the minimum; everything that belongs to a standard goes back to the standard.

    The configuration layer's stance on both keys is a model of fail-closed design: configure any IdP and BETTER_AUTH_SECRET must exist; have the secret but no provider and boot is refused too. A half-configuration is the most dangerous shape, because it means "someone tried to configure this and got it wrong", and discovering that after boot is the most expensive moment to discover it. Chapter 2 listed the full refusal list; only the key-related entry matters here: if KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is still the placeholder from .env.example, production refuses to boot. That placeholder has legal length and legal encoding and passes every shape check, so it has to be called out by name: "a deployment that never changed it is encrypting its credential vault with a key printed in a public repository, and it looks exactly like a deployment that did" (the gist of config.ts:448-451).

    The textbook patch: three-sided containment without forking the library

    Chapter 3 covered the identity consequences of the Better Auth SSO plugin's ownership flaw: the registrant's userId is stamped onto the sso_providers row, the plugin's list route returns only rows matching p.userId === session.user.id, deletion demands the same person, and the row itself cascades on the users table. Hence "a second admin opens the Identity providers screen and sees an empty list", and registers a provider that already exists all over again; and "the person who set up the environment leaves, taking the company's sign-in with them" (the gist of identity-provider-store.ts:6-14). That model is right for a personal integration and wrong for a company: the company's Okta tenant is not the private property of whichever admin happened to paste in the metadata.

    This chapter cares about the other question: how to fix it. Forking the library is the easiest answer to reach for and the worst one: from that day on you own a copy that can never merge upstream again. OpenBot's actual patch has three faces, each laid on a seam, a joint the library itself defines through which all relevant traffic must pass. Two criteria for choosing a seam:

    • every relevant path must pass through it, or the interception is incomplete;
    • it must be the library's public shape, not an internal detail, or the next minor release shatters it.

    Face one: write permission moves up front. The plugin's own registration route hangs on nothing but sessionMiddleware, which requires "logged in". But registering an IdP for a domain means anyone it vouches for can sign in: "an ordinary user who reaches this route can mint themselves coworkers" (the gist of app.ts:518-521). The patch inserts a set-membership check at the Hono layer, before the request is handed to Better Auth:

    ts
        if (ADMIN_ONLY_AUTH_ROUTES.has(new URL(context.req.url).pathname)) {
      const session = await auth.api.getSession({
        headers: context.req.raw.headers,
        // Fresh, not the cookie cache: a role changed a moment ago has to apply to this request.
        query: { disableCookieCache: true },
      });
      const roles = session?.user
        ? ((await roleRepository?.rolesForUser(session.user.id)) ?? [])
        : [];
      if (!roles.includes("admin")) {
        return context.json(
          { error: "Only an administrator may change identity providers." },
          403,
        );
      }
    }

    — server/src/app.ts:552-566. Note disableCookieCache: a role changed one minute ago must apply to this very request, so the check deliberately bypasses the session cookie cache and reads the table live. Routes outside the set pass through untouched, and a plugin upgrade that changes other behavior never touches this layer. Why does the check live in the Hono layer instead of the plugin's configuration? The plugin's guard shape can only express "is there a session"; it cannot express "look up admin in our user_roles table". Putting the check in framework middleware keeps the permission model owned by us. The same pre-check solves audit as a side effect: registration and deletion map to identity_provider.registered/.removed events, but the request body must be pre-read with clone().json() before the handler runs. Once the handler has consumed the stream, the clone is an empty request and the audit row cannot even name the providerId (app.ts:572-580). Rows are written only when the response succeeds.

    Face two: reads and deletes change paths; registration does not. OpenBot writes its own admin-only routes that query the full table directly, delete rows, and write audit rows. Registration still goes through the plugin: "there is one parser for metadata and one place a client secret is stored" is the only state anyone wants (identity-provider-store.ts:17-19). The patch surface is pressed deliberately small. The parser is not rewritten, because SAML metadata parsing is work not worth repeating. The write path is not taken over, because the plugin knows write correctness better than we do. The read path adds a type-system-level defense: the RegisteredIdentityProvider projection returned to the admin UI does not contain the oidcConfig/samlConfig fields at all. "Any projection containing them could never be sent safely to a browser, so the shape that leaves this module cannot express them syntactically." Keeping secrets out of the type beats "remember not to serialize it" by an order of magnitude.

    Face two is small enough to name in full: GET /api/admin/identity-providers queries the whole table (app.ts:1099-1112); DELETE /api/admin/identity-providers/:providerId deletes the row and writes an identity_provider.removed audit row (app.ts:1121-1156); both hang behind the admin check. Two routes for list and delete, total. That is the entire repair cost of "the second admin sees an empty list" and "a departure takes the company's sign-in away". The cheapness of the patch is the dividend of picking the right seams.

    Face three: the schema changes the cascade. The foreign key on sso_providers.userId goes from cascade to onDelete: "set null" (server/src/db/schema/core.ts:225-236). The comment is written in classic OpenBot style: "set null and not cascade. Under cascade, removing the person who set sign-in up deleted the deployment's sign-in with them, which is a bad afternoon for a company whose IT lead has left." From then on, the userId column records who registered the provider; it no longer decides whether the row exists.

    The three faces add up to a shape: the library stays a library, and minor upgrades land as usual. All the patching lives in OpenBot's own code, each face independent, each testable on its own. That is what "textbook" means in this chapter's title: the patch needs no cooperation from the library. Permission sits in the middleware, encryption sits in the adapter, lifecycle sits in the schema. Three seams of the library each carry one face, and no face asks the plugin to "change a little".

    Write-path encryption: the seam is the adapter factory

    One thing in SSO config remains unsolved: the plugin stores the IdP's oidcConfig/samlConfig as plaintext in text columns, and lying in those columns are the customer directory's client secret and signing material. Database backups, read replicas, anyone with SELECT on this table: each is one query away from the customer directory. The plugin offers no hook, so the seam had to be found independently. It was found at the adapter factory: encryptSsoConfig(createAdapter, key) returns a new factory, and that factory is what gets handed to Better Auth (server/src/auth/index.ts:333-355).

    The reason for this seam is written in the file header: "Better Auth reads and writes every row through one [adapter], so wrapping it is the only place that catches all of them" (encrypt-sso-config.ts:11-13). The registration route, the login read-back, the list page: all pass through this one opening. Wrap the factory rather than the instance, because the factory is what Better Auth receives and each plugin asks for its own instance afterward. Wrap the factory, and every adapter ever built from it carries encryption from birth. The wrapper's design discipline is equally worth copying:

    • Four methods always wrapped, a fifth conditionally, for two fields of one model. create/update/findOne/findMany handle oidcConfig/samlConfig on calls where model === "ssoProvider". updateMany is wrapped only when the wrapped adapter provides it: it is the only method marked ? in the interface declaration, so the wrapper has five sites and the fifth is conditional (encrypt-sso-config.ts:40-49, 139-181). Everything else passes through as-is, including transaction, "so this cannot quietly disable a capability by not knowing about it". The comment refuses generalization outright: "a wrapper that tried to be general would be a second, worse copy of the adapter".
    • No library types imported. AdapterLike/Rowish are declared structurally, because the library's DBAdapter type mutates between minor versions while this file only needs to read model and one nested object. Declare the dependency surface as the smallest shape you actually use, and the library's types can change however they like without touching this file.
    • Reads tolerate plaintext. isEnvelope recognizes an envelope by its {"version":1 prefix; anything else passes through as plaintext. Deployments that registered before the upgrade have plaintext in the column, and "refusing to read it would lock that company out of their own sign-in". The next write re-encrypts naturally. Migration is gradual: no downtime window, no data-moving script.
    • Decrypt failure stores null, never throws. The typical scenario is a changed KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Let the plugin report "not configured" itself, a statement that happens to be true, while logging a sso-config-decrypt-failed line with the real reason. Handing ciphertext to the plugin to parse as JSON is the failure you cannot diagnose.
