    • create returns plaintext. The registration route echoes back what was stored: "the encryption is about the column rather than about the request".

    The credential vault: atomic rotation and honest errors

    credentials.ts is KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY's largest consumer: model API keys and connector tokens live as envelopes in credentials.encrypted_value. Its design revolves around one invariant: at most one live credential per key, enforced at the database layer by a partial unique index (server/drizzle/0015_credentials_one_live_key.sql: (kind, provider, key_id) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL). All the rotation logic in the application layer exists to deserve that constraint under multi-replica concurrency.

    CredentialStore's verb surface is deliberately small: create, updateSecret, rotate, revoke, plus isLive and findLiveByKey on the query side (credentials.ts:281-433). Six verbs state the whole behavior of a vault. The smaller the verb surface, the easier the invariant holds: every write path passes through one of these six doors, and every door knows the partial unique index.

    Rotation takes the textbook shape: inside a single transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the old row, identity is verified, then revoke, then insert:

    ts
            const [previous] = await transaction
          .select({
            revokedAt: credentials.revokedAt,
            kind: credentials.kind,
            provider: credentials.provider,
            keyId: credentials.keyId,
          })
          .from(credentials)
          .where(eq(credentials.id, input.previousCredentialId))
          .for("update");

    — server/src/credentials.ts:327-336. Three details deserve a pause. First, the old row is locked for the scenario where two replicas rotate the same key at the same time: without the lock, both sides read "live", both act, and the constraint is down to luck. Second, kind/provider/keyId are read out along with the state and verified: "a rotation aimed at the wrong id is refused rather than silently retiring a secret the caller never named". Third, the order is revoke then insert: "this one never holds two live rows for one key even in the middle of it". That is exactly the invariant the partial unique index depends on. The constraint and the code keep each other's promise instead of each making its own wish.

    Why one transaction instead of two calls? The comment writes the answer out as reasoning (credentials.ts:91-98): retiring the old secret and storing the new one are the same decision, so they must be the same write, because "an UPDATE can commit and still throw on the way back, and no compensating revoke survives the process being killed between them". This is the same respect for "dying halfway" as Chapter 6's audit rows, "write the row first, then act": any operation that cannot tolerate a half-done state goes inside one transaction boundary.

    Updates that do not touch the whole row take another path: updateSecret is a single UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND revoked_at IS NULL (credentials.ts:299-315). "One statement, so nothing can revoke the row between a check and the write." The cost: "row does not exist" and "row already revoked" get the same answer, so the error message names both; the caller's response to either is identical anyway: refuse the call. revoke likewise only timestamps live rows. A second revoke that overwrote the first one's timestamp and reported success would be indefensible in an audit trail.

    Two more defensive decisions, both paid for by incidents. First, encryption happens outside the transaction (credentials.ts:597-600): the envelope is built in memory first, the transaction only makes two writes, and "no database connection is held while it runs". WebCrypto is asynchronous; putting async cryptography inside a transaction mortgages the connection pool to coroutine scheduling. Second, the UI has only Add and Revoke buttons, no Rotate. So Adding to an existing key automatically becomes a rotation (credentials.ts:560-574), because "refusing that would leave no way to replace a key at all". The product shape dictated the storage semantics, not the reverse. The credential family therefore has four audit events: credential.created/.rotated/.rotation_refused/.revoked. Refused rotations get their own row: "the refusals are the interesting ones".

    The vault has a second layer of honesty: CredentialRefusedError carries an HTTP status (404 or 409). Clicking Revoke on an already-revoked credential gets "it is gone", not a bare 500. Otherwise the second click reads as "the deployment broke" rather than "the credential was long gone" (credentials.ts:225-239). Errors must be classified, and classified finely enough that the UI does not lie.

    Errors must be classes, not messages

    The sharpest comment in the vault argues one small thing: why CredentialUnusableError must be its own error class, not "a plain Error whose message contains revoked". When drizzle reports a failed query, the message begins Failed query: select "encrypted_value", "revoked_at" from "credentials" …. The column names this very function reads happen to stuff the substring "revoked" into every database failure of this read operation. So the old code, which classified by wording, reported Postgres being down, a mistyped address, and a canceled statement all as "an administrator revoked the credential", to people, to the model, and to ops (credentials.ts:196-216).

    The lesson is engraved verbatim in the comment: "A class cannot be produced by accident that way, and it survives a reworded sentence." A class cannot be produced by accident, and it survives rewording; message text does neither. Never build security semantics on error message text. In OpenBot this rule is not a style preference; it was patched in.

    Rotation refusal reasons obey the same commandment: they pass through reasonWithoutStatement, which strips the statement and every bound value out of the drizzle error, before they may enter the audit payload (credentials.ts:626-648). The insert statement binds the freshly minted ciphertext envelope itself, and the audit table is trigger-enforced append-only: ciphertext must never enter an audit row. This rule came from a real incident where "the comment testified against itself"; Chapter 6 has the full incident report.

    Desktop credentials: defending against an attacker who is never in the room

    The desktop form factor poses a different question for security design: the model's OAuth refresh token must sit on the user's computer, and that same computer runs the local agent processes the user installed, exactly the things that need to use the model but must never touch the real token. OpenBot's answer turns the server into a local proxy: the desktop Rust side writes the credential into a file, sets OPENBOT_MODEL_OAUTH_FILE to point at it, and sets OPENAI_API_KEY to a proxy_token; the server mounts POST /api/model-provider/v1/chat/completions only when it sees that variable (server/src/index.ts:2401-2403). What a local agent receives as its "API key" is a proxy token; the real refresh token never leaves the server process. Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoint accepts API keys, not user OAuth tokens, so the server side also carries a protocol translation layer that preserves the local agents' Chat Completions contract. A Deep Dive later in this chapter covers it (see "Deep Dive: The Google protocol translation layer"); all that matters here is that the proxy endpoint's entire reason to exist is making the real credential unnecessary.

    First, name this section's attacker: not a stranger on the network, but other local processes on the same machine under the same UID. A malicious npm package, a poisoned build script. File permission bits and symlink defenses are designed for exactly this attacker; against root and the kernel they can do nothing, and that is outside the declared defense perimeter. An honest boundary statement follows the same line as Chapter 8's egress proxy: saying who you defend against beats pretending to defend against everyone.

    The attack surface then shrinks to one question: how many checks must this file, and the person presenting the token, each pass before either deserves belief?

    ts
      const handle = await open(file, constants.O_RDONLY | constants.O_NOFOLLOW);
  try {
    const info = await handle.stat({ bigint: true });
    if (before && (before.dev !== info.dev || before.ino !== info.ino))
      throw new Error("The private model credential path changed while opening.");
    if (
      !info.isFile() ||
      info.size > 64n * 1024n ||
      (process.platform !== "win32" && (info.mode & 0o077n) !== 0n)
    )
      throw new Error("The private model credential file is not valid.");

    — server/src/provider-oauth.ts:74-84. O_NOFOLLOW refuses symlinks. Windows ignores the flag, so an lstat records dev/ino first, and after the open the handle's stat is compared a second time; a swap between check and open gets caught by this second look. It is the textbook TOCTOU double-check. Size and permission bits are compared as bigints (64n * 1024n, 0o077n), because in stat's bigint mode the precision is not something a Number can safely express.

    This refusal chain is not a unilateral demand from the server side; the desktop writer cooperates to the same specification (desktop/src-tauri/src/provider_oauth.rs:548-581): the credential directory refuses symlinks and gets mode 0700, and since Windows has no chmod semantics, a PowerShell call gives the directory an owner-only inherited DACL. The read chain dares to refuse this hard because the write chain first lays the file down in a shape that passes inspection. A specification written once on each side would of course drift, so the spec facts (64KB, 0600, regular file) name each other in the comments on both sides.

    The check on the person is an independent local bearer: the caller presents the proxyToken from the file, and comparison goes through sameToken (server/src/agents/callback-token.ts:68-73). Lengths first, then timingSafeEqual; unequal length counts as malformed input, not "almost guessed right", and returns false directly. This function is the repository's only token-comparison primitive; host-access and the agent profile store both reuse it. A constant-time comparison primitive can exist exactly once per repository; two copies would drift.

    The path upstream is nailed down the same way: token and chat endpoints are a hardcoded table of literals, and every upstream fetch carries redirect: "error". A redirect is a failure; SSRF gets no detour. A 401 triggers exactly one refresh retry; a failed refresh records a desktop connection failure signal and answers 401. The refresh defenses are equally thorough: a token counts as expired 120 seconds early, leaving slack for slow requests; when the upstream returns no new refresh_token, the old one stays in use; a token_type other than bearer is refused outright.

    The "desktop connection failure signal" deserves an expansion, because it is this link's only output to the operations surface. desktop-connection-failure.ts compresses failures into three session-scoped signals, authentication failures for model, intelligence, and organization, one stored per kind, and "Never retains provider messages or credentials" (desktop-connection-failure.ts:6-27). The desktop shell polls it via GET /api/desktop/connection-failure: comparing x-openbot-desktop-host-token uses the same two steps, length first then timingSafeEqual, inlined into the route here; responses always carry Cache-Control: no-store; and when the host token is not configured, the route is not mounted at all (desktop-connection-failure.ts:30-43; the mount point is app.ts:452). An absent configuration maps to an absent endpoint, not to an endpoint that 401s forever. Signal creation and clearing both hang on real traffic: observeModelConnection listens to the AG-UI event stream, records a failure on RUN_ERROR/OPENBOT_MODEL_AUTH_REQUIRED, and clears on TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT or TOOL_CALL_START, the model producing work again (desktop-connection-failure.ts:65-95). The judgment is deliberately narrow: only the SDK's AI_APICallError with a 401 and our own error classes count, because "a harness HTTP 401 is a different credential". The signal heals itself with traffic; nobody ever has to click "mark read".

    Rotation: disk first, use second

    After a successful refresh, the persistence order of the new credential is the most fastidious passage in the whole endpoint: write file.<uuid>.tmp (0600, wx exclusive create) → sync() → atomic rename replacement, with the temp file deleted in a finally (provider-oauth.ts:106-127). Before writing, the file is read one more time and both sessionId and refreshToken are compared. A changed sessionId means the user has signed in again; answer SignInRequired directly. A changed accessToken means a concurrent request already rotated; use the new one. The principle in one line: "Do not use a rotated pair until it is durable; a failed save requires sign-in again" (provider-oauth.ts:201). Better to make a person sign in again than to spend a token pair that never reached disk. Spending it means the old refresh token is void while the new one exists only in the memory of a process that just got killed.

    Concurrency control has two layers: an in-process Map<sessionId, Promise> deduplicates so one session refreshes once; across processes, the file lock from the next section takes over. Inside the lock there is another re-read: by the time you hold the lock, the world may already belong to another session.

    The cross-process lock: flock, and a graceful exit on Windows

    Several processes on the same machine may refresh the same credential, and the in-process Map cannot govern them, so a cross-process lock is needed (server/src/provider-oauth-lock.ts). The lock's shape is a ${file}.lock directory next to the credential file (mkdir 0700) with an owner.lock file inside. On Unix, bun:ffi dlopens libSystem.B.dylib (macOS) or libc.so.6 (Linux) directly to call flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB), with a 5-second deadline, 25-millisecond backoff, and every error other than EWOULDBLOCK failing outright. The lock file's number-one rule is written at the top of the file:

    Both writers keep this directory and inode permanently. Never remove a held lock: another opener could then lock a different inode.

    — provider-oauth-lock.ts:7-8. Delete a held lock file and the next opener locks a different inode; two "locks" then hold at once. So the lock file is never deleted and the lock directory is 0700. A pre-existing legacy 0755 directory is tolerated (only the owner can change entries inside it), but the lock file itself must be 0600. Lenient with history, strict with new writes; the two do not contradict.

    The Windows side of the story is more instructive still. Bun 1.3 has no FFI for Windows ARM64, so instead it spawns powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive running an embedded C# snippet (CreateFileW with share=0 for an exclusive open). stdout prints the locked handshake, and stdin EOF releases the lock: "EOF on this pipe also releases it when the Bun parent dies". The parent crashes, the pipe breaks, the lock releases itself: the correct default for crash safety, with no watchdog needed. The path reaches the child process through an environment variable, and the comment names it: "The path is environment data, never interpolated code." Every failure is wrapped uniformly as CredentialLockUnavailable, and the endpoint answers 503 "credential store is busy". When the lock cannot be taken, say it is unavailable, plainly, rather than running naked.

    Admission to the lock directory itself follows the same paranoia: an existing directory must pass lstat: it must be a directory, not a symlink, with no group/other write bits (provider-oauth-lock.ts:20-28). The Windows exclusive open comes with a GetFileInformationByHandleEx check, confirming what is in hand is neither a reparse point nor a directory. Releasing the lock is likewise an explicit act: close stdin, wait for the child to exit, and a non-zero exit code throws "Could not release credential lock." (provider-oauth-lock.ts:171-175). "Failed to release" must be seen just like "failed to acquire". A lock whose release fails silently is more dangerous than no lock, because it gives the next comer a false sense of safety.

    Deep Dive: The Google protocol translation layer

    The translation layer mentioned at the start of this section deserves a closer look. It sits on the credential path, so every side of it is written as boundary code, not compatibility glue. Its reason to exist is two sentences, in the file header: "Google's OpenAI endpoint accepts API keys, not the desktop's user OAuth token. Keep the local agents' Chat Completions contract while using the native API." (google-oauth-transport.ts:4-5). Local agents speak Chat Completions; Google's native API speaks the Gemini shape. This file translates both ways, and it makes "translation" an act of narrowing:

    • A strict zod whitelist at the entrance. The request body recognizes only five roles (system/developer/user/assistant/tool) and the specified tools/tool_choice/stream parameters; extra fields never reach the upstream. The model name must pass a regex, because it gets interpolated into the Google-side URL (google-oauth-transport.ts:6-60). The narrower the translation layer's input surface, the less room the proxy endpoint has to be abused as an open proxy.
    • The upstream address is assembled, never received. Google's chat URL is built from the regex-passed model name interpolated into a literal template, https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/<model>:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse (streaming) or generateContent (non-streaming, google-oauth-transport.ts:230-238); the token endpoint is likewise a hardcoded literal table (provider-oauth.ts:53-61). Addresses always come from the code, never from the request. SSRF has no raw material at this layer.
    • Images in exactly two forms. data:image/*;base64 (shape-checked by regex) or an https URL; every other scheme throws (google-oauth-transport.ts:106-133). This is the same gesture as the mime whitelist for user content earlier in this chapter, this time guarding the outbound side.
    • thoughtSignature travels in the tool call id, never in model text. Gemini 3's thought signatures must ride back with function calls; this file copies the compatibility trick maintained by LiteLLM, splicing the opaque signature into the tool call id with the separator __thought__. The comment gives the upstream link and pins the discipline: "only the opaque signature travels in the ID, never model text or tool arguments" (google-oauth-transport.ts:135-137). The signature is protocol litter, not content; the content channel should not make way for protocol litter. For the same reason, function call ids are returned only for the gemini-3 family (google-oauth-transport.ts:164-166): older models do not know the field, and giving it to them is noise.
    • The SSE translator fails explicitly on any line it does not recognize. The hand-written TransformStream frames by line: data: goes into a buffer, an empty line triggers assembly, event:/id:/retry:/comment lines pass through, and any other line calls fail() directly, sending the client an incomplete_model_stream error frame. Residual buffer at flush, or a whole stream with no finishReason, also fails (google-oauth-transport.ts:360-455). An explicit error beats a silent truncation: a truncated stream looks to the client like "the model finished" when it has not; an explicit error frame at least gives the failure a name.
    • cache-control: no-store on every exit. The streaming and non-streaming paths share one headers object (google-oauth-transport.ts:315-324). This is a credential channel: no response leaving it should ever be cached.

    The body of the two-way translation rules compresses into one table (google-oauth-transport.ts:140-277):

    Chat Completions side Gemini side
    system / developer messages (text only) merged into systemInstruction
    user text and images text / inlineData / fileData (https only) in contents
    assistant tool_calls functionCall; id returned only for the gemini-3 family, thought signature appended to the id
    tool result messages functionResponse; text that parses as JSON becomes an object, images must be inline
    consecutive same-role messages merged into the parts of one content
    temperature / top_p / max_tokens / stop synonymous generationConfig fields
    response_format (json_object / json_schema) responseMimeType + responseJsonSchema
    tool_choice (auto/none/required/named) functionCallingConfig AUTO / NONE / ANY (named carries allowedFunctionNames)

    The return trip is field by field too (google-oauth-transport.ts:278-310): MAX_TOKENS becomes length, abnormal finishes other than STOP become content_filter, normal finishes with tool calls become tool_calls. usageMetadata folds back into OpenAI's usage shape, with thinking tokens broken out into completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens. The table's meaning is not the field-by-field correspondence; it is the completeness discipline. Every field either has an explicit counterpart or never gets through the door. The translation layer is not a "close enough" format converter; it is part of the contract.

    The translation layer does not change the proxy endpoint's threat model: it takes the same proxyToken, walks the same refusal chain, and simply speaks one more dialect. Keeping it on the server side, written as boundary code, leaves the local agents' Chat Completions contract intact. It is one instance of "the contract holds; dialects translate themselves".

    Two shaping passes before egress: user content and telemetry

    The last two boundaries are not about keys or files; they are about the shape of data leaving the trust domain.

    The first is user attachments going into the model. An image part's source.value gets assembled into a data: URL and sent straight to the model provider, so shared/user-content.ts whitelist-shapes it before the protocol payload forms:

    ts
        if (
      item.type === "image" &&
      source?.type === "data" &&
      typeof source.value === "string" &&
      source.value.trim() &&
      /^[A-Za-z0-9+/]*={0,2}$/.test(source.value.replace(/\s/g, "")) &&
      typeof source.mimeType === "string" &&
      ["image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/gif", "image/webp"].includes(
        source.mimeType.trim().toLowerCase(),
      )
    ) {

    — shared/user-content.ts:39-49. The mime whitelist has four bitmap formats, compared after trimming and lowercasing; the base64 shape gets whitespace stripped before the regex test. text/html, smuggled whitespace and quotes, empty values: none of them pass. But what fails is not discarded; it is named, degraded to a placeholder text like [image]. The file header gives the reason (user-content.ts:15-18): a model told [audio] can say "there is an attachment I cannot hear", while a model that received nothing answers as if nobody pasted anything. The first is honest degradation; the second breeds hallucination. The same rule recurs in the resultText of MCP tool results, and both Bot harnesses share this one declaration, "the two cannot drift". This is input-channel hygiene, not injection detection. What it guarantees: an untrusted attachment cannot become protocol payload sent to the provider in an arbitrary mime and encoding.

    The companion regression test writes the threat model verbatim into a comment (user-content-hardening.test.ts:7-10): the mime would be spliced into the data: URL sent to the model provider without a whitelist, the value would go on the road without a shape check. text/html, smuggled whitespace, and empty values now degrade to named placeholders instead of provider payload. The test's naming and comments pin down "why this regex exists"; the next person who wants to loosen the whitelist hits this threat model first.

    The second is telemetry egress. The command field in an audit row is the action itself and must stay inside the deployment in full. But the copy sent to the SIEM over OTEL cannot carry the credentials typed into commands, so before export, every command key at any depth of the payload goes through scrubCommand (server/src/telemetry/otel.ts:82-99): a gitleaks-style family of regexes. Well-known token prefixes (AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe…), credential-by-parameter-name, URL userinfo; a hit becomes [REDACTED]. Every outbound record also carries an openbot.surface classification (bot/identity/control_plane), and events whose names contain refused, failed, or revoked are all raised to WARN, so the SIEM side can read the bad news first without learning OpenBot's vocabulary.

    The tap point itself has discipline: addAuditTap fires only after the insert succeeds, so "nothing is streamed that the trail does not hold". A tap that throws only gets logged: "streaming a row must never fail writing it". With no OTEL environment variables configured, nothing loads at all; OPENBOT_OTEL_EXPORT=off is the explicit off switch. The scrubbing philosophy is one sentence: "Deliberately over-eager. A redacted word that was not a secret costs a reader a guess; a secret that survived costs a rotation" (telemetry/scrub.ts:10-11). A false positive costs a reader a guess; a survivor costs the whole company a key rotation. The asymmetry leaves nothing to discuss.

    Two hand-written special cases in the rule family deserve naming: mysql's -psecret and the various forms of curl's -u user:password. The username is kept; only the password is scrubbed (scrub.ts:71-76). The same scrub has two consumers: the OTEL export and the admin-side Action Recording (admin/controls.ts:303, 767). Two egress paths share one scrubbing rule, the same principle as sameToken: a security primitive exists exactly once per repository; two copies would drift.

    The exporter itself times out at 10 seconds, every emit is wrapped in a try/catch that only logs, and the header comment nails the priority down: "Never fatal. An unreachable collector drops records after the SDK's own retries, and the audit row in PostgreSQL is still the record of truth." (otel.ts:19-21, 159, 195-203). Telemetry may die; the audit row may not.

    Desktop telemetry runs in the opposite direction: an enumeration whitelist. platform/arch/engine accept only fixed enum values, and version strings must be ≤32 characters of pure dot-separated digits (server/src/desktop-telemetry.ts). The desktop-side documentation writes the refusal list as a promise: no prompts, no answers, no credentials, no filenames, no paths, no hostnames, no emails. The install identity is a random UUID, never derived from the machine. Opting out clears the queued state and the identity, with zero HTTP sent. Environment variables are untrusted input: schema first, then transmit.

    The server side's handling of this metadata is equally restrained: it invents no events, only merging the desktop shell's closed set of properties into the runtime's existing telemetry events. The comment states it plainly, "Adds no events of its own" (copilot.ts:1788-1793), and the merge also lets each event be told apart from other deployments' traffic. Disabling goes through two variables: COPILOTKIT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true or DO_NOT_TRACK=1; either one stops it. Telemetry restraint is two-way: the desktop does not offer, and the server does not add.

    Deep Dive: The trailing-space incident

    config.ts contains a three-line function, isProduction, and the reason it exists is a real incident (config.ts:424-443). Two security gates both need to answer "is this production": the placeholder encryption key check and the private-network browsing check. One read NODE_ENV through optional() (compared after a trim); the other compared the raw value directly. NODE_ENV=production with a trailing space is invisible in an env file, and Docker's env_file and every vendor console's text box preserve it as-is. So it tripped one gate and slipped past the other, and the one it slipped past happened to be the one deciding whether the credential vault may be encrypted with the key printed in a public repository (the gist of config.ts:431-435).

    The fix was not to add a trim at the second site; it was to fold the question into one helper: "so the next gate that needs this question cannot pick the wrong way to ask it." There must be exactly one way to parse a security judgment. A second optional() call site is itself new attack surface, because whoever writes it may forget the trim again. Every gate in Chapter 2's refusal list goes through this one function; Chapter 2's reachOf() three-way address classification works the same way, one copy in the entire codebase. The case's value is not the space; it is the discipline it demonstrates: the moment a security judgment appears twice, drift has begun. Token comparison, domain normalization, production detection: every security primitive should be greppable in the repository exactly once.

    Every mechanism in this chapter connects back to the book's thesis. Two keys, the envelope format, the partial unique index, the lock file: the boundary lives in the deployment, in the physical location of keys, in database constraints, in filesystem permission bits. It does not live in any model behavior. The three-sided SSO patch is another reading of governance riding the protocol: the patch rides seams the library itself defines, the middleware chain, the adapter factory, the schema constraint, so it survives library upgrades. What OpenBot did not build argues the same case: no fork of Better Auth, no unified "super key", no general-purpose encryption wrapper, no second home-grown token comparison. The maturity of security engineering shows in what was held back, not in what was built.

    The restraint list has one more entry that belongs to honesty rather than omission: the channels.allowed_groups field is declared in the tenant package and stored in the database, but it is not part of any authorization decision. No login path populates users.groups, so group-based rules have no input to evaluate. The documentation positions it as "a declaration waiting on group membership from the identity provider, not as a control that is running" (docs/architecture.md:174-177). A control that does not exist in the data is honestly marked as unwired, instead of sitting in the config schema pretending to enforce. This is Chapter 8's "honest boundary statement" applied to the authorization layer.

    Apply This

    If you build any system where secrets land in storage, an agent platform, CI, internal developer tooling, these five patterns transfer directly.

    Split keys by format ownership. The problem: one master key encrypts everything, so any party changing format, library, or lifecycle holds all the rest hostage. To adapt it: inventory your encryption-at-rest objects and group them by "who owns the read/write format of this data". Data with your own invented envelope goes to your own key; data in a third-party library's internal storage goes to the library's own mechanism; sub-purposes derive one-way with HKDF or labeled HMAC. The pitfall: hand-rolling encryption inside somebody else's storage layer. You cannot intercept all its write paths, and one format change in a library upgrade yields permanently unreadable rows. Also verify whether the library's mechanism tolerates existing plaintext; if it does not, the day you switch it on is the day everyone gets signed out.

    Patch at seams, not in a fork. The problem: a dependency's wrong domain model (ownership, permission, serialization) directly damages your security posture, but forking it means never merging upstream again. To adapt it: first find the single choke point the library itself defines, an adapter factory, a middleware chain, a serialization hook, and lay the patch there. The wrapper intercepts only the methods and fields you name; everything else passes through, including capabilities you do not know about. Declare types as the smallest structure you actually use; do not import the library's full types. The pitfall: writing the wrapper "general-purpose", which makes it a second, worse adapter. And when the patch has more than one face, resist merging them into one layer for speed: three independent faces each survive library upgrades on their own and each test on their own.

    Express security semantics as types, never as message text. The problem: distinguishing "credential revoked" from "database failure" by error.message.includes(...), when the dependency's error messages happen to contain your keyword. To adapt it: one error class (or error code) per failure kind that needs different handling; callers branch on instanceof. Message text is for humans to read and never enters control flow. The pitfall: assuming "our identifiers will never appear in the library's messages". drizzle puts the whole statement and all bound values into the message, including your column and table names. And when a dependency upgrade rewords the message, your classifier silently flips, usually toward the unsafe direction.

    Disk first, use second. The problem: rotation-style operations (credentials, tokens, configuration) have a window between "in effect" and "persisted" where the process can be killed, and a new secret spent inside that window dies with the process. To adapt it: write a temp file (wx exclusive, 0600) → sync() → atomic rename; the consumer re-reads and re-verifies the file before use; cross-process coordination uses mechanisms with "parent death releases" semantics (flock, stdin EOF), and lock files are never deleted, to prevent inode races. The pitfall: renaming without sync() first (after a crash you have a directory entry and no contents), and deleting a lock file "for tidiness". What you deleted is a lock someone else is holding.

    Name it, don't drop it. The problem: input shaping silently drops content that cannot be carried, so the model hallucinates that nothing was sent, or worse, the attachment was actually blocked while the answer pretends to have seen it. To adapt it: after whitelist filtering, replace what failed with a named placeholder ([image], [audio]) in the context, so the model can say "there is an attachment I cannot process". The placeholder is a text protocol between sender and renderer, with exactly one declaration on each side. The pitfall: filtering after the protocol payload has formed. Once the data: URL is assembled it is too late; the whitelist belongs before assembly. And placeholder wording that is vague: the model must be able to read "this is a degraded attachment" from it.

    The next chapter steps outside the core product: the desktop shell, mobile, and voice. How the two keys get packed into an installer, and how the boundary reaches the user's hands.
